**The entry directly above got this wrong twice, inside the paragraph whose entire subject is that the exact line matters, and that is worth more here than either mistake.** It asserts that running the script in full form *"IS A DIFFERENCE FROM EVERY EARLIER ENTRY IN THIS FILE RATHER THAN A DETAIL"* and that *"Every previous entry that runs this script quotes the other closing line."* One command refutes both: at `217cb7a`, `git grep -c 'all configs green' 217cb7a -- docs/superpowers/plans/2026-07-19-redextape-roadmap.md` reads **2**, not 1. The *"PLAN 5d-i CLOSES"* entry of 2026-08-11 — **31 `####` entries earlier in the same file** — already recorded `scripts/check-all.sh` **all configs green — base, LLVM and browser** in its own verification block. The same command for `green, but PARTIAL` reads **15**, so the partial line really is the norm; what was not checked was the universal. **And the quotation is not a quotation:** that entry renders the line as `all configs green -- base, LLVM and browser`, two ASCII hyphens where line 667 emits an em dash. **This is the identical defect that entry's own CI paragraph confesses to** — its first draft claimed *"every previous slice added its CI paragraph on the branch once the first run went green"* and measurement *"refutes twice over"* — so one entry made two unchecked universal claims about the file it was being appended to, caught one by measuring it, and shipped the other in a paragraph two screens above. This file's own rule covers it exactly: **write the value, never the relationship.** *"Every earlier entry"* is not an observation, it is a `grep` nobody ran.

**No CI paragraph appears here, and this time the reason is stated as a property rather than as a fact about the present moment.** At `217cb7a`, `grep -c '^#### '` reads 74 entries in this file and `grep -c 'Run [0-9]\+ '` reads 6, so a CI paragraph is the exception here rather than the rule. The entry directly above records what happened the last time one of these entries asserted the state of a run at the time of writing: *"no pull request exists at the time of writing and no run has happened"* — true when written, false within the hour. A sentence whose truth depends on when it is read does not belong in an append-only log, so none is written.

#### THE NULLABILITY OVERRIDE CLASS GETS A GATE IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, THE ANCHOR THE SPEC PRESCRIBED HAD A HOLE AT EACH END AND THE PLAN FOUND BOTH BY MEASURING IT RATHER THAN READING IT, A COUNT THIS BRANCH WROTE WAS FALSIFIED BY THE PARAGRAPH THAT REPORTED IT, AND THREE WHOLE-BRANCH REVIEWS COMPILED FOUR ORDINARY SPELLINGS THE FINISHED GATE PASSED IN SILENCE — EACH PAIR SITTING IN THE FIX FOR THE ONE BEFORE — UNTIL THE RULE STOPPED SCANNING RUST AND STARTED PARSING IT (2026-09-03, branch `nullability-override-gate`, `13f9ad3..eef2c26`, 16 commits, plus the entry commits)

Design: [`../specs/2026-09-03-nullability-override-gate-design.md`](../specs/2026-09-03-nullability-override-gate-design.md). Plan: [`2026-09-03-nullability-override-gate.md`](2026-09-03-nullability-override-gate.md).

Opened by PR #71's own WHAT STAYS OPEN list — its third bullet, the class that entry says the wire-type slice opened rather than closed. `ts(type = "...")` substitutes the WHOLE field type, `Option` and all, so an override on an `Option<u64>` generates `number` and drops the `| null` that `None` puts on the wire while both Rust gates stay green. Two checks land, at two different links in the chain. `assert_overrides_match_field_nullability` in `redextape-test-support::ts_derive_scan` refuses the disagreement at the DERIVE SITE, in both directions — an `Option` field whose override does not admit null, and a bare field whose override invents one — and both crates' `tests/ts_bindings.rs` call the one implementation, taking each gate binary from 2 tests to 3. `web/tests/node/bindings-contract.test.ts` pins the eleven nullable sites against the GENERATED file, which `pnpm run typecheck` builds before `tsc` runs. Neither substitutes for the other and the entry below says where each is blind.

##### THE ANCHOR THE SPEC PRESCRIBED HAD A HOLE AT EACH END, AND THE PLAN FOUND BOTH BY RUNNING THE GREP THE SPEC HAD ONLY DESCRIBED

The design said to anchor on lines whose trimmed form starts with `#[` and contain the bytes `ts(`. Writing the plan meant measuring that anchor, and it is wrong in opposite directions at once. **A `#[` prefix skips an override split across two lines** — `#[cfg_attr(feature = "ts",` on one and `    ts(type = "number"))]` on the next — which compiles, and whose second line begins with `ts(` rather than `#[`. That is a silent skip, the one outcome a gate cannot afford, and it is the shape the scanner module's own history is made of. **And the bytes alone are unusable in the other direction**: `ts(` is the tail of every identifier ending in `ts` followed by an open paren, so `sweep_targets(`, `list_of_nats(`, `simulate_counts(` and `reduce_trace_shares_its_snapshots(` all match. The anchor that ships is the byte pattern with a word boundary before the `t`, minus comment lines, minus the caller's own gate file, minus the canonical derive line — a narrowing the design's §1 now tabulates with a command per row. **`\b` is not available without a regex dependency this crate does not have**; the check is a comparison against the preceding byte.

**The comment exclusion is not tidiness and the tree proves it.** `redextape-wasm`'s `TmStatus::total_steps` carries a doc comment quoting `ts(type = "number")` — the wrong form — four times, directly above the field, in order to explain why it is wrong. An anchor that read comment lines would fail on the prose written to prevent this exact bug.

**The class this belongs to is the one PR #71 named and paid for.** That branch shipped *"That script needs no change"* as prose asserting a mechanism nobody had measured, and it hid a path that destroyed the bindings at exit 0. This branch's design shipped an anchor as prose asserting a mechanism nobody had measured. The difference is only that this one was measured one step earlier — at plan time rather than at review time — and the reason it was measured at all is that the design's §1 demanded a command per figure, so writing the plan meant running greps that the anchor then failed.

##### RESOLUTION IS FORWARD, AND THE CLEAN TREE IS THE TEST THAT SAYS SO

`redextape-core`'s `viewmodel.rs` declares `pub cut: Option<Cut>,` then the override, then `pub step: u64,`. A scan resolving backward, or taking the nearest field line in either direction, reads `Option<Cut>` for an override belonging to a bare `u64` and demands a `| null` that must not be there — so it fails on the UNMODIFIED tree, before any sabotage is applied. Both gates reporting `3 tests run: 3 passed` on a clean tree is therefore a measurement rather than a formality, and it is recorded before the sabotages rather than after.

##### SIXTEEN SABOTAGES AT THE DERIVE SITE, TWO AT THE TYPESCRIPT END, AND THE TWO THAT DID NOT DO WHAT THE PLAN PREDICTED

Each applied, measured, reverted, and **every one of them re-run against the fixed rule after the review round below** rather than assumed to have survived a change to the resolver — the rule this file already carries, and the one PR #71 followed when it moved this module's sibling scanner. Sabotages 8 through 13 are the reviews' silent passes and the third's `optional` finding promoted into the real tree, each confirmed to COMPILE before its result was read — a sabotage that does not build has measured nothing; the plan wrote seven. **All thirteen were then re-run a final time against the `syn` rewrite below**, which replaced the mechanism every one of them had been measured against. Under sabotages 1 to 6, 8 and 9 the two PRE-EXISTING tests in the failing binary reported passing every time, which is the argument of this slice measured rather than asserted.

1. `ts(type = "number")` on `TmStatus::total_steps` — the defect PR #71 measured. `redextape-wasm`'s gate reports `3 tests run: 2 passed, 1 failed`, naming the file, line 272, `total_steps: Option<u64>`, and both accepted forms. `redextape-core`'s gate stays at `3 passed`.
2. `ts(type = "number | null")` on `TmState::step`, a bare `u64`. `redextape-core`'s gate reports `2 passed, 1 failed` with the reverse remedy. `redextape-wasm`'s stays at `3 passed`.
3. `ts(as = "u32")` on `TmStatus::total_steps`. Fires — and its output is what found the defect two sections below.
4. `ts(type="number")`, no spaces. Fires as a RULE violation rather than as an unparseable line: the parse tolerates whitespace around `=`, because `cargo fmt` normalises it and a gate treating formatting as an unrecognized spelling would be noise.
5. The same wrong override split across two lines. `cargo check -p redextape-wasm --features ts` exits 0 — it really compiles — and the gate fires at line 273, the continuation line. This is the case a `#[`-prefix anchor passes in silence.
6. `ts(type = r#"number"#)`. **The plan left this between two acceptable outcomes rather than predicting one**, and the outcome is: the crate COMPILES, and the gate refuses it with `cannot parse`, naming the file and line. A silent pass was the only result that would have failed this sabotage.
7. `#[cfg_attr(feature = "ts", ts(rename = "renamedStep"))]` added above `TmState::step`. `redextape-core`'s gate stays at `3 tests run: 3 passed` — a key that is neither `type` nor `as` makes no nullability claim, and firing on it would be a false positive rather than a caught defect.
8. `#[cfg_attr(feature = "ts", ts(rename = "totalSteps"), ts(type = "number"))]` on `TmStatus::total_steps` — TWO `ts(...)` groups on one line. `cargo check -p redextape-wasm --features ts` reports no errors, so it is ordinary Rust, and the gate as shipped to review **went green on it**. Now `2 passed, 1 failed`.
9. `pub total_steps: std::option::Option<u64>` carrying `ts(type = "number")`. Compiles, and **went green on it**. Now `2 passed, 1 failed`.
10. The anchor sitting inside an attribute opened two lines above it — `#[cfg_attr(` / `feature = "ts",` / `ts(type = "number"),` / `serde(rename = "crate::de::opt")` / `)]`. Compiles, and **the FIX for sabotages 8 and 9 went green on it**. Now `2 passed, 1 failed`, naming `total_steps: Option<u64>` rather than the field name it used to fabricate out of that `::`.
11. `ts(as = "std::option::Option<u32>")` on `TmState::step`, a bare `u64` — an override inventing a null the wire never carries. Compiles, and **also went green on the fix**, because the `as` arm kept its own prefix test. Now `2 passed, 1 failed`.
12. `#[cfg_attr(feature = "ts", ts(optional))]` on `TmStatus::total_steps`. Now `1 passed, 2 failed` — both this rule and `no_generated_type_carries_bigint`, the latter because removing the type override lets the `u64` generate `bigint` again. The overlap is real and worth naming: on this one shape the two gates agree, and on every other shape in this list the older gate is silent.
13. `#[cfg_attr(feature = "ts", ts(optional = nullable))]` on the same field — the CORRECT form of that key, and the control for sabotage 12. This rule passes it; `no_generated_type_carries_bigint` fails, because there is no type override left and the `u64` generates `bigint`. **The gate that fires is named here rather than the count quoted**, because `2 failed` and `1 failed` say nothing about which rule spoke.
14. `#[cfg_attr(feature = "serde", cfg_attr(feature = "ts", ts(type = "number")))]` on `TmStatus::total_steps` — a NESTED `cfg_attr`. Compiles, and the parser-based rule **went green on it** while looking one level in. Now `1 passed, 2 failed`, this rule and the `bigint` gate together.
15. A `pub struct Inner` declared inside `Session::tm_status`'s body, carrying the canonical derive and a field with `ts(type = "number")` on an `Option<u64>`. Compiles. **Both gates fail now — and that is the finding, not the failure.** `the_gate_covers_every_exported_type` fails because the sibling line-based scan resolves forward to that `pub struct` and finds it; before this branch's fourth fix round, `no_override_misstates_a_field_s_nullability` PASSED on the same tree, because it descended into `mod` and not into a function body. Two gates in one binary, disagreeing about whether the same type existed.
16. A `pub(crate) struct HiddenHere` appended to `redextape-wasm`'s own gate file, carrying the canonical derive and a field with `ts(type = "number")` on an `Option<u64>`. **The fifth review ran this and got `4 passed; 0 failed`, with `web/bindings/HiddenHere.ts` really written** — the guard on the whole-file skip matched `pub struct ` and `pub enum ` as line prefixes and a restricted visibility walked through it. At this head the same construction fails two of the four: the sibling coverage gate, and the guard itself.

##### THE THREE-VERSUS-FOUR QUESTION IS SETTLED, AND BOTH FIGURES WERE RIGHT ABOUT DIFFERENT QUANTITIES

PR #71's entry records THREE `TS2322` errors under sabotage 1 at `2df9a58`. A `grep -rn 'total_steps: null' web/tests web/src` at `13f9ad3` returns FOUR sites. The design refused to reconcile them by reasoning and handed the question to a measurement. Sabotage 1 applied at this branch's head, followed by `cd web && pnpm run typecheck`, exits 1 and prints exactly four errors:

```
tests/node/bindings-contract.test.ts(37,11): error TS2322: Type 'null' is not assignable to type 'number'.
tests/node/replies.test.ts(99,59): error TS2322: Type 'null' is not assignable to type 'number'.
tests/node/results.test.ts(111,9): error TS2322: Type 'null' is not assignable to type 'number'.
tests/node/session-client.test.ts(152,67): error TS2322: Type 'null' is not assignable to type 'number'.
```

Three of them are the fixtures PR #71 named — `replies`, `results`, `session-client` — and the fourth is the pin this branch adds. **`web/tests/node/sessions.test.ts` produces no error at all**, which is what closes the gap between the two figures: its `total_steps: null` sits in an `as const` object literal that is never checked against `TmStatus`, so it is an assignment site and was never a check. Neither figure was stale; a grep for assignments and a count of type errors are different quantities, and the difference is one line that looks like a check and is not.

**The pin is named among those four, which is the property that matters** — a pin resolving to a stale or widened type would have passed vacuously. And with the pin's own `total_steps` constant deleted and the sabotage still applied, `pnpm run typecheck` still exits 1 on the remaining three fixtures: no single line in the pin is load-bearing.

##### THE GATE'S OWN PANIC EXPLAINED THE WRONG MECHANISM FOR ITS `as` ARM, FOUND BY READING OUTPUT RATHER THAN A DIFF

The panic told every reader that *"`ts(type = ...)` replaces the WHOLE field type, `Option` and all"* — correct for the `type` arm and quietly false for the `as` arm, which routes the field through the named Rust type's own `TS` impl, so it is THAT type's optionality reaching the wire type rather than the field's. Both arms had been tested and both fired; what was wrong was the explanation the failing gate hands to the person who tripped it. **It was found by reading sabotage 3's output, not by reading the diff** — the diff shows an assertion message that is true of the case it was written for. This is the same shape as PR #71's finding that `redextape-core`'s `bigint` gate was handing out the override that branch had just disproved: a failing gate's own words are the instruction the next person follows, and a gate that explains the wrong mechanism teaches the defect while refusing it.

**AND THAT FIX WAS HALF A FIX, WHICH THE WHOLE-BRANCH REVIEW FOUND ONE BINDING BELOW IT.** The panic builds two strings: `mechanism`, which the fix above split on the key, and `remedy`, which it left branching on whether the field is an `Option` alone. So `ts(as = "Option<u32>")` on a bare `u64` printed a correct mechanism followed by *"drop the `| null`"* — naming something the attribute in front of the reader does not contain, when what has to go is the `Option<...>` wrapper. The commit fixing the first string is what makes this worth recording: **the class was identified, named in its own commit subject, and then closed at exactly one of its two sites**, with the second sitting four lines below it in the same function. The remedy now has four arms rather than two. This file already carries the rule — fix the class, not the instance — and this is what missing it looks like from the inside.

##### A COUNT THIS BRANCH WROTE WAS FALSIFIED BY THE PARAGRAPH THAT REPORTED IT

`assert_overrides_match_field_nullability`'s doc comment quoted the anchor's narrowing as it was measured at `13f9ad3`: 184 occurrences of `ts(`, 41 with a word boundary, 27 after comment lines, 21 after the gate files, 4 after the canonical derive line. At `cff309c` the same commands read **186 and 43** for the first two rows. Nothing regressed — the two extra lines are the doc comments THIS branch added to the two gate files, each of which mentions `ts(` while explaining the rule. **The paragraph reporting the count was one of the things changing it.** The counts now live in the design's §1 table, where every row names its command and the table is dated to the commit it was measured at; what stays in the doc comment is the shape, which nothing this branch did can move: identifier tails are the largest class, comments the second, and what survives both exclusions plus the canonical derive line is the set of real override sites. The last three rows are unchanged at 27, 21 and 4, because the added lines are comments and the comment exclusion is where they leave.

##### THE WHOLE-BRANCH REVIEW COMPILED TWO ORDINARY SPELLINGS THE FINISHED GATE PASSED IN SILENCE, AND ITS METHOD IS WHY IT FOUND THEM

Every sabotage the plan wrote had fired, both gates were green, and the full local gate had run twice. The whole-branch review did not read the diff and agree: it **appended probe fixtures to the rule's own test module, ran them, and reverted**. Two of five went green on the defect this gate exists to refuse — the outcome the function's own doc calls unaffordable, three paragraphs above the code that produced it.

**`#[cfg_attr(feature = "ts", ts(rename = "totalSteps"), ts(type = "number"))]`.** Two `ts(...)` groups on one line, which is ordinary Rust and which `cargo check` accepts. The anchor returned the FIRST offset, the parser read `rename` and stopped at that group's closing paren, no `type` or `as` key was found, and the scan moved on to the next LINE — leaving the override in the second group unread, on the very field this rule was built for. Nothing panicked. The anchor now returns every group on a line.

**`pub total_steps: std::option::Option<u64>`.** The `Option` test was `field_type.starts_with("Option<")`, so a qualified path read as not-an-`Option`, and `ts(type = "number")` then agreed with a rule that had already decided the field could not be null. **This is the same prefix-versus-spelling shape the sibling scanner in this very module spends four paragraphs describing as what defeated each of its own earlier revisions** — the lesson was written down, in the file, immediately above the code that repeated it. Option-ness is now the last segment of the type's path, which closes every qualified spelling at once rather than the ones somebody has thought of; a `type` alias for an `Option` is named as a boundary and pinned by a test rather than left to be discovered by being bitten.

**Two false REDS on correct source came with them, and they are the same class read from the other side.** A trailing comma inside the attribute, and an attribute spread over several lines. The branch had taught the ANCHOR to read a split attribute — sabotage 5 exists for exactly that — and left the RESOLVER unable to cross one, so `#[cfg_attr(` / `feature = "ts",` / `ts(type = "number | null")` / `)]` panicked on valid code, as did a multi-line `#[serde(` between the override and its field. The resolver now tracks bracket depth, counted outside string literals so that a bracket inside `ts(type = "Array<[Span, TokenClass]>")` cannot push it past the field it is looking for.

**And a whole-file skip was sitting underneath a claim that this function never skips.** The doc credited the comment exclusion with saving the callers' assertion strings. It does not: those are `panic!` string continuations rather than comments, they anchor, and the parser then dies on their escaped quotes. What saves them is `scanner_path`, the whole-file exclusion both walks perform — and the new walk had shipped it **without the guard its sibling carries**, the assertion that the excluded file declares no `pub struct`/`pub enum` for a derive or an override to attach to. That guard is now one function called from both walks rather than a property of one of them, and the doc says which exclusion does what.

**The measurement ran both ways.** The review re-ran every figure in the VERIFICATION block below and every row of the design's §1 table, at the commits they are dated to, and found them correct; it sabotaged `web/bindings/RuleView.ts` to confirm the TypeScript pin fires, including on the `Vec<Option<Symbol>>` case the derive-site rule explicitly cannot see. Its own measurement is also what refuted a sentence this branch had written into `lib.rs`: deleting `#![cfg_attr(test, allow(clippy::pedantic))]` and running `cargo clippy -p redextape-test-support --all-targets` emits zero warnings, because the module below already allows that lint. *"The attribute now does real work"* was false, and it had replaced a sentence that was accurate.

**THE ENTRY ABOVE THIS SECTION WAS WRITTEN AND COMMITTED BEFORE THE REVIEW RAN, AND THAT ORDERING IS THE THING HERE MOST WORTH CARRYING FORWARD.** At `93e6d3f` this file held a finished record of a finished branch — `all configs green — base, LLVM and browser` behind it, nine tests green, three of its own defects already found and written up — describing a gate that an attribute with one extra key group walked straight past. A branch summary written before its whole-branch review is a report on work that nothing has yet tried adversarially, and it reads exactly like a report on work that has.

##### THE SECOND WHOLE-BRANCH REVIEW FOUND TWO MORE SILENT PASSES, AND BOTH OF THEM WERE SITTING IN THE FIX FOR THE FIRST TWO

The fix round above was substantial — a new anchor, a new resolver, a new `Option` test, a shared guard — so it was reviewed rather than trusted, on the strength of a line this file already carries about a fix round that introduced a Critical. It had. **Both new silent passes are defects in the fix, not defects the fix missed.**

**The depth seeding was half-done.** The first round taught `resolve_field` to cross an attribute that OPENS after the anchor, and left it starting at depth zero — with no way to know the anchor might itself sit inside an attribute opened two lines earlier. Given `#[cfg_attr(` / `feature = "ts",` / `ts(type = "number"),` / `serde(rename = "crate::de::opt")` / `)]`, it took the `serde` continuation for a field declaration, split it on the `::`, and produced a field named `serde(rename = "crate` of type `:de::opt")`. Not an `Option`; the override claiming no null agreed with it; **green**, and the real `Option<u64>` two lines below was never read. The depth is now seeded from a running attribute depth kept by the caller, **and a resolved name that is not an identifier is now a panic** — because the first defence is a heuristic and the second is a property, and it was the absence of the second that turned a resolution error into a silent pass.

**And the `as` arm kept the exact test the same round had just removed from the field side.** `is_option_type` was written in that round precisely because `starts_with("Option<")` had been defeated by `std::option::Option<u64>` — and four lines below it, the `as` arm still read `value.starts_with("Option<")`. `ts(as = "std::option::Option<u32>")` on a bare `u64` walked straight through. **That is the same class recurring for the third time on this branch**, and the third time it was the fix for the second time. The rule this file carries — fix the class, not the instance — turns out to need a mechanical reading: not "fix every site you can think of" but "make there be one site". There is one predicate now, and both sides call it.

**A third key makes a nullability claim and nothing had named it.** `#[ts(optional)]` turns `t: Option<T>` into `t?: T`; only `#[ts(optional = nullable)]` keeps the null. That is not a subtlety — it is `FieldAttr`'s own doc comment in `ts-rs-macros` 10.1.0, which the review read and neither the design nor the plan nor two fix rounds had. A rule about nullability that checks two of the three keys that change it is not a rule about nullability. `skip` and `flatten` are now named as a different defect rather than left to be inferred safe from a short list.

**Two more false reds on correct source, and one of them was worse than a false red.** `ts(type = "null | number")` and `ts(type = "number|null")` both admit null and both were refused — and the design's argument for the exact suffix does not survive being stated plainly: `CANONICAL_TS_DERIVE` is a string THIS REPOSITORY writes, so demanding one spelling costs nothing, while a TypeScript type is a string TYPESCRIPT defines. The check is a top-level union member now. And the comment test — `trimmed.starts_with("//")` — missed an interior block-comment line and a trailing comment after code; the second **anchored and reported a violation against the NEXT field**, naming an override that field does not carry. Comments are blanked once per file now, offsets preserved, rather than tested for at each site.

**The pin's own header claimed something the pin does not do.** It said `pnpm run test` checks the annotations. `web/vite.config.ts` sets no `test.typecheck`, so vitest transpiles them away and every assertion in that file becomes `expect(null).toBeNull()`. Only `tsc` holds the pin — via `pnpm run typecheck` and CI's `web` job. The header says that now, including that sabotaging a binding and running only `pnpm run test` proves nothing about it.

**THE HONEST SUMMARY OF THIS BRANCH IS THAT ITS GATE WAS DEFEATED BY ORDINARY RUST FOUR TIMES, AND THAT EVERY ONE OF THOSE WAS FOUND BY SOMETHING THAT RAN CODE.** Not by reading the diff, not by re-reading the doc, not by the fixtures — which were green throughout, at 15, then 22, then 31. Both reviews built inputs and executed them: the first appended probes to the test module, the second extracted the private functions into a standalone harness. Every defect this branch shipped past its own tests was found the same way, and the two that were found by reading — the design's anchor and the `as`-arm message — were found by reading OUTPUT, not source.

##### THE THIRD REVIEW FOUND THE FOURTH SILENT PASS, AND THE ANSWER WAS TO STOP SCANNING RUST AND PARSE IT

The second fix round was reviewed for the same reason the first was, and it had the same result: a defect in the fix. **`code_only` carried block-comment state across lines and reset string state at every line**, so a `/*` inside a multi-line raw string opened a comment that never closed and blanked the rest of the file — every override after it invisible, nothing panicking. And it did not lex char literals, so `chars[i] == '"'` — which is live at `redextape-core`'s `three_way_oracle.rs` — flipped it into string mode for the rest of the line.

**That is four silent passes, in three rounds, from one cause.** A qualified `std::option::Option`. Two `ts(...)` groups on one line. An anchor inside an already-open attribute. A comment lexer meeting a char literal. Each fix was correct about its instance and each left the mechanism intact, and the mechanism was reading Rust as text.

**THE DECISION THIS MIRRORS IS RECORDED TWENTY LINES ABOVE IT IN THE SAME FILE.** `ts_deriving_type_names_in_crate`'s doc describes four widenings of a different text scan and the decision not to attempt a fifth — *"a blacklist can only ever enumerate the spellings someone has already thought of, and there is always one more"* — and inverts to a whitelist. The same judgement applied here reaches a different answer, and the difference is worth stating because it is not inconsistency: **that scan asks whether a line IS one exact string, a question with no grammar in it. This rule asks what type a field has and which attributes sit on it, which only a parser can answer.** The inversion available here was not a wider scan; it was `syn` — the crate `ts-rs` itself uses to read these same attributes.

**The rewrite deletes the surface rather than patching it.** `code_only`, `bracket_delta`, `anchored_ts_calls`, `parse_ts_keys`, `resolve_field` and the string-matching `Option` test are gone, and with them four of the third review's six findings — not fixed but made unrepresentable. An attribute sharing a line with its field, a `pub(super)` field, a raw string, a char literal, a nested block comment: none of these is a case the new rule handles, because none of them is a case it can see. The two findings that survive as real questions — `optional`'s spelling and the arrow type in a union — are small and are fixed.

**THE SHARPEST FINDING WAS THAT THE `optional` SUPPORT COULD NEVER HAVE WORKED, AND ITS TEST AGREED WITH IT.** `ts-rs` reads that key's argument with `Ident::parse`, so `#[ts(optional = nullable)]` — unquoted — is the only spelling that compiles. The parser demanded a string literal, so it panicked `cannot parse` on every tree that could exist, and **the panic then told the reader to write the spelling that had just panicked**. The fixture claiming to prove the good case passed used `ts(optional = "nullable")`, which `ts-rs` rejects at compile time. The parser and its test agreed with each other about a shape no compiling tree can hold, which is why 31 green fixtures said nothing about it — the same class as this file's entry on a harness that supplied the thing under test.

**Correcting one of those fixtures found a boundary nobody had looked for.** Two tests had put their attribute on an enum VARIANT rather than on the variant's field, and passed — vacuously, because field attributes are what this rule reads. Chasing why turned up `VariantAttr` in `ts-rs-macros`, which carries `type` and `as` of its own: a variant-level override is a real override this rule does not see. It is named in WHAT STAYS OPEN and pinned by a test that asserts the hole, rather than guessed at. **A test that passes for the wrong reason is a bug report about the thing it was testing.**

**WHAT THE PARSER COSTS, PER CRATE, BECAUSE THE FIRST VERSION OF THIS PARAGRAPH SAID "EVERY CONSUMER" AND WAS FALSE.** `syn` joins `redextape-test-support`'s `[dependencies]`; it was already in `Cargo.lock` via `wasm-bindgen-macro-support`, and what is new is this crate depending on it. `redextape-wasm` declares `redextape-test-support` under `[target.'cfg(not(target_arch = "wasm32"))'.dev-dependencies]`, so nothing reaches the graph that matters — `cargo tree -i redextape-test-support --target wasm32-unknown-unknown -p redextape-wasm --edges normal,build,dev` prints `nothing to print`, and `cargo check --target wasm32-unknown-unknown -p redextape-wasm --all-targets` exits 0. **`redextape-core`, `redextape-native` and `redextape-grammar-check` declare it under a plain `[dev-dependencies]`, so `syn` and `quote` ARE in their wasm32 dev graphs.** Those graphs do not build for wasm32 and did not before this slice: `redextape-core`'s manifest records the reason above its `proptest` entry, and `cargo check --target wasm32-unknown-unknown -p redextape-core --all-targets` fails on `wait-timeout` at this head as it did at `main`. What ships is unaffected either way, because `wasm-pack build` compiles no dev-dependencies — which is why the paragraph above runs that command rather than reading a manifest. **The original claim was checked with one query against the one crate where it held**, which is how a sentence about every consumer got written from evidence about one. Panic messages now name the file, the owning type and the field instead of a line number, which this repository's own citation gate would prefer in any case.

##### THE FOURTH REVIEW FOUND TWO MORE, NARROWER, AND ONE OF THEM CAME WITH A WITNESS

The parser closed the class the text scan kept losing to; it did not close every question about where to look. **A nested `cfg_attr` was a silent pass.** `#[cfg_attr(feature = "a", cfg_attr(feature = "ts", ts(type = "number")))]` is ordinary Rust, reaches the derive with both features on, and drops the `| null` exactly as the flat form does — and the scan looked one level inside `cfg_attr` and stopped. It recurses now, to any depth rather than to the one depth somebody had thought of, which is the shape of fix this module's history keeps arriving at. The same path also held a silent `continue` on a `cfg_attr` whose contents would not parse, in a module whose stated rule is that an unreadable attribute is a panic; it panics now.

**AND A TYPE DECLARED INSIDE A FUNCTION BODY WAS NEVER VISITED, WHICH IS THE FIRST DEFECT ON THIS BRANCH TO ARRIVE WITH A WITNESS RATHER THAN ONLY A FIXTURE.** The walk descended into `mod` and not into `fn`. What makes it more than an omission is that **the sibling scan in the same binary DOES find such a type** — it is line-based, and resolves forward from a derive line to the next `pub struct NAME` wherever that sits. So a struct declared inside a function with the canonical derive and a bad override was, at once, listed as covered by `the_gate_covers_every_exported_type` and invisible to `no_override_misstates_a_field_s_nullability`. Sabotage 15 above is that construction in the real tree: it compiles, and at this head both gates fail, where before the fix only one did. **Two gates disagreeing about whether the same type exists is the exact condition each of them was written to make impossible**, and neither could have reported it — it is only visible from outside both.

**A CLAIM THIS BRANCH MADE ABOUT DEPENDENCIES WAS CHECKED AGAINST ONE CRATE AND WRITTEN ABOUT EVERY CRATE.** The justification for the new `syn` dependency said this crate is declared under `[target.'cfg(not(target_arch = "wasm32"))'.dev-dependencies]` *by every consumer that has one*. Only `redextape-wasm` does. `redextape-core`, `redextape-native` and `redextape-grammar-check` use a plain `[dev-dependencies]`, so `syn` and `quote` are in their wasm32 dev graphs — graphs that already did not build for wasm32, as `redextape-core`'s own manifest records above its `proptest` entry, and which `cargo check --target wasm32-unknown-unknown -p redextape-core --all-targets` still fails on `wait-timeout` exactly as it did at `main`. Nothing that ships changed, because `wasm-pack build` compiles no dev-dependencies. **The defect is the reasoning, not the outcome**: one `cargo tree` query was run, against the one crate where the sentence held, and the sentence was then written about all of them. All three copies of it — manifest comment, design §4.1a, and the paragraph above — now say it per crate. This is the same shape as the entry above this one, whose *"every previous entry"* was a `grep` nobody ran.

**AND SIXTY-FIVE LINES OF THE PRE-`syn` DOC COMMENT WERE STILL ATTACHED TO THE FUNCTION.** The rewrite replaced the body and left the old doc block above the new one, with no separator, so rustdoc concatenated two mutually exclusive descriptions onto one item — the dead half still asserting that the anchor is a byte pattern with a word boundary, that the comment exclusion is load-bearing, and naming two functions the same commit had deleted. The design document got an explicit supersede note for exactly this hazard; the function's own doc did not, and the reviewer found the omission by reading what rustdoc would render rather than what the diff showed.

##### THE FIFTH REVIEW WALKED A TYPE THROUGH THE GUARD ON THE WHOLE-FILE SKIP, AND THE DESCENT HAD TO STOP BEING HAND-WRITTEN

Two findings, both silent passes, both narrower than the round before — and one of them is the sharpest single result of the five rounds, because it was carried all the way to a generated file.

**THE GUARD ON THE WHOLE-FILE SKIP MATCHED TWO LINE PREFIXES.** `assert_scanner_file_declares_no_types` is the only thing that makes skipping the caller's gate file safe, and it asked whether any trimmed line began `pub struct ` or `pub enum `. The review appended a **`pub(crate) struct`** to `redextape-wasm`'s gate file, with the canonical derive and a bad override on an `Option<u64>` field, and ran the binary: **`4 passed; 0 failed`, and `web/bindings/HiddenHere.ts` was really written.** Every gate silent, through the guard, on precisely the sabotage the exclusion's own comment says it assumes never happens — and a private `struct`, a `pub(super)`, a `union`, or a declaration not starting its line would each have done the same. The guard parses the file now and refuses a `struct`, `enum` or `union` at any visibility; sabotage 16 above is that construction at this head, failing two of the four tests where it used to fail none.

**AND THE HAND-WRITTEN DESCENT WAS ON ITS THIRD ROUND OF THE SAME MISTAKE.** "Descend into `mod`", then "and into `fn` bodies", then "and into `impl` methods": each correct, each leaving out the next container. A type in a nested block, in a closure body, in a match arm, in a `const _: () = { … }` initializer, or a `union` — all ordinary Rust, all silent passes, all with the same witness as round four's, since the sibling scan finds a derive wherever it sits. **The walk is `syn`'s own `Visit` now**, overriding the three item kinds that have fields and letting the default traversal reach everywhere else, so "did you remember to descend into X" stops being a question this code can answer wrongly. That is the second time on this branch that the fix was to stop enumerating and let something else own the traversal — the first was replacing the text scan with a parser at all.

**THE GUARD ADDED IN ROUND FOUR CREATED ITS OWN SIBLING, WHICH IS THE THIRD TIME THAT HAPPENED HERE.** Round four taught `union_admits_null` that a `>` following `=` closes no generic, so that `((x: number) => void) | null` would split correctly. `(x: number) => void | null` — the same shape without the outer parentheses — then split at top level too, and TypeScript binds that `| null` to the RETURN type, so the scan read a non-nullable override as nullable on an `Option` field. A top-level arrow ends the member search now. **Every one of the three "the fix carried the next defect" instances on this branch has been a guard that was right about the case it was written for and silent about the case one token away from it.**

**TWO MORE SILENT SKIPS BECAME PANICS**, in the module whose stated rule is that an unreadable attribute is a panic and never a skip — the same shape round four fixed one call above them. And `lib.rs`'s claim that this module "is plain `std`, so a consumer that opts out of `proptest` compiles it at no dependency cost" went false the moment the parser arrived; it now carries the `cargo tree` output showing `syn` reaching `redextape-cli`, the one consumer that declares `default-features = false` specifically to avoid paying for what it does not use.

**THE ROUND FIVE FIX ITSELF IS UNREVIEWED, AND THIS ENTRY SAYS SO RATHER THAN LEAVING IT TO BE ASSUMED.** Five rounds ran; each found defects in the one before, including this one. The decision to stop here was made deliberately and not because a round came back clean: severity fell across the five (High, High, High, Medium, Medium), the last round's two fixes both replaced an enumeration with something else owning the traversal, and the remaining named holes are pinned by tests that assert them. **What is not claimed is that a sixth round would have found nothing.** On this branch's evidence, the honest expectation is that it would have found something, and the reason to stop is that the something left is getting smaller while the cost is not.

##### THE `docker` JOB'S PR EXEMPTION, RESTATED PER PR 1'S OWN INSTRUCTION TO SAY SO EVERY TIME

`docker` does not run on pull requests and is absent from `gate`'s `needs`, so a pull request goes green on a `Dockerfile` this branch broke and the failure appears only on the post-merge push to `main`. **Checked from the diff rather than from memory, and the answer CHANGED while this entry sat in the file.** `git diff --name-only main..eef2c26` lists ten files: three under `crates/redextape-test-support/`, one gate file in each of `redextape-core` and `redextape-wasm`, one new file under `web/tests/node/`, three under `docs/`, and **`Cargo.lock`**. None is a `Dockerfile`, a `.dockerignore`, a `.forgejo/` workflow, a compose file, or `web/package.json`, so no stage's command changed — **but an earlier version of this paragraph said "no `Cargo.toml` or `Cargo.lock` moved either", and the `syn` rewrite falsified it.** That sentence was true at `cff309c` and false three commits later, in the entry whose own subject is claims going stale.

So the manifest claim is made the way PR 1 of the wire-type slice learned to make it — **by running the command the image's first stage runs, rather than by reading the manifest**. `wasm-pack build crates/redextape-wasm --release --target web` exits 0 at this head and writes a complete `pkg` (the `.wasm`, its `.d.ts`, the JS shim and `package.json`), with `git status --porcelain` empty afterward — **re-run at `55837ad` rather than carried from the earlier commit where it was first measured**, because the manifest moved again after that when `syn` gained its `visit` feature. That is the stage that could have been affected, and it was not: the new dependency is in `redextape-test-support`'s `[dependencies]`, and that crate enters no graph `wasm-pack build` compiles. `cargo check --target wasm32-unknown-unknown -p redextape-wasm --all-targets` also exits 0, with `--all-targets` rather than `--lib` because dev-dependencies appear only there.

##### WHAT STAYS OPEN

- **An `Option` field with NO override is watched by the eleven named constants in `bindings-contract.test.ts` and by no rule.** `ts-rs` maps `Option` to `| null` on its own and the derive-site gate never looks at a field without an override, so a twelfth nullable field entering the boundary is unwatched and nothing fires to say so. The pin's own header says this rather than leaving it to be discovered.
- **Both walks in `ts_derive_scan` skip the caller's gate file entirely**, which is a whole-file skip sitting in a module whose doc says an unreadable attribute is a panic and never a skip. It is guarded — the excluded file is read and refused if it declares a `pub struct` or `pub enum` — and the guard is one function shared by both walks, but the skip itself remains. **The clause that used to follow this one, about a `ts(...)` attribute quoted inside a string literal failing as unparseable, was true of the text scan and is false of the parser**: `syn` sees a string literal as a literal and never as an attribute, so no such file is refused. It was left standing here as a live limitation of a mechanism that no longer exists.
- **An override written on an enum VARIANT is not read by this rule.** `ts-rs-macros`'s `VariantAttr` carries `type` and `as` keys of its own, so that is a real override rather than a mistake the compiler catches; this rule reads field attributes only. What a variant-level override does to its payload's nullability has not been measured, and a rule guessing at it would be the unmeasured mechanism this branch spent three review rounds learning not to write. Found while correcting a fixture in this module that had put its attribute on the variant by mistake and passed vacuously because of it — the fixture was the bug report.
- **A `type` alias for an `Option` reads as not-an-`Option`.** `syn` parses one file and resolves no names, so `type MaybeSteps = Option<u64>;` with `pub total_steps: MaybeSteps` passes. Pinned by a test that asserts the hole.
- **`#[ts(skip)]` and `#[ts(flatten)]` are named as a different defect rather than as safe.** `skip` removes a field from the generated type that the wire still sends, which is wrong about the boundary in a way this rule does not describe; `flatten` restructures. Neither is checked here, and `NULLABILITY_KEYS`'s doc says so rather than leaving a reader to infer from a three-element list that every other key is harmless.
- **Nullability INSIDE a generic is invisible to the derive-site rule.** `RuleView::read` and `RuleView::write` are `Vec<Option<Symbol>>` generating `Array<string | null>`; an override rewriting the element type passes a rule that reads only the outermost `Option<`. Closing it means parsing the Rust type rather than matching its prefix — a different mechanism, not a wider prefix.
- **Nothing compares the generated types against the measured wire.** Unchanged from PRs #69, #70 and #71: `crates/redextape-wasm/tests/browser.rs` measures shapes out of a real browser and the generator asserts them, and no test compares the two. The pin added here checks one property of the generated output against a hand-written list; it is not that comparison.
- **The coverage scan's three named routes** — a `Cargo.toml` rename of the ts-rs dependency, a macro expanding to the marker only at its call site, and a `#[path]` resolving outside the crate root — are inherited unchanged by the new scan, which walks the same files by the same rule. Named, not closed.
- **`LinkIndexWire` stays hand-written and unwatched**, and **`TermTree`/`TermNode` stay serialized with no `TS` derive and no schedule**, both unchanged from PR #71's list.
- **`web/bindings/` is generated and gitignored, so a stale one still typechecks.** `assertTokenClasses` remains the check that compares against the loaded wasm module rather than against a file on disk.

They have now been measured six times on this branch — at `cff309c`, `dd3fb90`, `a5d4a2e`, `eef2c26`, `3b79d0d` and here — because every review round moved the code underneath the previous set, one of them replaced the mechanism outright, and **one set was left standing one round behind and caught by the fifth review rather than by the person who wrote it**.
