**THAT IS THE FULL CLOSING LINE, NOT THE PARTIAL ONE, AND IT WAS RUN SIX TIMES ON PURPOSE.** The script's other closing line reports itself `green, but PARTIAL` when the LLVM or browser tier is skipped; none of these runs skipped either. It ran at `3f91d7a`, at `cff309c`, at `dd3fb90` after the first review round, at `a5d4a2e` after the second, at `eef2c26` after the third replaced the mechanism, and at `55837ad` after the fifth. The second run is the one worth defending: the argument for skipping it was available and mechanical — `git diff 3f91d7a..cff309c -U0` changes no line that is not a `///` or `//` comment — and the entry directly above this one records what happens when an entry reasons about a diff instead of re-running, a paragraph claiming nothing but the roadmap had moved that was refuted by its own fix round. **The runs after the first two are what that habit bought**, because between `cff309c` and `55837ad` the review rounds rewrote the anchor, the field resolver, the `Option` predicate, the comment handling, the key list and the panic text, deleted all of it in favour of a parser, and then replaced the parser's hand-written descent with `syn`'s visitor and its two-prefix guard with a parse. A green gate on any earlier tree would have said nothing about this one. At the time this entry is committed the working tree differs from `55837ad` in this file alone, which `git status --porcelain` shows.

**`git status --porcelain` is empty at this head**, after every sabotage above was reverted, and `find crates -maxdepth 2 -iname bindings -type d`, `find crates -maxdepth 2 -iname pkg -type d` and `find web -maxdepth 1 -iname 'bindings.*'` all print nothing — `web/bindings`, gitignored and expected, is the one generated directory in the tree, holding 17 files.

**THAT SENTENCE WAS FALSE FOR SEVERAL HOURS AND `git status` COULD NOT HAVE TOLD ANYONE.** It was measured, correctly, before sabotage 16 was run — and sabotage 16 is the one that makes a gate file declare a type, so `export_bindings_hiddenhere` actually executed and wrote `crates/redextape-wasm/bindings/HiddenHere.ts`. **Reverting the source file does not remove a file a test wrote**, and both paths are gitignored, so the working tree read clean the entire time. The same run left a `crates/redextape-wasm/pkg` behind from the `wasm-pack` invocation above, where PR 1 of the wire-type slice had written its `pkg` outside the repository for exactly this reason. Both were removed and every check above re-run afterward. **The operational rule this yields is narrow and worth keeping**: a sabotage that causes generation must be followed by a check *by name*, because `git status` is blind to every path this repository deliberately ignores — which is the same reason PR 2's entry gave for checking by name, applied to a case that entry did not have.

**AND THE IMAGE WAS BUILT, NOT REASONED ABOUT.** `docker` does not run on a pull request, so the paragraph above argues from the diff that no stage's command changed and runs `wasm-pack build` — stage 1's command — to check the one thing that did move. That argument is now unnecessary rather than merely supported: **`docker build .` was run at this head and exits 0**, building every stage. PR 1 of the wire-type slice broke the image in precisely this blind spot and had it found by a human running the build; running it is cheaper than the paragraph explaining why it was not run.

##### CI RUN 353 WAS GREEN ON `082781e`, AND THAT SHA WAS READ FROM PULL REQUEST 75'S OWN `head.sha` RATHER THAN ASSUMED FROM THE BRANCH

This file's convention since entry 61, and it holds here for the usual reason plus a sharper one: the commit adding this paragraph necessarily sits outside the run it reports, and **this branch's history was rewritten after an earlier run had already gone green**, so the sha of that run is not merely a different commit — it is not in this history at all. Every job in run 353 reached a terminal status and none failed: `detect`, `linear-history`, `rust`, `rust-slow`, `rust-llvm`, `rust-browser`, `web` and `gate` all `success`; `rust-scoped` skipped because the unscoped `rust` ran instead; `docker` skipped, as the paragraph above covers. The run NUMBER from the `html_url` is 353 and the API's own id is `1384`; both are recorded because neither can be guessed from the other, and the offset is not constant — 350/`1380`, 351/`1382`, 352/`1383` and 353/`1384` give 1030, 1031, 1031 and 1031.

**THE RUN THIS PARAGRAPH ORIGINALLY REPORTED WAS DELETED RATHER THAN REMAPPED, AND THAT IS THE POINT WORTH KEEPING.** As first committed it named run 348 as green on `63a1c0b`. The 24 commits then had their messages rewritten to strip attribution trailers this repository forbids, which changed every id on the branch, and a script remapped 27 sha references in this entry by matching commit subjects. **The CI paragraph was the one thing that must not be remapped**: `63a1c0b`'s rewritten counterpart exists, but run 348 never saw it, and a paragraph naming a run against a commit that run never built is worse than no paragraph — it reads exactly like evidence while being none. So it was removed, a fresh run was allowed to complete on the rewritten head, and this is that run. **A sha rewrite invalidates every claim anchored to a sha, and the ones it invalidates hardest are the ones about things that happened outside the repository.**

**NO PER-JOB DURATIONS ARE QUOTED HERE, AND THE REASON IS THAT NOTHING THIS ENTRY RAN MEASURED THEM.** The Forgejo API route this entry used, `list_run_jobs`, returns each job's `status`, its ids and its `needs`, and carries no timing fields at all. Quoting numbers nobody here observed would be this branch's own lesson committed inside the paragraph reporting it.

**THE THREE TIERS THIS BRANCH HAD MOST REASON TO WANT RUN RATHER THAN ASSUMED ALL RAN GREEN, AND SO DID THE ONE MOST LIKELY TO OBJECT TO A REWRITE.** `rust-llvm` carries the `--fail-under-lines 90` coverage gate against a branch that added forty-nine fixtures and two dependencies to `redextape-test-support`. `rust-browser` exercises `#[wasm_bindgen]`'s generated glue for the types whose overrides this rule guards. `web` runs `pnpm run typecheck`, which is **the only thing that enforces the TypeScript pin at all**. And `linear-history` passed on a `filter-branch`-rewritten history, which is the job that would have caught a rewrite that produced anything other than a straight line.

**THIS ENTRY WAS COMMITTED SAYING NO CI PARAGRAPH APPEARED IN IT, AND THEN ONE WAS ADDED DIRECTLY ABOVE THIS LINE.** The sentence read *"No CI paragraph appears here, and the reason is a property rather than a fact about the present moment"*, and it went on to count 76 entries against six carrying such a paragraph, so that a reader would not take the absence as an oversight. It was true when written and false one commit later, for the plainest possible reason: the pull request had not been opened yet, and then it was. **This is the third time in three consecutive entries that a sentence about the state of CI has gone stale inside this file**, and the previous two are recorded above — one asserting *"no run has happened"* which was false within the hour, and one reasoning about a diff instead of re-running. The rule that survives all three is not about CI at all: **a sentence whose truth depends on when it is read does not belong in an append-only log, and "none is written" is exactly such a sentence.** The frequency figures were the sound half and are kept: at `55837ad` this file held 76 `####` entries and six CI paragraphs, so carrying one remains the exception.

#### THE GUARD PR #75 SHIPPED REPLACED A CHECK INSTEAD OF COMBINING IT AND REOPENED THE HOLE IT CLOSED, THE ONE COMMIT THAT WENT IN UNREVIEWED IS WHERE THE CRITICAL WAS, AND THE STOPPING RULE THAT LET IT SHIP WAS WRONG IN THE WAY IT WAS MOST CONFIDENT (2026-09-03, branch `nullability-guard-macro-hole`, `c2bff2f..f634ce9`, 1 commit, plus the entry commits)

Design and plan: none. This is a defect fix against [the entry above](#), whose own closing section recorded that its fifth and final fix round had shipped without a whole-branch review — and a sixth review of exactly that commit, run after the merge, found a Critical in it.

##### THE FIX SWAPPED ONE HOLE FOR ANOTHER, AND THE SIGNATURE IT PRODUCED IS THE ONE ITS COMMIT MESSAGE CLAIMED TO HAVE CLOSED

`assert_scanner_file_declares_no_types` is the only thing that makes the whole-file skip of each crate's gate file safe. PR #75's fifth round replaced its test — trimmed lines beginning `pub struct ` or `pub enum ` — with a `syn` parse, because the fifth review had walked a `pub(crate) struct` through the prefixes. The parse does refuse that. **It does not refuse a type declared inside an item-position macro**, because `syn` reads the invocation as `Item::Macro` and never enters its token stream — while the prefix check found exactly that case, since the words are literally present in the file.

Demonstrated on the real tree, not argued: `macro_rules! declare_it { ($($t:tt)*) => { $($t)* }; }` followed by `declare_it! { #[cfg_attr(feature = "ts", derive(ts_rs::TS), ts(export))] pub struct SneakyViaMacro { #[cfg_attr(feature = "ts", ts(type = "number"))] pub total_steps: Option<u64>, } }` appended to `redextape-core`'s gate file gives **`4 passed; 0 failed`** — including `export_bindings_sneakyviamacro` — and writes `crates/redextape-core/bindings/SneakyViaMacro.ts` reading `export type SneakyViaMacro = { total_steps: number, };`. The `| null` gone, every gate silent, a binding really on disk. **That is byte for byte the signature the round-five commit message cited as the thing it had closed.**

**THE LESSON IS THE VERB.** The fifth review reported a hole in a guard; the fix REPLACED the guard. Nobody asked what the old check had been catching that the new one would not, because the old check looked crude and the new one looked principled — a parse is obviously better than two string prefixes, and it is, at the thing it does. A guard replaced is not a guard fixed, and "the new mechanism is strictly better" is a claim about coverage that needs measuring exactly like a count does.

##### THE GUARD IS THREE LAYERS NOW, AND EACH CLOSES SOMETHING THE OTHER TWO STRUCTURALLY CANNOT

The parse catches a type declared plainly at any visibility. A text check — `struct`, `enum` or `union` followed by a name, on a line that is not a comment — catches one declared inside a macro invocation **this file spells out**, which is the case above. And a refusal of item-position macro invocations outright catches the third route, where the macro's body lives in another file and the words appear nowhere here, so neither reading the file nor parsing it can see the result. Each layer names, in its own comment, the route it exists for. **The text layer costs nothing today**: neither gate file contains the words `struct`, `enum` or `union` at all, in prose or otherwise, and their only macro invocations — `vec!` and `assert!` — are statement-position and untouched. **A macro in STATEMENT position inside a `#[test] fn` could still declare a type none of the three sees**, and that is named rather than closed.

##### THREE MORE FROM THE SAME REVIEW, AND ONE OF THEM IS A GUARD THAT CREATED ITS OWN SIBLING FOR THE SECOND TIME

**The parse failed OPEN.** `if let Ok(parsed) = syn::parse_file(…)` left the flag false when the gate file did not parse, silently re-blessing the skip — ten lines from `check_source`, which panics on the identical condition and carries a comment explaining why a parse failure must never be a skip. The one guard on the one skip that hides a file from every gate in the binary was the place that fell back to a pass.

**`union_admits_null` lost quoted spans.** Round five taught it that a depth-zero `=>` ENDS the member search, because everything after an arrow is the return type. A TypeScript string-literal type may contain any character, so `'=>' | null` and `'>' | null` — both genuinely nullable — terminated the scan before reaching `null`. Both returned `true` before that change and `false` after: a false red panicking the gate on correct source. **This is the second time on this slice that the guard added in one round created its sibling in the next**, and both times the new guard was right about the case it was written for.

**And `FieldWalk`'s doc over-claimed.** It said the visitor makes the two gates in one binary unable to answer differently about the same type. Still false for an item macro: the sibling line-based scan resolves forward to the `pub struct` inside one and finds it, the visitor does not. The wording is corrected rather than softened, and points at the layer that protects the gate file specifically.

##### THE STOPPING RULE WAS WRONG, AND IT WAS WRONG IN THE DIRECTION IT WAS MOST CONFIDENT

PR #75 stopped after five review rounds on a stated argument: severity had fallen — High, High, High, Medium, Medium — the last round's fixes had replaced enumerations with something else owning the traversal, and what remained named was pinned. That reasoning is recorded in that entry, along with the caveat that the fifth fix round was itself unreviewed and that a sixth would probably find something. **A sixth found a Critical, and it was in that exact commit.** So the trend was real and the inference from it was worthless: five rounds of falling severity said nothing whatever about the one change nobody had looked at. **The severity of past rounds is a property of the code that WAS reviewed. The risk lives entirely in the code that was not, and no trend can speak to it.** The honest stopping rule is not "severity is falling" but "every change has been reviewed by something that ran it" — a condition PR #75 explicitly did not meet and said so, which is the only reason this was ever found.

##### AND THE FIX FOR THAT WAS REVIEWED BEFORE IT SHIPPED, WHICH IS THE WHOLE POINT — IT GOT A TYPE PAST ALL THREE LAYERS

The three-layer guard above was itself sent to a whole-branch review before this branch was opened, because the section directly above retracts the stopping rule that let an unreviewed commit ship. It found two Highs, and the first is the third appearance of the same signature.

**`#[path = "../../elsewhere.rs"] mod m;` walked past all three layers.** It declares no type, so the parse sees nothing. It spells no type NAME, so the text scan sees nothing. It is not a macro, so the item-macro refusal sees nothing. And `#[path]` resolves it outside `crate_root`, which is one of the three routes the sibling scanner has named as outside its own reach since PR #70 — so neither walk ever opens the file. Measured on the real tree: `4 passed; 0 failed` with `web/bindings/SneakyViaPathMod.ts` written as `total_steps: number`. **Three rounds of asking "does this file declare a type" produced three holes**, because that question is answered by looking at the file, and every one of these routes puts the declaration somewhere else.

**So the question changed.** The guard now asks what the file can PRODUCE, and refuses every construct that can bring a declaration in from anywhere: a `struct`/`enum`/`union`, a `mod`, an item-position macro, or an item attribute that is not on a whitelist of attributes known to expand to nothing. **The whitelist is the only construction that refuses an attribute proc-macro**, which `syn` reports as an ordinary `Item::Fn`/`Item::Mod`/`Item::Const` carrying an attribute — indistinguishable from an inert one by any amount of parsing. The two gate files carry exactly `#![allow]`, `#![cfg]` and `#[test]`, and no `mod`, so the whitelist costs nothing today.

**THE TEXT LAYER WAS DELETED RATHER THAN FIXED, AND THE REASON IT COULD BE IS THAT SOMEBODY MEASURED IT.** The review's second High was that it false-positived on prose: adding one natural sentence containing *"Every struct or enum in this crate"* to an existing `assert!` message reddened both gates with a message asserting that a macro was declaring a type, when none existed — in files that are almost entirely long prose assertion messages. Before patching its lexer, the layer was disabled and the macro sabotage re-run: **it still failed**, because refusing item macros already covered that case. The layer bought nothing and cost a false-positive surface aimed squarely at the next person to edit those messages.

**Its own justification is the part worth keeping.** The comment read *"Neither gate file contains these words at all today, in prose or otherwise, so this costs no false positives"* — a fact about today's bytes, offered as a property, in a file whose entry two sections above is about exactly that failure. The diagnosis and the instance were written hours apart by the same hand. **A guard justified by what a file happens to contain is not justified; it is scheduled to fail when someone edits the file.**

Three smaller findings from the same review: escapes were not honoured inside quoted union members, so `'it\'s' | null` closed the span at the backslashed quote and swallowed the top-level `|`; the layer messages named a diagnosis rather than what fired, when `syn` reports a `macro_rules!` DEFINITION as `Item::Macro` too; and three lines exceeded the repo's `max_width = 120`, which `cargo fmt --check` cannot catch because it rewraps neither doc comments nor string literals.

##### AND THEN THE GUARD STOPPED BEING NEEDED, BECAUSE THE SKIP IT PROTECTED HAD OUTLIVED ITS REASON BY THREE ROUNDS

Everything above describes guards on a whole-file exclusion. **The exclusion was unnecessary.** Both walks in `ts_derive_scan` skipped each crate's gate file because that file quotes `ts(type = "number")` inside its own assertion messages — text a scanner would anchor on. The nullability rule stopped scanning text and started parsing Rust in PR #75, and **a parser does not care**: those seven occurrences are string literals and doc comments, and not one of them is an attribute. Nobody checked. The skip predated the parser and outlived its reason by three review rounds, each of which spent itself finding a way past the guard defending it — a `pub(crate) struct` past two line prefixes, a `macro_rules!` body past a parse, a `#[path] mod` past a parse plus a text scan plus an item-macro refusal.

**Measured before removing it rather than after**, which is the only order in which the measurement means anything: with the exclusion deleted from that walk, both crates' gates report `3 tests run: 3 passed`. So the walk now reads every `.rs` file in the crate, and **the class closes instead of its members being refused one at a time — including the members nobody has found yet.** `assert_scanner_file_declares_no_types` survives for `ts_deriving_type_names_in_crate` alone, which is textual by design and genuinely cannot read a gate file's `use ts_rs::TS;` without failing its own canonical-line check; its doc now ends by asking whether that scan could stop needing it too.

**WHAT THE REMOVAL BOUGHT IS A CHECK THAT DID NOT EXIST, NOT MERELY A SIMPLER GUARD.** A bad override on a type declared IN a gate file is now caught by the rule itself. Measured in the real tree: a `pub(crate) struct` there with `ts(type = "number")` on an `Option<u64>` fails BOTH `the_gate_covers_every_exported_type` and `no_override_misstates_a_field_s_nullability`, where before it failed only the sibling's guard — because that file was never read by this walk at all. The `scanner_path` parameter is gone from the signature, so both call sites lost an argument that had stopped meaning anything.

**THIS IS THE THIRD TIME ON THIS SLICE THAT THE ANSWER WAS TO REMOVE THE THING BEING WIDENED**, and the three are worth reading together because they are the same move at increasing distance from the code. Text-scanning Rust became a parser. A hand-written descent became `syn`'s visitor. And a guard on an exclusion became no exclusion. Each time the preceding rounds had been correct about their instances and had left the mechanism intact; each time the question that broke the cycle was not "what else can get past this" but **"why does this exist"** — which nobody asks of a thing that has been there longer than the reason for it.

##### THE EIGHTH REVIEW COULD NOT BREAK THE REMOVAL, AND FOUND EVERYTHING ELSE IN THE GUARD THAT SURVIVED IT

Its own summary is the result worth recording: *"I could not get a bad override past the unskipped nullability walk by any route the module does not already name, and I could not make it false-positive. The holes are all in the surviving guard."* **That is the first change on this slice to come through a round intact, and it is the one that deleted a mechanism rather than adding to one.** Both real gate files parse and pass; the claimed benefit was re-measured; every VERIFICATION figure reproduced.

**The HIGH is a class this file had already fixed eighty lines away.** `#[cfg_attr(all(), wasm_bindgen::prelude::wasm_bindgen)]` — a real proc macro on the real tree — compiled, expanded, and left `redextape-wasm`'s gate file at `3 passed; 0 failed`. `visit_attribute` sees only the OUTER attribute and `cfg_attr` is on the inert whitelist, so nothing ever looked at what was nested inside it. `ts_keys_under`, in this same module, carries a doc paragraph headed *"A NESTED `cfg_attr` WAS A SILENT PASS, AND IT IS ORDINARY RUST"* and recurses to any depth — written during PR #75's fourth round. **The layer whose entire stated purpose is that the whitelist is the only construction refusing an attribute proc-macro was bypassed by the one construct the whitelist itself admits, and the fix for it was already in the file.** Fixing a class in one function and not in its neighbour is the mechanism by which this module keeps paying for the same lesson.

**And the whitelist matched only the last path segment**, so `#[tokio::test]`, `#[async_std::test]` and `#[actix_rt::test]` — ordinary attribute proc-macros that expand to arbitrary items — all answered to `test`. A path must be a single segment now; a qualified one is refused whatever its tail says, which also refuses `#[rustfmt::skip]`. That is the safe direction, and the message names the construct so the next person adds it deliberately rather than discovering the gate is quiet.

Three smaller ones, each the same shape as something already recorded above it. `type_is_option` did not unwrap `Type::Paren`, so `(Option<u64>)` was a silent pass on the field side and `ts(as = "(Option<u32>)")` a false red on the other — the third appearance of "this predicate does not recognise an ordinary spelling", after the bare prefix and the qualified path. `union_admits_null` rejected `number | (null)`, splitting the member correctly and then failing a bare string comparison. And **five comments and panic messages still said the guard serves "both walks"**, which the commit before them had made false — including one telling the reader that the other walk *"excludes the same file for the same reason"*, when as of that commit it excludes nothing. Those are the sentences an engineer reads at the moment the gate fires.

**One figure was wrong in the way this file has a memory for.** The paragraph explaining why the skip was unnecessary said *"those seven occurrences"* and then generalised in its next clause to *"both gate files"*. `grep -c 'ts(type'` reads **7** in `redextape-core`'s gate file and **5** in `redextape-wasm`'s. Nothing gates either number, so the sentence now states the property it actually needs — every one of them is a string literal or a doc comment and not one is an attribute — rather than a count that was true of the file it was written while looking at.

##### THE NINTH REVIEW REOPENED THE EIGHTH'S FINDING WITH ONE KEYWORD, AND THE FIX FOR ITS OTHER HALF BROKE BOTH REAL GATES

**`syn::Meta` CANNOT PARSE THE KEYWORD `true`.** Round eight taught `check_meta` to recurse through `cfg_attr` by parsing its whole argument list as `Punctuated<Meta, Comma>`; `#[cfg_attr(true, wasm_bindgen::prelude::wasm_bindgen)]` compiles, that parse fails on the predicate, and an `if let Ok` dropped the attribute entirely. A real proc macro walked past the whitelist the round before had just tightened — `3 passed; 0 failed` in `redextape-wasm`'s gate file. **It was the one place in this module that skipped rather than refused**, in a file whose rule everywhere else is that an attribute it cannot read is a panic. A shared `CfgAttrTail` parser now consumes the predicate as opaque token trees up to the first top-level comma and reads only the tail, which repairs the same defect on the FIELD side from the opposite direction: a correct override written `#[cfg_attr(true, ts(type = "number | null"))]` used to panic both gates on source that compiles, and the skip removal had widened that blast radius to every file in both crates.

**AND ITEM POSITION WAS NEVER THE ONLY MACRO POSITION.** A `macro_rules!` invoked in STATEMENT position inside a `#[test] fn` declares a type into that scope; measured on the real tree, one did, and `export_all()` wrote the binding with all three gates silent. Expression, `impl`, trait, `extern` and type positions are the same construct. **The roadmap named this gap under WHAT STAYS OPEN while the code comment three lines from the check denied it** — *"refuses every CONSTRUCT that can bring a declaration in from anywhere"* — and the comment is what a reader meets at the moment the gate does not fire. All six positions are checked now.

**THE FIX FOR THAT PRODUCED THIS BRANCH'S OWN BEST EXAMPLE OF A FIXTURE PROVING NOTHING.** Statement macros cannot be refused outright — `vec!` and `assert!` are statement macros and these files are full of them — so a whitelist applies. The fixture written for it listed `vec!` and `assert!`, passed, and **both real gates went red**: the gate files call `env!` for `CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR`, and the fixture's author did not think of it. A list built from imagination is not the list built from need. The fixture now carries every macro those files actually invoke, and `INERT` gained `forbid` beside its three siblings plus `must_use`, `track_caller` and five more built-ins that were reds on source a gate file could legitimately grow.

Three smaller ones, each a sibling of something fixed the round before. `union_admits_null` rejected a union parenthesised as a WHOLE — `(number | null)` — the round after it learned to accept a parenthesised MEMBER; and the first fix for that then failed on `number | (null | undefined)`, a member that is itself a union, so the check recurses now. `type_is_option` unwrapped exactly one layer of parens, so `((Option<u64>))` was a silent pass. **Every one of these is the same shape: a predicate taught one spelling in one round and meeting its neighbour in the next.**

**AND THE ENTRY'S OWN NO-STRAYS CLAIM WAS FALSE AGAIN, IN THE PARAGRAPH THAT DOCUMENTS IT BEING FALSE THE FIRST TIME.** `crates/redextape-core/bindings/SneakyInGate.ts` was on disk with an mtime nine minutes BEFORE the commit that asserted `find crates -maxdepth 2 \( -iname bindings -o -iname pkg \) -type d` prints nothing — left by a sabotage, gitignored, so `git status` stayed empty exactly as that paragraph warns. Twice on one branch, the second time under the sentence explaining the first. **The rule is not "check by name after a sabotage"; it is that a sabotage which causes generation leaves evidence the revert does not remove, so the check belongs in the same breath as the revert rather than at the end of the session.**

##### THE TENTH REVIEW DELETED A LAYER THE NINTH HAD ADDED, BECAUSE THE MEASUREMENT THAT JUSTIFIED IT WAS NEVER CHECKED AND DOES NOT REPRODUCE

Scoped to the guard alone, since the unskipped walk had survived three rounds. It found the usual next spelling — and underneath it, that the layer those spellings lived in should never have existed.

**ROUND NINE ADDED CHECKS FOR MACROS IN STATEMENT, EXPRESSION, `impl`, TRAIT, `extern` AND TYPE POSITION ON A REPORT NOBODY VERIFIED.** That report said a statement-position macro had declared a type and written a real binding with every gate silent. It was implemented as written. **Round ten measured the opposite, and the measurement was then repeated here rather than taken on trust a second time**: a canonically-derived type declared inside a `#[test] fn` in the real gate file yields `warning: unnameable_test_items`, four tests, **no `export_bindings_*` and no `bindings/` directory at all**. `rustc` does not collect `#[test]` items nested in a function body, so ts-rs's generated export test never runs. None of those six positions can place an item at module scope, and module scope is the only scope that produces a binding.

So the layer bought nothing, while costing false reds on `env!`, `debug_assert_eq!`, `format_args!` and every `std::`-qualified spelling — and the `env!` one **reddened both real gates** before it was caught, because the fixture written for that whitelist was built from imagination and the gate files were built from need. **It is deleted rather than extended**, and a fixture now pins the measured fact so a later round does not add it back. That also disposes of the round's HIGH, which was that any refused construct could be hidden inside a whitelisted macro's token stream: with no whitelist there is no hiding place, and the constructs were only ever reachable at a scope that generates nothing.

**THIS FILE ALREADY CARRIED THE RULE THAT WAS BROKEN.** PR #71's entry records a fix round whose own research subagent reported two claims false, and the round overrode it by reading the code and confirming the claims were true — *"a subagent's result is a claim to check, not a result."* That paragraph was read during this very branch. A review's finding is evidence about where to look, not a measurement; the two look identical in a report and differ entirely in what they license.

**THE FOURTH REMOVAL ON THIS SLICE, AND THE FIRST WHERE THE THING REMOVED WAS ONE ROUND OLD.** Text scan to parser; hand-written descent to visitor; guard-on-an-exclusion to no exclusion; and now a layer to nothing at all. Three of the four were mechanisms that had outlived their reason by rounds or by a whole PR. This one had outlived it by a single review, which is the shortest possible span and the easiest to miss, because nothing about it had yet had time to look load-bearing.

One real fix survives the deletion: **`#[unsafe(no_mangle)]` is edition 2024's REQUIRED spelling** of otherwise-inert built-in attributes, and the guard refused it while naming `#[unsafe]` — a construct the author did not write. It descends into the wrapper now, and the three attributes it wraps are on the inert list.

**AND THE ASSISTANT CLAIMED TO HAVE RUN THE FULL GATE ON THIS ROUND AND HAD NOT**, which the human caught by asking. The figures quoted alongside it — 70 fixtures, 1378 workspace tests, clippy clean, both `ts_bindings` binaries green — were all real and all run; `scripts/check-all.sh` was not, and its last run had been two commits earlier, before this round's deletion. **A false sentence surrounded by true ones is the shape this entire entry is about**, and it turns out to be as available for a claim about one's own actions as for a claim about a mechanism. The gate has since been run at `36b9abe` and its closing line is in the block below.

##### WHAT STAYS OPEN

- **The guard still stands between `ts_deriving_type_names_in_crate` and its own gate file**, and everything above about ways past it applies to that scan alone now. **The open question its doc asks is whether that scan could stop needing the skip too**, the way the nullability walk did — it cannot today, because its rule refuses any non-canonical mention of `ts_rs` including prose, and the gate files discuss `ts_rs` in prose at length.
- **Two whitelists, and a whitelist is a list that goes stale.** One names the attributes known to expand to nothing, the other the `std` macros known to expand to an expression. Both refuse anything unlisted, which is the safe direction, and both name the construct in the refusal so the next addition is deliberate. The macro one already cost a round: its first fixture omitted `env!`, which both real gate files use.
- Everything the entry above lists stays open unchanged: an override on an enum VARIANT, a `type` alias for an `Option`, a macro-generated field anywhere outside the gate files, nullability inside a generic, and an `Option` field with no override watched only by the eleven named constants in the TypeScript pin.

##### VERIFICATION

Figures measured at `36b9abe`, the branch's last commit before the one that adds this entry — re-measured there rather than carried from any of `f634ce9`, `154789d`, `3ce6f34`, `8053f5f` or `8f37c2d`, because a review round moved the code after every one of them. **The insertion count FELL between the last two**, from +782 to +755, which is what a round that deletes more than it adds looks like in this column.

```
11                      commits                      git rev-list --count main..36b9abe
6 files, +755/-65       whole-branch diff            git diff --shortstat main..36b9abe
70 passed, 0 skipped    source fixtures on the rule  cargo nextest run -p redextape-test-support
                          (49 before this branch)
3 passed, 0 skipped     ts_bindings, each crate      cargo nextest run -p redextape-core --features ts
                                                      -E 'binary(ts_bindings)'  (and -p redextape-wasm)
1378 passed, 10 skipped workspace                    cargo nextest run --workspace
0                       clippy findings              cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets
```

```
$ scripts/check-all.sh
all configs green — base, LLVM and browser
[exited with code 0]
```

**Four guard routes were sabotaged in the real tree and each fires, the prose case that used to redden them is green, and the check the skip's removal created was sabotaged too.** A `pub(crate) struct` fails on the type check; `declare_it! { pub struct … }` on the item-macro check; `#[path = "../../sneaky_probe.rs"] mod sneaky_probe;` on the module check; `#[emit_a_type] fn helper() {}` on the attribute whitelist. Adding a sentence containing "struct or enum" to an existing `assert!` message leaves all three tests passing. And a `pub(crate) struct` in a gate file carrying `ts(type = "number")` on an `Option<u64>` now fails TWO tests — the sibling's guard and the nullability rule reading that file for the first time. `git status --porcelain` is empty at this head and `find crates -maxdepth 2 \( -iname bindings -o -iname pkg \) -type d` prints nothing — checked by name, because both are gitignored and the sabotage above really does write a binding file, which is how the entry above came to carry a false no-strays claim for several hours.

#### THE `.tm` AND `.asm` TEXT FORMS KEEP THEIR COMMENTS, THE TWO FORMS GET DIFFERENT GUARANTEES BECAUSE THE TM PRINTER FABRICATES LABELS AND TWO OF ITS ANCHORS WERE NAMED FROM A FAMILY OF LINES RATHER THAN ONE, A SECOND `tapes` LINE HAD BEEN SILENTLY OVERWRITING THE FIRST SINCE LONG BEFORE THIS BRANCH AND WAS FOUND BY AN OUT-OF-TREE PROBE AFTER A REVIEW CHALLENGED A DOC COMMENT'S SELF-EVIDENT CLAIM RATHER THAN BY THE PROPERTY, WHICH WAS AND REMAINS STRUCTURALLY BLIND TO THE SHAPE, AND FOUR TIMES A GREEN TEST STRUCTURALLY COULD NOT REACH THE CASE THAT WOULD HAVE FALSIFIED IT WHILE LOOKING COMPREHENSIVE BECAUSE IT NAMED EVERY VARIANT (2026-09-04, branch `redextape-lsp`, `ebb1970..4135ef7`, 28 commits, plus the entry commit)

Design: [`../specs/2026-09-04-redextape-lsp-design.md`](../specs/2026-09-04-redextape-lsp-design.md). Plan: [`2026-09-04-tm-asm-comment-retention.md`](2026-09-04-tm-asm-comment-retention.md).

PR A of a two-PR design, and the half the other half needs first. A formatter cannot be pointed at a hand-written `.tm` or `.asm` file while the parsers throw its comments on the floor, so `parse_tm_full` and `parse_asm_full` now return `TmDocument` and `AsmDocument` — the machine or program, the header, the diagnostics, and a `Vec<AnchoredComment<A>>` — and `print_tm_doc` / `print_asm_doc` write the comments back. **The comments are a SIDE CHANNEL, and `Machine` and `Program` gain no field**: a machine that came out of `lower_tm` has no comments and must print exactly what the listing golden pins, so comments must not reach the compiler's output path at all. Each `AnchoredComment` carries the trimmed body, the printed line it sits against, and whether only whitespace separated it from the previous newline. **An anchor rather than a span, and that is the whole design decision.** `token::Comment` can carry a `Span` because the `.rxt` formatter walks tokens and can order a comment against them; the TM and asm printers walk a `Machine` and a `Program` and never see a token, so a byte offset into the text a comment CAME from cannot say where to write it in the text being produced. Naming the printed line is what survives reformatting.

`print_tm`, `print_tm_with`, `print_asm` and `print_asm_with` are unchanged in behaviour by construction rather than by test: every one of them reaches a single inner printer with `comments` as `&[]`, `CommentWriter::new` buckets an empty slice into two empty maps, `HashMap::get` on an empty map is `None` for every key so `own_line` and `trailing` write nothing, and `HashMap::contains_key` on an empty map is `false` for every key so `has_trailing` answers `false` for every anchor too, which is what keeps `write_header`'s generated `; reg` label in `print_tm_with`'s output rather than suppressing it — `print_tm_inner`'s own doc states both halves of this argument, and this entry now follows that wording. **`.rxt` already retained comments and λ has no comment syntax at all** — nothing under `crates/redextape-core/src/lambda/` contains a `';'` character literal or a `";"` string literal, so no byte of λ source is ever compared against a semicolon, let alone read as opening a comment — so this is two forms and not three.

##### THE TWO FORMS GET DIFFERENT GUARANTEES, AND BOTH MECHANISMS THAT FORCE THE DIFFERENCE ARE ABSENT ON THE ASM SIDE

`.asm` gets the **strict round trip**: `parse_asm_full(print_asm_doc(d))` agrees with `d` on `program`, `header` and `comments` exactly. `.tm` gets only **idempotence**: `print_tm_doc(parse_tm_full(print_tm_doc(parse_tm_full(x))))` equals `print_tm_doc(parse_tm_full(x))`. Formatting a `.tm` file once may change it; formatting it again changes nothing.

**The strict round trip is false on `.tm`, and it is false for exactly the files this slice exists to serve.** `write_header` labels a `tape <i>` line with a comment `tape_name` generates — `; reg`, `; work`, `; stack`, `; heap`, `; box` — whenever that anchor carries no AUTHORED trailing comment, `CommentWriter::has_trailing` being what decides "authored". A hand-written file is not obliged to comment its `tape` lines, so a `tape 0` line with nothing after it parses with no comment on that anchor and prints **with** `; reg`; reparsing that output records an `AnchoredComment` anchored to `Directive(Tape(0))` that was never in the source. `d` and its round trip differ by a comment the printer invented. This is a property of every generated label, not a count of which tape indices happen to trigger it.

**The second mechanism is subtler, and it is what the duplicate-line diagnostic below exists for.** `TmAnchor::Tapes` and `TmAnchor::Start` were each named by `parse_tm_full` from a **family** of lines — every `tapes ...` line, every `start ...` line — rather than from one fixed line, unlike `Directive`, `State` and `Rule`, which are keyed by an identity of their own. `CommentWriter::trailing` joins several trailing comments on one anchor with `" ; "`, and that join is not a fixed point when a body is empty, so a second line in either family made the first print and the second print differ.

**Neither mechanism has a counterpart in asm, and that was verified rather than assumed.** The asm printer fabricates no comment. `AsmAnchor::Label(i)` and `AsmAnchor::Instr(i)` are positional — `labels.len() - 1` and `code.len() - 1` at the moment of the push — so no two lines in one clean parse can share an index. A second `result` directive is already a diagnostic, on either of two branches, and `parse_asm_full`'s single tail check empties `comments` for the whole document whichever fired. And `AsmAnchor::Eof` is never a `trailing` argument at all: the parser only ever drains `pending` into it own-line, matching the printer's own `Eof` call, which has no `trailing` counterpart. So the asm property does not have to weaken to idempotence and does not have to drop to a sub-multiset check on `comments`.

**Why idempotence is the right statement for `.tm` rather than a retreat.** After the first print the generated label is ordinary text sitting on that line. Reparsing records it as an AUTHORED trailing comment on the same anchor — parsing cannot tell a generated label from a hand-typed one, they are the same bytes — and on the second print `has_trailing` takes the displacement branch, writes the recorded text, and never calls `tape_name` again. The generated path and the authored path converge on identical bytes. That convergence is a property of the displacement rule, so the section's two rules hold each other up instead of sitting side by side. And idempotence is what a formatter actually needs: *"running the formatter twice differs from running it once"* is the defect a user meets, while *"a hand-authored file is not a fixed point of the printer"* is what every formatter does the first time it touches a file.

**`CommentWriter` is generic over its anchor type, so the doc states two things a THIRD instantiation must still establish rather than a fact about today's tree**: one line holds at most one trailing comment, AND every anchor variant names at most one line. The second is the one that was false for `TmAnchor`, and it is the one a reader is most likely to assume — but for `AsmAnchor`, which has already shipped, the doc does not stop at naming `parse_asm_full`'s duplicate-`result` diagnostic and its positional anchors as a starting point: it states the argument discharged, the same argument `printing_and_reparsing_all_anchors_recovers_the_document_exactly`'s doc comment writes out in full.

##### A PRODUCTION BUG OLDER THAN THIS BRANCH, FOUND BY AN OUT-OF-TREE PROBE AFTER A REVIEW CHALLENGED A DOC COMMENT'S SELF-EVIDENT CLAIM, IN A CODE PATH THAT HAS NOTHING TO DO WITH COMMENTS

`tapes 1` followed by `tapes 5` silently yielded a five-tape machine. `start q0` followed by `start q1` silently started at `q1`. Both with zero diagnostics, neither diagnosed, neither tested, and both predating this branch by a long way. **The rule they were outside of was already written down**: `HeaderParts::directive` refuses a second `version`, `encoding`, `width`, `slots`, `result` or `tape <i>` directive on the argument that a file states a thing once, so a second line — even one that agrees with the first — is refused rather than silently taken as last-wins. The two leading lines had simply never been brought under it. `parse_tm_full` now reports `duplicate \`tapes\` line` and `duplicate \`start\` line`, with the span pinned to the SECOND line, which is the only observable trace of the keep-the-first choice. The first line **that parses** is the one that wins: a malformed first `tapes` line sets nothing and reports only its own error, so a well-formed second line is then the one that counts.

**The idempotence property did not find this, and structurally could not have.** Its generator emits exactly one `tapes` line and one `start` line per document, at every commit on this branch — `render` in `crates/redextape-core/tests/tm_comments.rs` is the function that builds its input, and it calls `emit` for `tapes` and for `start` exactly once each. No case the property can draw ever contains the duplicate, so it never went red on this defect and remains blind to it today, a fact this entry documents twice more below. What actually found it was an out-of-tree probe, "found by a probe rather than by reasoning" in `dfc150c`'s own words, written after a review challenged `CommentWriter::trailing`'s doc comment — it had stated as self-evident that a parse can never attach two trailing comments to one anchor, and that claim was false for exactly this shape: `TmAnchor::Tapes` and `TmAnchor::Start` are each named from a family of lines rather than one, so a duplicate `tapes` or `start` line attached a second trailing comment to the same anchor, and the `" ; "` join is not a fixed point when a body is empty. The correctness bug underneath — a second `tapes` or `start` line silently overwriting the first — was found on the way to the fix, not by the fix's own test suite.

##### FOUR TIMES A GREEN TEST STRUCTURALLY COULD NOT REACH THE CASE THAT WOULD HAVE FALSIFIED IT, AND EACH TIME IT LOOKED COMPREHENSIVE BECAUSE IT NAMED EVERY VARIANT

This is the most valuable thing on the branch, so it is recorded as four instances and one general form.

1. **The round-trip property appended its generated comments after a fixed skeleton.** So every comment it drew landed on `TmAnchor::Eof`, and the property never met a `tape` line at all. It was strengthened to range densely over every anchor and both `own_line` values **because a review said it was weak**, and it went RED on the first run of the strengthened form — against real, previously-untested printer behaviour rather than a generator artifact. That red is the false round-trip guarantee above.

2. **The same property emits exactly one `tapes` line and one `start` line per document, and still does today.** So no case it can draw contains the duplicate, and strengthening it in the first direction did not reach this: the generator would have had to gain the ability to write a second line in either family before the anchor-family defect could appear to it at all — and nothing on this branch gave it that ability. The property never met this case; the defect above was found by a probe built outside it, not by any strengthening of it.

3. **A `.tm` emission test used a header-less fixture, so `write_header` was never called by the test that appeared to cover printing.** Five of the six `TmDirective` variants — `Version`, `Encoding`, `Width`, `Slots`, `Result` — were parsed by a test and printed by none. The same test also asserted only that each comment's text appeared SOMEWHERE in the whole document, so moving a comment onto a neighbouring anchor left it green; it now compares the entire printed output against a frozen expected string in one `assert_eq!`, which pins placement, indentation and ordering at once, and a second test gives every directive variant a comment against `write_header`'s actual fixed order.

4. **An `.asm` fixture put every whole-line comment above a `result` line or a label line**, each of which drains `pending` before any instruction is reached. So the ordinary case — a whole-line comment directly above an unlabeled instruction — was untested, in a fixture whose entire purpose was to reach every `AsmAnchor` variant. It now carries a second instruction with a comment directly above it and no label or directive between, asserting `AsmAnchor::Instr(1)` so the index cannot be a hardcoded `0`.

**THE GENERAL FORM: coverage is a property of a fixture's SHAPE, not of the list of things it mentions.** All four of these tests named the variants they were supposed to cover. The generator drew from every anchor; the emission test had a comment for each; the asm fixture listed `Result`, `Label`, `Instr` and `Eof` by name. What none of them had was a document whose shape put a comment anywhere but the end, or a second `tapes` line, or a header, or an instruction with nothing above it. **512 passing cases said nothing, twice**: the same property, at the same `ProptestConfig::with_cases(512)`, was green while blind to the duplicate `tapes` line AND green while blind to a printer that stably dropped every comment. The number of documents was never the variable.

##### THE STOPPING RULE IS SHARPER THAN "THE SABOTAGE REDDENED IT", AND THE SHARPER FORM IS WHAT EXPOSED AN ASSERTION THAT COULD NOT FAIL

**A sabotage that reddens an assertion proves less than a sabotage that reddens one assertion while leaving another green.** The first shows a test can fail. The second shows WHICH test carries the weight, and that its neighbours are not carrying it for it. Three on this branch, each applied, measured and reverted:

- **Removing `write_header`'s call reddens the header assertion and nothing else.** The case aborts there, and the machine is built from `tapes`, `start` and the states, which still print.
- **No-op'ing `CommentWriter::own_line` and `CommentWriter::trailing` reddens the survival assertion while byte-level idempotence stays GREEN.** A printer that stably drops every comment prints the same bytes twice, so idempotence is structurally blind to it.
- **Dropping the `accept` keyword reddens the machine assertion while idempotence is likewise blind.**

**The middle one is what forced the survival assertion to exist.** The property had excluded `comments` from its comparison entirely, so a printer that stably dropped every comment satisfied all three of its assertions. `is_sub_multiset` closes that — a SUB-MULTISET rather than a subset, because two comments with identical text are two obligations for the printer to preserve, and set containment is satisfied by one copy surviving while the other silently vanishes.

**And the assertion it replaced could not fail at all.** The property compared `parse_tm_full` of the twice-printed text against `parse_tm_full` of the once-printed text — but once byte idempotence holds, those are the same string fed to a pure function, so every field agrees by construction. Nothing then related the printed output to the ORIGINAL parse in any way; a printer that stably dropped the whole header would have satisfied it too. The assertions now relate the reparse back to the parse of the source the generator actually wrote.

##### FOUR SENTENCES IN THE DESIGN DOCUMENT WERE FALSE, AND EACH WAS WRITTEN WHILE CORRECTING THE PREVIOUS ONE

§2.4 of the design is one short section, and it was wrong four times in sequence with every correction introducing the next error:

1. The guarantee was stated as the strict round trip `parse_tm_full(print_tm_doc(d)) == d`. False, for the reason in the first section above.
2. Correcting that, the replacement said the document round trip *"does hold from the first print onward"*, comparing the once-printed text with the twice-printed one. A tautology, as the section above records.
3. Correcting THAT, the paragraph read *"the comments do not [survive]"* — which says comments may be lost, the exact opposite of what this whole slice guarantees. The distinction it was missing is the direction: survival holds, equality does not.
4. And the paragraph explaining the duplicate-line defect said the sequence stabilised *"only from the third print"*, counting the first print that equals its predecessor rather than the number of distinct values. Hand reconstruction gives exactly two, for `Start` as well as for `Tapes` and for any number of empty trailing comments.

A fifth in the same section: **one sabotage was credited with proving three assertions, and it reddens exactly one of them** — the rule of the section above, broken inside the paragraph that states it.

**AND THE SAME FALSE SENTENCE WAS FIXED IN THE SPEC AND LEFT STANDING IN THE PLAN, FROM WHICH AN IMPLEMENTER INHERITED IT INTO SHIPPED CODE.** §2.4's clean-parse clause argued that a document carrying diagnostics reprints to text that parses clean, so its round trip returns an empty `diagnostics` and fails equality — an argument from a comparison the property does not perform. The real reason is different and stronger: every diagnostic under the TM module is `Severity::Error`, so any diagnostic at all leaves `machine: None`, `print_tm_doc` returns `None` through its `?`, and the guard is load-bearing **against a panic** rather than against a failed comparison. That correction was applied to the spec and not to the plan's Task 8, which stated the identical false mechanism; Task 8's implementer inherited it, wrote it into the property's doc comment, and it shipped until a review checked it in one line. **A class fixed in one document and not in its neighbour** — the failure this file already carries a diagnosis of, committed again on the branch that was reading it.

##### WHAT STAYS OPEN

- **λ gains no comment syntax, and that is a property rather than a gap.** Its text form has no comment token at all, so there is nothing to retain and nothing to add here. It is why this slice is two forms and not three.
- **Comment placement WITHIN a line is not preserved.** The body is trimmed and reprinted as `; body`, so `;x` and `;    x` come back alike and column is not recorded anywhere. **That is what makes the round trip a fixed point rather than a best effort**, and it is a choice rather than a limitation waiting to be fixed.
- **Blank lines are not preserved.** The printer decides where those go, as it always has. Only comments are recovered.
- **CLOSED — `redextape fmt` now accepts `.tm` and `.asm` alongside `.rxt`.** This bullet named it as the natural follow-on once comment retention made it possible without data loss; it has since been designed, planned, implemented and merged as branch `cli-fmt-tm-asm`. See the entry at the end of this file for what it covers and what stays open.
- **The obligation `CommentWriter`'s doc states for a third anchor type is prose, not a gate.** Nothing mechanical stops a future instantiation whose anchor variants name a family of lines, which is exactly the shape that produced the defect above.
- **CLOSED — PR B is the `redextape-lsp` crate, and it shipped.** This was PR A of a two-PR design, and it read "The `redextape-lsp` crate is PR B, and it has no plan yet" until PR B had one. It has since been planned, implemented, reviewed and merged as branch `redextape-lsp-crate`; see the entry below for what it covers and what it leaves open. **The bolded lead says the closure first**, on the rule the very next bullet in this same list already states in full and this file has been caught by more than once: a bullet under a WHAT STAYS OPEN heading is read by its first clause, and burying the fact that PR B now exists inside a sentence that still opens on "no plan yet" would leave a scanning reader with the stale half.
- **CLOSED BEFORE MERGE — `parse_tm_full`'s six hand-rolled copies of "content up to the first `;`" now go through `comments::content_before_comment`.** It is left in this list rather than moved out of it because the finding, the reason it was deferred, and the reason that reversed are one story; what follows is its history. **The bolded lead said the opposite until a review pointed out that a bullet under a WHAT STAYS OPEN heading is read by its first clause**, and burying `CLOSED` forty per cent into a long paragraph leaves a scanning reader with the false half. The original description: `parse_tm_full` re-derived "content up to the first `;`" six times over, independently of `comments::split_trailing`. `parse_cells`, `HeaderParts::directive`, `parse_rule_line` and three sites inside `parse_tm_full` itself each call `.split(';').next()` by hand to strip a trailing comment before reading the content that precedes it, rather than going through the one shared splitter `attach` already uses for the comment side of the same line. `parse_asm_full` does not have this shape today, and **it carried the seventh copy until this branch folded it.** Before the comment-retention task it spelled the same thing character-for-character; that task replaced it with a single `split_trailing` call feeding both halves, because it needed the comment half for the first time and a second independent split would have been the duplication being described here. So the pre-branch tree held seven copies, this branch folded the asm one as a side effect of the feature, and the six named above were folded last. The six TM sites and `split_trailing` agree today because both split on the first `;`, but nothing enforces that agreement; a change to either side (an escaped `;` in a comment body, say) could desynchronize what a line's content is taken to be from what its comment is taken to be, with no test positioned to catch the drift since the six sites predate this branch and comment recovery only reads their output after the fact. **CLOSED before merge, at the repository owner's call, and the measurement is why it was cheap.** The six spellings are provably interchangeable rather than merely agreeing in practice: `str::split` always yields at least one item, so each site's `unwrap_or("")` arm is unreachable, and both forms answer with the prefix before the first `;` or the whole string when there is none. All six now call `comments::content_before_comment`, which is `split_trailing`'s first half trimmed — so a line's content and that same line's comment are derived from one function for both grammars, which is what `parse_asm_full` already did. `git grep "split(';')" crates/redextape-core/src` matches exactly one line afterwards, inside the new function's own doc comment explaining what it replaced. The workspace suite is unchanged at 1403 passed — **and that figure proves less than the sentence here first claimed.** It read "the property that matters for a fold justified on equivalence: not that the tests still pass, but that not one expected value moved". Since the two spellings are extensionally equal on every input, no expected value *could* have moved, so the count has no discriminating power whatever over the equivalence claim it was offered for. What it does rule out is a mechanical slip across six edits — the wrong receiver threaded at one site — which is a real property and a different one. **This file's own entry above documents four cases of a measurement credited with more than it can see, and this is the fifth, written while closing the branch that documents them.**

#### THE LANGUAGE SERVER SHIPS DIAGNOSTICS AND FORMATTING FOR ALL FOUR TEXT FORMS OVER STDIO, AND THREE OF THE BRANCH'S OWN REVIEW FINDINGS WERE TESTS WRITTEN TO LOOK THOROUGH THAT STRUCTURALLY COULD NOT HAVE FAILED (2026-09-05, branch `redextape-lsp-crate`, `2ea57a4..da277ee`, 17 commits, plus the entry commit)

Design: [`../specs/2026-09-04-redextape-lsp-design.md`](../specs/2026-09-04-redextape-lsp-design.md). Plan: [`2026-09-05-redextape-lsp-crate.md`](2026-09-05-redextape-lsp-crate.md).

PR B of the two-PR design the entry above opened, and the half that makes PR A's comment retention reachable from an editor rather than only from a test. `redextape-lsp` is a new workspace crate: a stdio binary serving diagnostics (push, `publishDiagnostics`) and whole-document formatting for `.rxt`, `.rxlambda`, `.tm` and `.asm` over the Language Server Protocol, wired into Neovim by four lines appended to `plugin/redextape.lua`.

**The crate is split so that `lsp-server` — the transport — is confined to `main.rs`, and that is checked mechanically rather than asserted** (figure below). Everything else is `Server::handle(&mut self, RequestObject) -> Vec<Outgoing>`, a pure function from one client message and the server's own state to the messages that go back — no stdio, no threads, no channels — which is what lets the crate's tests call it directly and is what holds the workspace's 90%-line coverage floor with a new crate in the tree. `gen-lsp-types` supplies both the payload types and the JSON-RPC envelope (`RequestObject`/`ResponseObject`), so the pure half never names `lsp-server` at all. Dispatch is a four-arm match on the `languageId` Neovim already sends — the same four filetypes `plugin/redextape.lua` already registers — with an unrecognised language answered empty rather than guessed. Formatting is `print ∘ parse` for all four forms: `.rxt` and `.rxlambda` through their existing printers, `.tm` and `.asm` through PR A's `print_tm_doc`/`print_asm_doc`, which is why formatting these two forms was unsafe before that PR landed and is safe now that it has. Position encoding is negotiated per the design's §4 — `utf-8` when the client offers it, `utf-16` otherwise, and Neovim offers `utf-8` — and the one test that earns its place there formats `λ` on its own line: two bytes, one UTF-16 code unit, one codepoint, three different numbers for one character under the two encodings.

**Three of this branch's own review findings were tests written to look thorough that structurally could not have failed, and that is this branch's most transferable lesson.** `did_close` originally hand-built its `publishDiagnostics` notification instead of calling `Server::publish`, so `documents.close()` was exercised by the test that names it but never verified by it — the hand-built notification answered an empty diagnostics list unconditionally, regardless of whether the document was actually removed, so deleting `documents.close()` from `did_close` would have broken nothing in that test. Routing `did_close` through `publish` instead makes the same assertion DERIVE the empty list from the document map, so a broken `close` now surfaces as the document's real diagnostics coming back rather than as silence. The formatting test's three `.contains()` assertions each matched a comment substring the input fixture already held verbatim, so all three would have passed against a handler that returned `doc.text` unchanged; an `assert_ne!` against that same untouched fixture is what actually requires the printer to have run — it normalises the space before a trailing comment, so only real output can satisfy it. And `tests/protocol.rs` — the one test in the crate that sees the wire, written specifically because a handler test cannot see the framing — never sent an ordinary, id-bearing request: `initialize` and `shutdown` each bypass the main loop's `dispatch`/`to_message` response path through their own dedicated handling, so a version of this test carrying only those two ids never executed the arm that answers a normal request at all. A second document and a `textDocument/formatting` request with a real id closes that gap. All three were plan-authored test code that read as covering the exact case it did not cover.

**Ten further defects sat in the plan's own code blocks rather than its prose, and the gap between the two is why they survived to implementation.** The plan's **Verified fixtures** section exists because an out-of-tree probe ran every fixture STRING through the real parser before any task was dispatched — the first draft had invented all of them and every one was wrong (`_ -> _ R halt` is not TM rule syntax, `result Int` is not a value type, a hand-written `.rxt` "does not format" fixture turned out to format because a type error is not a parse error). No equivalent check ran the plan's CODE blocks through `rustc` before execution began, so a `use` path that does not resolve or a field access that does not match the real struct shape was caught only once a task actually compiled it: `gen_lsp_types::json_rpc::ErrorCodes` named a path that does not exist (the type is at the crate root); `Diagnostic.message` was assigned a bare `String` where the field is a `Message` enum; `DidChangeTextDocumentParams`'s `uri` was read as a direct field where `VersionedTextDocumentIdentifier` flattens it under `text_document_identifier`; `main.rs` omitted the `drop(connection)` that keeps `io_threads.join()` from hanging forever after `exit`; `Server::formatting` was typed `&mut self` where it mutates nothing; and a Task 4 instruction asked `rustfmt` to decide a re-export merge that `rustfmt.toml`'s absent `imports_granularity` means stable `rustfmt` can never decide on its own. The Neovim verification command in Task 9 named its probe file as a positional argument, which Neovim's `-c` flag always processes AFTER — regardless of where it sits on the command line — so the probe got the built-in `tcl` filetype before the plugin ever loaded; the fix opens the file with `-c 'edit <path>'` after sourcing the plugin instead. `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-09-05-redextape-lsp-crate.md` now records the corrected form of each in place, so a future reader copying a code block from that plan copies the version that compiles rather than rediscovering why it does not.

##### WHAT STAYS OPEN

- No navigation for any form. Go-to-definition on a TM state name is `SourceMap::tm_owner` then `SourceMap::source_span`, both of which already exist; it is a slice of its own.
- `analysis` still drops resolved symbols; every `.rxt` navigation feature waits on that.
- `classify_lambda`/`classify_tm` over *authored* text still do not exist. This slice advertises no semantic tokens, so it does not need them.
- No semantic tokens, deliberately — the four grammars already highlight all four forms in the target editor.
- Incremental text sync, deliberately: `FULL` is what the design chose and why.
- `web/` is not a consumer; the crate layout keeps that option open at no cost.
- **CLOSED — `redextape fmt` now takes `.tm` and `.asm`.** This bullet left the question open, in neither PR; it has since been designed, planned, implemented and merged as branch `cli-fmt-tm-asm`. See the entry at the end of this file.

- **`scripts/check-lua.sh`'s ORIGINAL `GRAMMARS`-to-C-symbol check still has no self-test, and this branch added a self-tested check directly beside it.** The new `FILETYPES`-to-`languageId` check is covered five ways (an agreeing pair accepted, an extra filetype rejected, an extra `languageId` rejected, and a renamed table or reshaped `from_language_id` failing rather than passing on an empty extraction). The older check that this file's own header calls the reason the script exists is covered by none of them — the self-test proves the syntax detector and the new detector detect, and says nothing about the one that guards the silent wrong-colour failure. **It is named here rather than fixed because it predates this branch**, and widening a language-server PR into the grammar gate is how a slice stops being reviewable. The factoring the new check introduced is the shape the old one would reuse.
- **That new check text-scans Rust with `awk`/`sed` rather than parsing it.** A shell gate cannot use `syn`, and this repository has a standing preference for parsing over scanning where a rule can be expressed either way — the nullability-override gate was moved off a text scan for exactly that reason. The mitigation here is that an extraction returning nothing is a failure rather than a pass, which is what the two "renamed table" self-test assertions pin; that closes the vacuous-pass hole, not the general fragility of the scan.
- **`tests/protocol.rs`'s `assert_eq!(reply["id"], 2)` on shutdown asserts `lsp-server`'s behaviour, not this crate's.** `Connection::handle_shutdown` answers the request itself before `dispatch` ever sees it, so `Server::handle`'s own `shutdown` arm is unreachable from the binary and reachable only from a caller that is not `lsp-server` — the wasm path §9 keeps open. Both module docs now record this; the assertion was deliberately left in place, because what it covers (the client gets an answer to id 2) is still worth covering even though the code answering it is the transport crate's.

#### `redextape fmt` LEARNS `.tm` AND `.asm`, THE SNIFFER IS THE PARSERS BECAUSE ONLY ONE OF THEM MAY HOLD AN OPINION ABOUT WHAT A `.tm` FILE IS, AND A VERIFICATION COMMAND'S OWN CORRECTION WAS ITSELF BLIND, IN A DIFFERENT DIRECTION, FOR TWO TASKS (2026-09-05, branch `cli-fmt-tm-asm`, 19 commits in the anchored range `7b4a1ff..748d5e6`, plus the entry and whole-branch-review-fix commits that follow it)

Design: [`../specs/2026-09-05-cli-fmt-tm-asm-design.md`](../specs/2026-09-05-cli-fmt-tm-asm-design.md). Plan: [`2026-09-05-cli-fmt-tm-asm.md`](2026-09-05-cli-fmt-tm-asm.md).

The follow-on both merged LSP entries named, closed: PR A's comment retention made a `.tm`/`.asm` round trip lossless enough to format, and this slice wires `fmt` to the two forms it could not touch before. A new `Form` type in `crates/redextape-cli/src/form.rs` names the three text forms `fmt` and `run` both read — `Rxt`, `Tm`, `Asm` — and the extension table that used to live only in `run.rs` moves there, so both commands read one table instead of keeping a second copy in agreement by hand. `Form::resolve` gives the precedence: an explicit `--form` wins over the path's extension, the extension wins over anything else, and for stdin only — where there is no extension to ask — content decides through `Form::sniff`; a bare `Rxt` default closes every case that answers none of the above. `fmt.rs`'s dispatch grew two arms alongside the existing `.rxt` call: `Tm` and `Asm` each go through `parse_tm_full`/`parse_asm_full` and `print_tm_doc`/`print_asm_doc`, the pair PR A shipped, with a `None` payload rendering the document's own diagnostics and failing exactly the way an unparsable `.rxt` file already does. `--width` is a line budget the `.rxt` printer alone reads; the two artifact printers lay out from their own content, so an explicit `--width` on either is refused — in `run`'s own voice, the same way `run` already refuses `--backend` on an artifact — rather than silently accepted and ignored, which would tell a user asking for a specific width that they got one.

##### THE SNIFFER IS THE PARSERS, NOT A PATTERN SET

`Form::sniff` holds no patterns at all: it runs `parse_tm_full` and asks whether a machine came back, then `parse_asm_full` and asks whether a program did, behind one guard for content that is only whitespace — the single case the two front ends' acceptance genuinely overlaps on, and the only case a precedence rule would have had to arbitrate. `plugin/redextape.lua` already sniffs `.tm` and `.asm` buffers by content, in Lua, over sixty buffer lines rather than whole stdin — and a second pattern set in Rust would be one rule in two languages with no gate able to hold them in step, because the two sniffers have different inputs and different fallbacks. Trial parsing has no rule to duplicate: the parser *is* the definition of the language, so the CLI and the plugin cannot disagree about what a `.tm` file is, because only one of them holds an opinion about it at all. **And a correct pattern rule was not writable anyway** — the obvious asm signal, a `result <Type>` line, is optional, and a checked-in fixture `run_asm` already exercises is two indented mnemonics with no header, no `result` and no label; a header-based sniffer would have missed its own test fixture. The cost is real and named rather than overlooked: sniffing runs up to two extra parses through the real front ends, and formatting parses the chosen content again once a form is settled on.

##### A VERIFICATION COMMAND'S OWN CORRECTION WAS ITSELF BLIND, IN A DIFFERENT DIRECTION, AND HID A RED SUITE FOR TWO TASKS

Task 1 found that `redextape-cli` is bin-only — a `[[bin]]` and no `[lib]` — so `cargo test -p redextape-cli --lib` matches nothing and reports zero tests, a green result reading exactly like a passing suite. The plan's correction was `cargo test -p redextape-cli --bin redextape`, and that command was itself blind in a different direction: it runs the binary's own unit tests and silently excludes everything under `crates/redextape-cli/tests/`, `trycmd` transcripts included. Adding `--form` changed `fmt --help`'s output and staled `tests/cmd/fmt_help.stdout`; from that commit onward `cargo test -p redextape-cli` exited 101, and nothing noticed for two tasks, because the pre-commit hook does not run tests at all — every task in between was verifying with a command structurally unable to see the failure. Two confident readings of the crate's test health, wrong in two different directions. The plan now names the fix in place of the command it replaced: `cargo nextest run -p redextape-cli`, which runs unit and integration tests together and is what this entry's own VERIFICATION block uses below, and the stale golden was regenerated with `TRYCMD=overwrite cargo test -p redextape-cli --test cli`. A later task then pinned the property the two commands' agreement had only ever been assumed for — `crates/redextape-cli/tests/form_agreement.rs` drives `run --backend` and `fmt --width` refusals from one classification table over six filenames, so `run` and `fmt` disagreeing about what a file is would now surface as a failing test rather than as two hand-kept copies quietly drifting apart.

##### THE WHOLE-BRANCH REVIEW FOUND TWO CLAIMS ABOUT THE CODE THAT THE CODE DID NOT SUPPORT, AND THE BETTER FIX FOR ONE OF THEM WAS TO MAKE THE CLAIM TRUE

Nine task reviews passed. The whole-branch review then returned two Important findings, both
documentation-against-code divergences spanning tasks, and neither visible to a diff-scoped review.

**`run` did not call `is_artifact`, and three documents said it did** — the method's own doc comment,
the design, and this entry. `run` asked the same question a different way, `Option::is_some` on
`from_extension`'s result, so "what counts as an artifact" was answered twice in two independently
written spellings that agreed only because `from_extension` never returns `Rxt` — an invariant held
by two `unreachable!` calls rather than by the type. **The fix was to make the sentence true rather
than to correct it**: collapsing `run`'s `Option<Form>` into a `Form` gives `is_artifact` its second
consumer, makes `run`'s dispatch total over the enum, and deletes one of the two panics. Behaviour was
held by differential rather than by argument — a binary built before the change and one built after
produce byte-identical exit status, stdout and stderr across fourteen cells, and no `run` test was
edited.

**And the agreement test asserted a boolean where the design asked for a form.** Its table read
`(filename, expected_form)`, but the only use of the second column was `expected != "rxt"` — so
`("p.asm", "asm")` and `("p.asm", "tm")` were the same test, and a defect mapping `.asm` onto
`Form::Tm` would have left the file green. The file whose whole purpose is the half of the
anti-divergence property a compiler cannot check had an inert column, and it was the column naming
the thing the file said it pinned. Each helper now parses the distinguishing noun its command prints
back into a form; the sabotage that proves it — remapping `.asm` to `Tm` in the shared table — fails
the new version on `run, p.asm: left Some("tm"), right Some("asm")` and passed the old one.

**Both are the shape this file keeps recording: a sentence that was true when written and was not
re-read against the code after the code moved.** The `is_artifact` claim was even corrected once, in
the plan, when the task boundary that produced it was fixed — and the correction never propagated to
the method's doc, the design, or this entry.

##### WHAT STAYS OPEN

- **`.rxlambda` is not formatted.** The CLI has no λ surface at all — `run` knows only `tm` and `asm`, and `crates/redextape-cli/src/emit.rs` still records that a `.rxlambda` file "stays read-only from the command line". Teaching `fmt` alone would create a new asymmetry — formatted by `fmt`, untouchable by `run` — rather than close the existing one. A follow-on slice should give the CLI a λ surface properly, across the subcommands that should have one, instead of bolting it onto whichever command is being edited.
- **`run` gains no `--form` and no sniffing, deliberately.** Sharing the whole resolution *policy* between `run` and `fmt` would change a shipped command's behaviour as a side effect of a formatting change — `cat p.tm | redextape run -` would begin sniffing stdin, where today it is unconditionally `.rxt`. `run` and `fmt` share the extension table and `is_artifact` only; the policy stays two callers, one shape apiece.
- **Sniffing costs up to two extra parses, and the format that follows parses again.** Chosen rather than overlooked: not worth optimising against the size of input that arrives through a pipe, and threading a parsed document out of resolution would couple identity to parsing for no real gain.

**AND THE TWO GIT FIGURES NAME A SHA BECAUSE ONLY THEY CAN MOVE — THE RULE, NOT THE NUMBER.** Writing this entry is itself a commit, and so is any later correction to it, so a count measured "at the branch head" is false the moment it is written down; the previous entry in this file chased that and had to be re-anchored. What ends the regress is that `main..19b5cda` is a fixed range whose answer does not change, plus one property a reader can check rather than trust: **every commit after `19b5cda` on this branch touches only Markdown** — verify with `git diff --name-only 19b5cda..HEAD | grep -v '\.md$'`, which prints nothing. **AND THE ESCAPE HATCH WENT STALE BEFORE ANY OF THE FIGURES IT PROTECTS DID.** This block was anchored at `748d5e6` and rested on the same property, spelled against that commit.
