Both were read off the same `TOTAL` row of one honest run — the percentage from the REGION column, the counts from the LINE column. `--fail-under-lines` gates lines, so the line column is the one this row is for, and the figures above are that column's own percentage beside its own counts, which a reader can now reconcile: `1 - 1150/23118` = 95.03%. **A figure can be measured, current, and still false, when the label names a different column from the number.**

#### THE LANGUAGE SERVER LEARNS TO NAVIGATE `.tm` AND `.asm`, AND THE SAME SPAN DEFECT SHIPPED TWICE — ONCE IN EACH PARSER, THE SECOND TIME UNDER A PARAGRAPH THIS ENTRY WROTE ASSERTING THE SECOND PARSER WAS IMMUNE, BOTH TIMES BECAUSE EVERY FIXTURE WAS A PRINTER LAYOUT WHILE THE POPULATION THIS FEATURE EXISTS FOR IS HAND-WRITTEN FILES; A MISSING RE-EXPORT PASSED EVERY IN-CRATE TEST BECAUSE `super::*` CANNOT SEE ONE, AND THE COMMAND WRITTEN TO PROVE THE FEATURE IN A REAL EDITOR COULD NOT HAVE OBSERVED IT — THE CORRECTION TO SLICE 1'S BLIND HARNESS WAS ITSELF BLIND IN THREE NEW WAYS (2026-09-06, branch `lsp-navigation`, 31 commits in the anchored range `64c1164..7b74f53`, which is all of them)

Design: [`../specs/2026-09-06-lsp-navigation-design.md`](../specs/2026-09-06-lsp-navigation-design.md). Plan: [`2026-09-06-lsp-navigation-tm-asm.md`](2026-09-06-lsp-navigation-tm-asm.md).

PR A of a two-PR design. `textDocument/definition`, `textDocument/references` and `textDocument/documentSymbol` for `.tm` and `.asm` buffers, served from a name-span index the two artifact parsers build while they are already scanning. A new `redextape-core` module `nav.rs` owns `NameIndex` — every name occurrence in one document, each a `Definition` or a `Reference { def: Option<usize> }`, references linked to the definition they name by INDEX rather than by string, so a shadowed name resolves to the binding actually in scope rather than to whichever definition happens to share its spelling. **The module holds no grammar at all**: it cannot answer "is this a state?", because the parsers are the only things in the crate that know where a name begins, and the server is the only thing that knows which language the buffer is. `parse_tm_nav` and `parse_asm_nav` return `(Document, NameIndex)` and mirror the `print_tm`/`print_tm_mapped` pair the same files already have, with `parse_tm_full`/`parse_asm_full` pinned by test as exactly the document half of each. `redextape-lsp` gained the inverse position conversion it had been missing — `LineIndex::offset`, `Position` → byte offset — three capability entries and three dispatch arms. `Server::handle` is still a pure function of one client message and the server's own state; nothing here touches transport, and `lsp-server` is still named in `main.rs` and nowhere else (figure below).

**An index outlives a failed parse, and that is the difference from the comment recovery the previous slice's PR A shipped.** Comment recovery is all-or-nothing across a document, because comments feed the printer and there is nothing to print for a file with an error. Navigation is per-occurrence: a jump from a `goto` to its `state` is right on its own terms, and nothing else in the file has to be true for it to be the right answer. A `.tm` file with an unknown `goto` target has `machine: None` and a diagnostic, and go-to-definition still works inside it — which is the case navigation is worth most in, because a file under active editing is a broken file.

##### A REAL DEFECT SHIPPED IN THE PLAN'S OWN CODE AND NO FIXTURE IN THE PLAN COULD SEE IT

`parse_asm_nav`'s label-operand span was computed with a term that measured what comment-stripping had removed from the **end** of the line. A span is measured from the line's start and a comment is removed from its end, so any offset derived from that strip pushes the span rightwards — into the comment. `jmp f ; go back` reported the `k` of `back` as the reference to `f`, and go-to-definition on a jump in any commented file landed on nothing or on the wrong thing.

**Not one fixture in the plan had a trailing comment.** Every `.asm` fixture in that file was a layout the printer emits — labels at column 0, no comments — because that is what every other test in the file needed, and the fixtures were reused. The population this feature exists for is the opposite one: navigation is for a file a human is editing, and hand-written `.asm` carries trailing comments constantly. The suite was green and structurally could not have been anything else.

**The fix asserts a general invariant instead of a table of offsets:** every occurrence's span must slice back to its own name — `src.get(occ.span.start..occ.span.end) == Some(occ.name)` — walked over every occurrence the fixture produces. A table of expected columns would have caught this bug and nothing else; the invariant catches every bug of its shape, including ones no fixture anticipates. The fixture was then widened to the cases the plan's own had missed: an indented label, a trailing comment on every line, and all three label-taking mnemonics rather than one, `jz` putting its label second where `jmp` and `call` put it first.

**AND THE SENTENCE THAT STOOD HERE WAS FALSE, IN THE PARAGRAPH ANNOUNCING THE LESSON IT VIOLATED.** It read: *"`.tm` was never affected — its arithmetic uses a leading pad, not a trailing difference."* The leading pad is real in the code and **dead in the data**. `trimmed_at` returns how far into its argument the trimmed text begins, and both `.tm` name sites fed it `comments::content_before_comment(..)`, which is `split_trailing(..).0.trim()` — an already-trimmed string, whose pad is structurally zero. So every `.tm` name span was correct only when exactly one space followed its keyword. Measured at the whole-branch review, all parsing clean with zero diagnostics: `start  scan` gave a span slicing to `" sca"`, and `   state   scan:` one slicing to `"  sc"`. `goto` was the sole survivor, because it alone **was** fed un-trimmed text and so was, before the fix, the only one of the four call sites with a live pad. After it, all three `.tm` sites are fed un-trimmed text; the fourth, the `.asm` label, still passes fully-trimmed text and is correct only because its `indent` term carries the whole offset independently.

**It is the same defect as the `.asm` one above, in the sibling parser, found by the same reasoning, and the paragraph asserting immunity is what carried it.** The `.asm` half was found because a fixture gained a trailing comment; the `.tm` half survived because its invariant test — the right assertion, every span slicing back to its own name — used a fixture with single spaces throughout. **Printer layout again.** The population is hand-written files and a human aligns state names, so the one spacing no `.tm` fixture in this branch contained is the one every hand-written file has. Eight task reviews passed over it.

Fixed by taking the pad from `comments::split_trailing(..).0`, which removes a trailing comment without touching the leading whitespace the offset is measured from; a comment is stripped from the END, so the two do not interact. The fixture now reads `start  scan`, `   state   scan:` and `goto   scan`, and restoring either old call site reddens it. `trimmed_at`'s doc now names the trap at the definition rather than leaving it to be rediscovered a third time.

**The transferable rule, since this file has now recorded the same shape twice in one branch: a fixture drawn from a printer's output cannot test a hand-writer's input, and "form A is unaffected" is a claim about data flow, not about code shape.** Reading that `.tm` uses a leading pad was true and useless — what mattered was whether anything ever reaches that pad with un-trimmed text.

##### THREE MORE GREEN RESULTS WERE NOT THE COVERAGE THEY LOOKED LIKE, AND IN NONE OF THE THREE COULD THE SUITE HAVE SAID SO

**`references_to_does_not_answer_by_name` used two definitions of DIFFERENT names, which is the one fixture shape that cannot distinguish the two implementations** — under a comment asserting it was the fixture that could. With one definition per name, `link` resolves every reference to that string's unique definition, so a name-matching `references_to` and a link-matching one always agree. Measured rather than reasoned: the old shape PASSES with the sabotage applied. Divergence needs a SHADOWED name — two definitions sharing one string, so that a name match on the second wrongly pulls in a reference that links to the first — and the replacement asserts exactly that, `references_to(1).count() == 0` despite the name matching.

**The obvious covering test for a third sabotage also could not cover.** Dropping `locate`'s language check reddened nothing, as the plan predicted it would not. The first fix was a fixture of arbitrary non-TM text under an unrecognised `languageId` — and that still answered `null` either way, because such text parses to an empty index whether the check is there or not. Only **valid `.tm` text under an unrecognised `languageId`** separates them: with the check, `null`; without it, a real `Location`. A covering test can be wrong about which axis it varies.

**And an in-crate `super::*` test cannot see a missing re-export, which is a narrower fact than the one this paragraph first claimed.** `parse_tm_nav` was added to `tm/syntax.rs` without adding it to `tm.rs`'s `pub use` list, so `redextape_core::tm::parse_tm_nav` — the path `redextape-lsp` was about to call — did not resolve. Both parsers' unit tests reach the function through `super::*`, which works whether or not the re-export exists, so nothing inside `redextape-core` could see it and the crate's own suite stayed green. `crates/redextape-core/tests/nav_reachable.rs` is what sees it: an integration test, compiled as a separate crate that can only reach the public surface, calling both entry points by the exact paths the server uses.

**THE LESSON THIS ENTRY FIRST WROTE DOWN WAS FALSE ABOUT THIS REPOSITORY, AND A FALSE TRANSFERABLE RULE IS WORSE THAN NONE IN A FILE WHOSE PURPOSE IS CARRYING THEM FORWARD.** It read *"a `pub fn` in a private module is not public"*. `tm.rs` declares `pub mod asm_syntax;` and `pub mod syntax;` — on `main` and on this branch — so those modules are not private and the longer path `redextape_core::tm::syntax::parse_tm_nav` resolved the whole time. `crates/redextape-core/tests/tm_comments.rs` already imports through exactly that path. What was actually missing was only the CONVENIENCE re-export that gives the short path, and the failure was never about visibility at all. The accurate rule was sitting two files away the whole time, in `nav_reachable.rs`'s own module doc, correctly stated — the entry generalised past it into something checkable and wrong. **The max-effort review caught it by running `git show main:crates/redextape-core/src/tm.rs`, which is the whole method: a claim about what a path resolves to is answerable by reading the file, and this one was not read.**

##### THE CRLF ROUND TRIP WAS FALSE IN THE PLAN'S OWN STATED INVARIANT, AND WHAT RESOLVED IT WAS READING ANOTHER PROJECT'S SOURCE RATHER THAN RECALLING IT

`LineIndex::offset` was specified as the inverse of the pre-existing `position`, under two requirements that cannot both hold on a CRLF file: a character column past the end of a line clamping BEFORE the `\r`, and `offset(position(o)) == o` for every `o`. `position` already counts a `\r` as line content — `LineIndex::new` records only `\n` positions and the column is the raw byte distance from the line start — so an `offset` that clamped before the `\r` disagreed with its own inverse at the `\n` of every `\r\n` pair. A plan defect rather than an implementer deviation: the plan asserted both.

**It was settled by reading rust-analyzer's `line-index` rather than by recalling what it does.** That crate contains no `\r` handling anywhere: it records only `\n`, computes a column as the raw distance from the line start, and treats a carriage return as ordinary content. **The property is written here and its line count is not**, deliberately — `line-index` is not a dependency of this workspace, so nothing in this tree can hold a figure about it, and an uncheckable number in this file is the failure this file has recorded against itself more than once. The property is checkable by anyone who opens that crate; a count is only checkable against the version that was open at the time. Matching it makes the two functions inverses again and puts this crate on the same rule as the reference implementation of the same conversion, rather than on a rule invented to satisfy whichever of the two requirements was written down second.

##### THE COMMAND WRITTEN TO PROVE THE FEATURE IN A REAL EDITOR COULD NOT HAVE OBSERVED IT, AND THE CORRECTION TO SLICE 1'S BLIND HARNESS WAS ITSELF BLIND IN THREE NEW WAYS

The design predicted no plugin change — `vim.lsp.buf.definition` dispatches off the capabilities the server advertises at `initialize` — and required PR A to confirm that in a real headless Neovim rather than assume it, specifically because slice 1 had recorded a verification command that silently tested the wrong thing. **The prediction was right, and the command written to test it was wrong in three separate ways**, each of which had to be found by running it.

- **It never moves the cursor.** It opens the probe and calls `vim.lsp.buf.definition()` where `:edit` leaves the cursor — line 1, column 0, on the `tapes` keyword, where `null` is the correct answer — then prints the cursor's line, which is the starting line under every implementation, working or broken. The step's own pass condition is *"the definition's line, not the cursor's starting line"*, so the command can neither satisfy it nor distinguish a working feature from a missing one. **The instrument reads the same number for both outcomes**, which is slice 1's failure again, one layer in from where the correction was applied.
- **`cargo build -p redextape-lsp` builds the debug binary and `plugin/redextape.lua` looks for `target/release/redextape-lsp`.** With nothing named `redextape-lsp` on `PATH` — measured, `which redextape-lsp` exits 1 — `server_cmd()` returns `nil`, the plugin emits its "no redextape-lsp binary found" warning, and no client ever attaches. `--release` is what the plugin's own resolution rule requires.
- **`-u NONE` turns filetype detection off, so the `-c` ordering the correction is about cannot matter yet.** `-u NONE` sets `loadplugins=false`, and Neovim's filetype detection lives in a bundled runtime *plugin*; with that unloaded, the plugin's `vim.filetype.add` registers a rule nothing ever triggers. Measured under the corrected `-c 'edit'` ordering: `vim.bo.filetype` is the empty string and `#vim.lsp.get_clients({bufnr=0})` is `0`. Slice 1's fix corrected the ordering trap sitting on top of a harness that was already inert.

**What was run instead, and what makes it evidence.** The runtimepath is pinned to `$VIMRUNTIME` plus this checkout, so no user configuration is reachable; `-c 'filetype on'` restores detection; the plugin is sourced; the probe is opened with `-c 'edit'` after it; and a Lua file that starts no client, registers no autocmd and sets no filetype does the observing. The probe files live outside the tree, at a path with no `/redextape/` component, so the plugin's path fallback cannot fire and its content sniffer has to do the work. **The control is that same command with the `source` line removed**, and it reports `filetype=tcl` — Neovim's own built-in mapping for `.tm`, the collision `plugin/redextape.lua`'s comment names — with zero LSP clients and the cursor where it started. The real run's answers are therefore the plugin's and the server's, not the harness's.

The real run attaches one client named `redextape` and reports `definitionProvider`, `referencesProvider` and `documentSymbolProvider` all `true` from the handshake. On the `.tm` probe, go-to-definition from the `scan` of `goto scan` moves the cursor from `4,35` to `3,6` — `state scan:`, not the `start scan` on line 2 that a string search finds first. Those are `nvim_win_get_cursor`'s coordinates, 1-based line and 0-based column, and so one line above the protocol's own numbering for the same two places. `references` with `includeDeclaration` returns three items and `documentSymbol` returns two flat `[Class]` symbols. **And the `.asm` probe is this branch's own defect, in the editor:** a file with a trailing comment on every line, cursor on the `f` of `jmp<TAB>f ; go back`, jumps to the `f` of the `f:` label — the character the shipped arithmetic would have missed.

**No plugin change was needed, and this entry records that prediction as confirmed rather than as assumed.** `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-09-06-lsp-navigation-tm-asm.md` now carries the command that works in place of the one that could not observe anything, for the reason the previous slice's plan carries its corrections in place: the next reader copies a command, not a caveat.

##### `tests/protocol.rs` GREW THE ONE EXCHANGE A HANDLER TEST STRUCTURALLY CANNOT SEE

Every other test in `redextape-lsp` calls `Server::handle` directly, which is what makes the workspace coverage floor reachable with a new crate in the tree and is also exactly why one test has to spawn the binary: a handler test cannot see the framing, the handshake or the write loop. That test now opens a third document over the wire and asks for a definition in it, so a `Location` has to survive serialization and the framed write loop, and a request answered after three `didOpen` notifications on one connection has to read the document it names. It also asserts `definitionProvider` on the `initialize` reply — the same field a handler test checks on an `InitializeResult` struct, but here as the JSON an editor actually reads, which is what `vim.lsp.buf.definition` dispatches off. Both new assertions were sabotage-run: `definition_provider: None` fails the capability one, and answering `nav.get(i)` instead of the definition it links to fails the position one with `left: Number(3), right: 2`.

##### WHAT STAYS OPEN

- **PR B — `.rxt` navigation.** Needs the binder-resolution pass `analysis` still does not keep, and the AST growing name spans for `Stmt::Let`, `Stmt::Fn` and `Stmt::Assign` — all three carry the statement's span today — and for the two `params: Vec<String>` fields, which carry no spans at all.
- **`.rxlambda` has no navigation and cannot cheaply get any.** `LambdaTerm` is de Bruijn: `Var(u32)` and an `Abs` name hint its own module doc marks print-only. There are no source positions in the term, and adding them means threading spans through an `Rc`-shared type used by `lower`, `decode`, `encode`, `syntax` and `reduce`. Go-to-binder is a real feature and a separate slice.
- **No cross-form navigation.** `SourceMap::tm_owner` returns `None` for any name this lowering never produced — including every name belonging to some other lowering of the same program — and `SourceMap::source_span` returns `None` for a map built by `build` rather than `build_from_program`. An authored `.tm` buffer therefore yields nothing without knowing which `.rxt` produced it and at which encoding. That is a design question, not a coding task.
- **No rename and no `documentHighlight`.** Every occurrence is known once the index exists, so intra-file rename is reachable — but it mutates the buffer, needs `prepareRename`, name validity and collision handling, and is the first thing in this crate that writes rather than answers. `documentHighlight` is the same data as `references` and is the cheapest follow-on named anywhere in this design.
- **`Language::Redextape | Language::Lambda => SymbolKind::Variable` is unreachable today and has no test.** `Language::nav` answers `None` for both forms, so `document_symbol` returns through the `?` before it ever selects a kind. The arm is answered rather than asserted precisely so that PR B adding `.rxt` cannot make it panic — which means PR B is also the moment it becomes reachable and wants a test, and until then it is a line nothing exercises.
- **`tests/protocol.rs` covers `definition` over the wire and not `references` or `documentSymbol`.** Deliberate: what that file exists for is the framing, the handshake and the write loop, and one id-bearing navigation request exercises all three. The two uncovered response shapes are `Vec<Location>` and a `DocumentSymbol` list, both serialized through the same `ResponseObject::from_success` path the covered one uses, and both asserted as JSON by the handler tests. It is named here because "the protocol test covers navigation" is a sentence that is true of one provider out of three.
- **Every existing caller of `parse_tm_full`/`parse_asm_full` now builds an index and throws it away, and the TIME cost of that is below measurement noise while the MEMORY cost is real and unmeasured.** The design argued the cost was "already paid, already accepted" by analogy to `print_tm`, which has always built a `Classified` and discarded it — an argument, not a measurement, and the whole-branch review flagged it as an unquantified regression. Measured since, on a generated 1,377,797-byte machine of 25,000 states, three runs each of `cargo nextest --release`: this branch 428/384/397 ms, `main` in a detached worktree 474/420/424 ms. **The branch is faster on the median, which is the honest way of saying the added work does not register against run-to-run variance at that size.**

**AND THAT MEASUREMENT WAS TRUE, GENERALISED, AND WRONG — IN THE VERY PARAGRAPH CORRECTING SOMEONE ELSE FOR QUOTING A FIGURE WITHOUT A BASELINE.** It measured `.tm` and stated a conclusion about "every existing caller", both forms included. The max-effort review measured `.asm` and found the opposite, which re-measuring confirms: a 377,791-byte, 20,000-label `.asm` file goes `2.37/2.10/2.14 ms` on `main` to `6.87/4.88/4.66 ms` on this branch — **+128% on the median, so the discarded index costs more than the entire parse it rides on.** The two forms differ because `.tm`'s parse does far more work per line for the index to hide behind, and `.asm`'s does almost none. **A baseline fixes the wrong half of the error: the first version had no baseline, the second had one and only one, and a claim about "every caller" needed a measurement per form.** The cost lands on `Language::diagnostics` (every `didChange`), `Language::format` (every save), `redextape-wasm`'s session (every browser edit), and `redextape-cli`'s content sniffer, which calls BOTH parsers on one source purely to test `.is_some()` and so builds and discards two indexes. What is NOT dismissed by that: the same input produces 50,001 `Occurrence`s, each carrying an owned `String`, plus a transient `HashMap` over all of them in `link`, for callers — `redextape fmt`, `Language::diagnostics`, `Language::format` — that never read one. Peak memory was not measured and no caller opts out; `parse_tm` and `parse_asm` remain the tuple-shaped wrappers and are equally affected.

- **Every navigation request re-parses the whole document.** `Language::nav` calls `parse_*_nav` afresh, so a `definition`, a `references` and a `documentSymbol` on one unchanged buffer parse it three times. `textDocumentSync` is `FULL`, so the server already re-parses on every keystroke for diagnostics; caching the index per document version is the obvious next move and is deliberately not in this slice.

- **Find-references from the SECOND of two definitions of one name reports it as unreferenced, and that is left standing on purpose.** `link` points every reference at the FIRST definition of its name, and `definition_of` answers a definition with itself — so with two `f:` labels and one `jmp f`, a cursor on the first gives the jump and a cursor on the second gives nothing. Which of two visually identical lines the caret sits on decides whether a used label looks used, on an `.asm` file with zero diagnostics. **It is also arguably the correct answer:** jumps resolve to the first label, so the second is dead and genuinely has no references; in `.tm` the same shape is a diagnosed error. **What rules out the obvious fix is PR B.** Canonicalising every definition of a name to the first is exactly wrong for `.rxt`, where two definitions of `x` are two bindings with two separate reference sets — the case §2.4 builds the whole index-linked design around. A correct fix needs a per-language notion of whether a duplicate name is one entity or two, which is real design work for a case that is an error in one form and dead code in the other. Filed rather than fixed, with the reasoning, so PR B decides it with the shadowing rules in hand instead of inheriting a rule it must unpick.

- **`scripts/check-lua.sh`'s `GRAMMARS`-to-C-symbol check still has no self-test.** Carried forward from slice 1, still out of scope for a language-server PR, and still the shape the `FILETYPES` check beside it already has.
- **Nine Minor findings were recorded across the task reviews: two are now closed and seven stand, none of them changing an answer the server gives. The seventh standing one is the bullet directly above this one; the other six are enumerated here.** The count is stated because a count is a claim like a number is — and the first attempt at this bullet said *five* against nine recorded, while the correction to it said *seven stand* above a list of six, because the arm in the bullet above was not counted as being in it. **A count is only a claim if the reader can check it, so this one names where every member is.** **Closed, and only one of the two by a fix:** `trimmed_at`'s doc omitted its non-underflow property — mis-triaged as cosmetic, since its subject is the function the Critical above lived in, and it now names the trap. The other was closed by observation rather than by an edit: the note that sabotage 2's captured output on `LineIndex::offset` showed only the column assertion failing, `assert_eq!` being fail-fast, so that run is not evidence for the round-trip half of its own claim — the two halves have shared one test since `ac937a3`, an implementation commit, and nothing in this round touched `position.rs`. **Standing, six:** the duplicated `let indent = …` in `parse_asm_nav`'s label and instruction branches, which could hoist once per loop iteration. And: `position.rs`'s CRLF round-trip loop runs only `Encoding::Utf8`, so the {CRLF, UTF-16} pair is unexercised — zero risk while the fixture is pure ASCII and `len_utf16` equals the byte length, and a real gap in the stated "every `o`, CRLF included" property the day that arm is edited. No test asserts that a duplicate `state <name>:` records a SECOND definition, which §3.1 claims and which the structurally identical unknown-goto path does cover. `definition_in_a_broken_file_still_answers` checks only `range.start` where its sibling checks the whole range and the URI. The `references` tests cover three cells of the (declaration/reference × include/exclude) square and not `(reference, true)`. And `document_symbol` re-derives the document, its language and its index rather than sharing `locate`'s — defensible, because `locate` also computes a cursor offset this handler has no position to compute one from.

**THE COVERAGE ROW IS THE LINE COLUMN'S OWN PERCENTAGE BESIDE THE LINE COLUMN'S OWN COUNTS, WHICH IS THE CORRECTION THE ENTRY ABOVE THIS ONE HAD TO MAKE.** `--fail-under-lines` gates lines, and `llvm-cov`'s `TOTAL` row carries a region percentage, a function percentage and a line percentage side by side; taking the percentage from one column and the counts from another produces three honest numbers that do not reconcile. These do: `1 - 1148/24012` = 95.22%. The same run's per-file rows put `redextape-core/src/nav.rs` at 100.00% lines (119 lines, 0 missed), `redextape-lsp/src/position.rs` at 100.00% (137 lines, 0 missed) and `redextape-lsp/src/lib.rs` at 98.58% (565 lines, 8 missed).

**THE TWO GIT FIGURES NAME A SHA BECAUSE ONLY THEY CAN MOVE — THE RULE, NOT THE NUMBER.** Writing this entry is itself a commit, and so is any later correction to it, so a count measured "at the branch head" is false the moment it is written down; two earlier entries in this file chased that and had to be re-anchored. What ends the regress is that `main..7b74f53` is a fixed range whose answer does not change, plus one property a reader can check rather than trust: **every commit after `7b74f53` on this branch touches only Markdown** — verify with `git diff --name-only 7b74f53..HEAD | grep -v '\.md$'`, which prints nothing. So the measured figures above are invariant under everything that has landed since, and only the two git figures move. The property is *Markdown* and not *`docs/`*, for the reason an earlier entry records: a correction to a crate README sits outside `docs/` and would falsify the narrower spelling while leaving every figure untouched.

**THIS BLOCK HAS BEEN RE-ANCHORED THREE TIMES, AND EVERY TIME THE PROPERTY WORKED.** The third was the max-effort review's fix round, which changed both crates. It first stood at `4fffa4f`. The whole-branch review found the Critical above and its fix changed `crates/redextape-core/src/tm/`; the re-review then found four of that fix's own prose corrections wrong about the code, and repairing two of them meant editing doc comments — **which live in `.rs` files**. Each time the grep began printing source paths where the paragraph promised nothing, and each time that is the property DOING ITS JOB: it is a tripwire, and a tripwire that fires is not a tripwire that failed. **A draft of this paragraph called those two breakages a reason to abandon the shape, and replaced it with "the figures were measured at the head as written" — which is the regress this whole block exists to end, since writing that sentence moves the head.** The shape stays; only the anchor moves.

**WHAT THE SECOND BREAKAGE ACTUALLY TAUGHT IS NARROWER AND WORTH MORE: A COMMENT CAN MOVE A COVERAGE FIGURE.** The line total went from 23,743 to 23,749 across a change that added no code, because `llvm-cov`'s line column counts source lines in the coverage map and a six-line comment is six of them. So "documentation-only" does not imply "figure-preserving" here, and the Markdown-only property is the right tripwire precisely because it fires on a `.rs` doc-comment edit that a `docs/`-only rule would have waved through. The percentage was unmoved at 95.15% and the missed count unmoved at 1,152; had only the percentage been quoted, nothing would have looked different and the denominator would have been silently stale.

**AND `redextape-core` STILL HAS ZERO DEPENDENCIES, WHICH IS WHAT ALLOWED `nav.rs` TO BE A NEW MODULE THERE RATHER THAN A NEW CRATE.** `cargo tree -p redextape-core --edges normal` prints one line, the crate itself. `nav.rs` uses `std::collections::HashMap` and `crate::Span`, and nothing further.

#### `.rxt` GETS PARSE RECOVERY SO A BROKEN FILE ANSWERS A TREE AND EVERY PARSE ERROR RATHER THAN NONE AND ONLY THE FIRST, THE PLAN'S OWN `parse_program` DROPPED THE CHECK THAT ITS LOOP ACTUALLY REACHED END OF INPUT, AND AN EXHAUSTIVE SWEEP FOUND IT DELETING SOURCE FROM 3,724 OF 30,941 SHORT TOKEN SEQUENCES WHILE 1,507 TESTS STAYED GREEN — FOUND BY A REVIEW THAT RAN `format` OVER GENERATED INPUT RATHER THAN READING THE DIFF (2026-09-07, branch `rxt-parse-recovery`, `fe3d34b..1b46a8b`, 17 commits, plus the entry and whole-branch-review-fix commits that follow it)

Design: [`../specs/2026-09-07-rxt-parse-recovery-design.md`](../specs/2026-09-07-rxt-parse-recovery-design.md). Plan: [`2026-09-07-rxt-parse-recovery.md`](2026-09-07-rxt-parse-recovery.md).

**PR B1 of the LSP track's third slice.** The navigation design's own §7 named one remaining PR, ".rxt navigation", and scoped it as span plumbing plus a binder-resolution pass. Working through it found a blocker that design did not see: `.rxt` had no parse recovery at all, while both artifact forms already did, and `nav.rs`'s own module doc states the property navigation is built around — the moment it is worth most is the moment the file is broken, which is what a buffer under active editing is. A `.rxt` index built from the existing `parse` would be empty for exactly the files it exists to serve. This PR clears that blocker without touching `redextape-lsp` at all; B2 is the follow-on that spends it.

`ast::Stmt::Error` and `ast::Expr::Error` now hold the source that did not parse. `parser::parse_recovering` always answers a tree; `parse_full` and `parse` keep answering `None` unless the parse was complete, which is the whole of the contract split and what keeps a lossy tree away from `format` — `format` is `print ∘ parse` and writes straight back over the author's buffer, so a `parse` that ever returned a partial tree would delete the parts of it that did not parse. Recovery itself is per statement: `resync` skips forward to the next `;` or `}` at the brace depth recovery started from, so a `}` closing a block nested inside the failed statement is not mistaken for the end of it; a progress bump guarantees the loop advances even on a token that starts no statement, backed by a hard iteration bound in the same shape `MAX_TOKENS` and `MAX_PARSE_DEPTH` already use; `parse_program` absorbs whatever tokens are left over into a trailing `Stmt::Error` rather than reporting a complete parse while they sit unconsumed; `let` and assignment recover a value that fails to parse into an `Expr::Error`, so the binding under the cursor survives losing only its right-hand side; and an unclosed block keeps the body it already collected — the property §1 of the design says the whole option turns on — instead of discarding the file from the open brace onward, which is the state of every buffer while its author is still inside the function they are writing. `Parser::record` counts every recovery unconditionally and caps what it *records* at `MAX_RECOVERED_DIAGNOSTICS = 100`; recovery does not stop at the cap, because B2's navigation reads the tree and not the diagnostic list, and a file of pure garbage recovering at roughly one construct per token would otherwise push up to `MAX_TOKENS` diagnostics to an editor that re-parses on every keystroke.

##### THE PLAN'S OWN `parse_program` DROPPED THE CHECK THAT MADE THIS SAFE, AND ONLY RUNNING `format` OVER GENERATED INPUT SURFACED IT

Task 3's `parse_program` shipped as `let block = self.parse_block_body(TokenKind::Eof); Program { block }`. The old, fallible version had ended with `self.expect(TokenKind::Eof, ...)?`; when `parse_block_body` became infallible that call was dropped and nothing took its place. `parse_block_body`'s `Tail` arm breaks its loop on the first token that cannot extend the tail expression — not on `close` or on `Eof` — so a program whose tail expression was followed by more tokens left the parser sitting mid-file with `self.recovered` still zero and `record()` never called. `parse_full` therefore answered `Some` for a tree that had lost source, and `format("1 2")` answered `Ok("1\n")` — the trailing `2` deleted outright, with nothing anywhere reporting that it had been. An exhaustive sweep over every token sequence of length ≤ 4 found 3,724 of 30,941 losing source this way, and the whole suite was green at 1,507 tests the entire time the defect was live in the tree.

**What found it was a review that ran `format` over generated input rather than reading the diff.** The code is not visibly wrong — `parse_program` reads as a two-line pass-through over an already-infallible call — and no amount of re-reading it would have surfaced a hole that exists only in the gap between where the loop actually stops and where its one caller assumed it stopped. This is the exact failure the whole design exists to prevent (§1: a lossy tree reaching `format`), reintroduced by the task whose brief opens by naming that as the single point of failure to avoid, and it shipped anyway because the two halves of the guarantee — "the loop stops where the caller expects" and "every exit that does not is covered" — were never restated at the one call site that had no caller of its own to enforce the second half. Fixed in `febe3db`: `parse_program` now checks `self.peek().kind != TokenKind::Eof` after the call and, if so, absorbs everything remaining into a trailing `Stmt::Error` and calls `record()` on the way — the check the old `expect(...)?` used to make, restated as an absorb-and-record because `parse_program` has nothing above it to propagate an `Err` to.

##### THE WHOLE-BRANCH REVIEW FOUND THREE MORE DEFECTS THAT SIX PER-TASK REVIEWS HAD EACH PASSED

Six task reviews passed. Asked specifically to search for siblings of defect classes this branch had already produced, the whole-branch review found three more, two of them exactly that.

**The recovered tree could read backwards.** `parse_program`'s trailing-token absorb — the same
mechanism the section above this one corrects, there for losing source outright rather than for this —
pushed its trailing `Stmt::Error` into `block.stmts` while a still-live tail expression sat in
`block.tail`, and `Block` prints `stmts` before `tail`. So a token that comes AFTER the tail in the
source printed BEFORE it in the tree: `parse_recovering("1 2")` gave `stmts=[Error@2..3]`,
`tail=Some(Nat@0..1)`, the `2` ahead of the `1` it follows in the source. A sibling of the Eof-check
defect: the same absorb mechanism, a second way for it to misrepresent the source it collected.

**One wrong rule, independently written at three separate call sites across three earlier tasks, let
sibling spans overlap.** `expect_or_record`, `parse_expr_recovering`, and `parse_block_body`'s own
end-span computation each answered a mismatched or unconsumed token's FULL span rather than a
zero-width span at its start, so a construct could claim source a following sibling also claimed:
`"let x = 1 let y = 2; y"` gave `Let(x)` the span `0..13` and `Let(y)` the overlapping span `10..20`.
A throwaway sweep over 5,000 generated damaged programs (3,506 needing recovery) measured 1,537
sibling-order violations and 2,566 overlap violations before the fix, and zero of each after.

**The third finding was a test's own comment arguing a policy its assertion contradicted.**
`lints.rs`'s `an_error_statement_warns_about_nothing` carried a comment saying the warning it asserts
would be "the parser's failure dressed up as one about the user's code" — while the test demanded
exactly that answer from the arm beside it. The arm is correct as written; the comment now explains why
the false positive it worried about cannot reach a real user (`analyze` never hands a program
containing this node to `check`) instead of arguing against the code it sits next to.

All three fixed in `c32b9e3`. **Per-task review could not see any of them because each task's diff was
correct in isolation.** The order defect lives in the interaction between the tail-expression exit and
the trailing-token absorb — two mechanisms from two different tasks, each fine reviewed alone. The
overlap defect lives in three separately-reviewed span computations agreeing on the same wrong rule,
which a diff-scoped review has no way to compare against each other. Only a review holding the whole
branch, and asked to look for siblings on purpose, found either.

##### WHAT STAYS OPEN

- ~~**PR B2 owns the rest of `.rxt` navigation.**~~ **CLOSED** by the entry below (`rxt-navigation-index`). Every item on this list shipped: name spans on `Stmt::Let`, `Stmt::Fn` and `Stmt::Assign`, and a `Param` type carrying one per parameter; the binder-resolution pass, which landed in a new `binder` module rather than in `analysis` as this item predicted; `Role::Definition`'s kind discriminant; `nav_rxt`; and both `Language` arms — `symbol_kind` did not gain an arm but was replaced outright by a per-`DefKind` `outline_kind`, on the reasoning that entry records.
- **The binder pass must be ITERATIVE.** `lints.rs`'s module doc records that its own recursive walk over the surface tree is safe only because both its current callers — `analyze` here, and `redextape-wasm`'s `Session::compile_with_caps` — run it after typechecking has added no error-severity diagnostic, and `typeck.rs`'s `MAX_TYPE_DEPTH` bounds any program deep enough to clear that gate to a nesting typeck itself can recurse over. A navigation pass runs BEFORE typechecking, over a tree that may not typecheck — or, now, even parse completely — at all, so it cannot borrow that guarantee, and a recursive walk over adversarial nesting is an uncatchable native stack overflow rather than a diagnostic. `desugar.rs`'s `free_member_refs` already walks the identical scoping shape iteratively, over an explicit worklist, and its own doc comment says why; that is the shape B2 should follow rather than reinvent.
- **`.rxlambda` still has no recovery and no navigation.** Nothing in this PR touches it. Its terms are de Bruijn-indexed and largely print-only past lowering, which the earlier navigation slice already recorded as its own, separate piece of design work.
- **The `"parser made no progress"` iteration bound in `parse_block_body` is unreachable by construction, and that is by design rather than an oversight.** Every turn of the loop either advances `self.pos` — the progress bump guarantees this on the recovery path, and an ordinary successful statement always consumes at least one token on the happy path — or it breaks the loop outright, so the bound sitting behind that `if turns > bound` can only fire if some future change breaks one of those two guarantees. It is this crate's established shape for turning an uncatchable failure into a diagnostic instead of a hang — the same shape `MAX_TOKENS` and `MAX_PARSE_DEPTH` already use — and it is a tripwire, not a live guard against anything reachable today: only a sabotage makes it observable, which is exactly what `recovery_makes_progress_on_a_token_it_cannot_start_a_statement_with`'s own sabotage run does, by deleting the progress bump it exists to protect.
- **`let x 1;` — a name present but the `=` missing — discards the binding exactly as a missing name does, and this is pre-existing, unchanged by anything in this branch.** `parse_let` calls `self.expect(TokenKind::Assign, "\`=\`")?` immediately after reading the name, and `expect`'s `?` propagates on any mismatch, turning the whole statement into a single `Stmt::Error` with the name nowhere left to recover from. This branch's recovery only reaches into the VALUE position — `let x = ;` keeps `x` and gives `value` an `Expr::Error` — because the value is the one sub-position with somewhere to put a placeholder; a missing `=` fails before there is a `Stmt::Let` to hold one. It is exactly the case B2's navigation will feel first, since the name a user just finished typing is the one thing a binder pass most wants to keep live through the keystroke that has not yet typed `=`.
- **`MAX_RECOVERED_DIAGNOSTICS` does not bound what an editor receives.** It caps only the parser's
  half. Lexer diagnostics are prepended in `parse_inner` uncapped, so 50,000 `$` characters produce
  50,000 diagnostics out of `parse_recovering`; adding 300 broken `let` statements behind them (capped
  to 100 plus a summary) measured 50,101 total. The cap is the correct answer for the half it covers
  and should stay — its own doc comment already states an editor-storm rationale that this measurement
  shows it only half achieves.
- **Recovery can stack duplicate diagnostics on one position.** `"{ { { 1"` yields three identical
  "expected `}`" diagnostics, all at `7..7`. `"let x = } 1;"` yields three diagnostics at `8..9`, two
  of them the identical message "expected an expression".
- **Above `MAX_TOKENS`, `parse_recovering` answers an entirely empty tree, not a partially recovered
  one.** The oversized-input path returns `Block { stmts: Vec::new(), tail: None, .. }` before the
  parser ever runs, covering none of the source with an error node. "Always answers a tree" holds only
  literally there — navigation gets nothing at all on the largest files, the ones a cap like this exists
  to protect.
- **The `Expr::Error` echo is invisible to the printer's own width probe.** `width_of` measures an
  element by printing it into a `Printer` built with an empty source string (`Printer::new("", &[])`);
  an `Expr::Error` arm reads its text out of `self.src`, so against an empty source it always echoes
  nothing and `width_of` reports 0 regardless of the error span's real size — measured directly: a
  500-byte `Expr::Error` span reports a width of 0. The arm's stated justification, that a formatter for
  broken files would have the mechanism, is only partly true: the mechanism is there, but the layout
  decision that would decide whether to USE it cannot see the text it would echo.

#### `.rxt` GETS NAVIGATION ON A SCOPE-AWARE BINDER PASS, AND THE BRANCH'S SHARPEST FINDING IS THAT SIX CLEAN PER-TASK REVIEWS WERE FOLLOWED BY FIVE FALSE LOAD-BEARING CLAIMS — EVERY ONE IN A FILE THE BRANCH NEVER EDITED, WHICH IS WHY NO DIFF-SCOPED REVIEW COULD SEE THEM; THREE OF THE DESIGN'S OWN TEST FIXTURES DID NOT HOLD THE PROPERTY THEIR TEST WOULD HAVE ASSERTED AND WERE CAUGHT ONLY BY RUNNING THEM BEFORE WRITING THEM DOWN, AND TWO SUCCESSIVE CORRECTION ROUNDS EACH INTRODUCED A NEW FALSE CLAIM WHILE FIXING ONE (2026-09-08, branch `rxt-navigation-index`, `1412686..a72aa01`, 15 commits, plus the entry commit that follows it)

Design: [`../specs/2026-09-08-rxt-navigation-index-design.md`](../specs/2026-09-08-rxt-navigation-index-design.md). Plan: [`2026-09-08-rxt-navigation-index.md`](2026-09-08-rxt-navigation-index.md).

**PR B2, the last of the LSP track's third slice.** `.tm` and `.asm` resolve a name by flat lookup, which `NameIndex::link` does for both. `.rxt` names are scoped, so an occurrence resolves to a *binding* — in `let x = 1; let x = x + 1;` the two `x`es on the second line resolve to different ones — and that needs a pass rather than a lookup. `binder.rs` is 479 lines and answers it: an explicit worklist over the tree `parse_recovering` hands back, a persistent scope arena where each work item carries its own scope index, and a final sort that turns walk order into source order. `redextape-core` still has zero dependencies; `cargo tree -p redextape-core --edges normal` prints one line.

The pass is **iterative**, and the reason is not visible at the call site: `lints.rs`'s module doc records that its own recursive walk is safe only because both callers run it after typechecking added no error-severity diagnostic, so `MAX_TYPE_DEPTH` has already rejected anything deep enough to matter. Navigation runs *before* typechecking, on a tree that may not typecheck and — since B1 — may not have parsed completely, so it cannot borrow that gate, and the failure it would buy is an uncatchable native stack overflow that takes the editor's server process with it. `desugar.rs`'s `free_member_refs` walks the identical scoping shape iteratively and says why; this follows it rather than reinventing it.

`Language::symbol_kind` is **gone**, not extended. It answered one fixed `SymbolKind` per language, and `every_form_with_an_index_has_a_symbol_kind` existed to stop it drifting from `nav` — because a form gaining an index without gaining a kind reports nothing in an outline, with no compile error. `DefKind` moves the answer to the push site, so `outline_kind` is exhaustive over kinds and a new one is a compile error. **That test was deleted on purpose**: the compiler now holds what it held. `DefKind::Param` maps to `None`, meaning "not an outline symbol" rather than "not indexed" — a parameter must be navigable, but an outline listing every parameter of every function as a flat sibling of the functions is noise.

##### THREE OF THE DESIGN'S OWN FIXTURES DID NOT HOLD THEIR PROPERTY, AND ONLY RUNNING THEM BEFORE WRITING THEM DOWN FOUND IT

Every fixture in the design's testing section was run through `parse_recovering` before being committed to prose. Three did not survive. `fn f(a) { a + ` was the broken-file fixture, chosen to show that an unparseable file still indexes: the trailing `+` makes recovery swallow the whole body into a single `Stmt::Error`, so the body's `a` the test would have asserted **is not in the tree at all**. `{ let y = 1; y } y` was the block-scope fixture: its trailing `y` parses as a `Stmt::Error`, so there is no occurrence to assert on. And the run-boundary negative named a fixture with no forward reference in it to be unresolved.

Each was chosen by reading the grammar, each looked right, and none held the property its test would have asserted. This is the same class as the previous slice's printer-layout fixtures, one layer earlier: there the fixtures were real but unrepresentative, here they were imagined. The replacements are `let x = ; x` and `fn f(a) { a`, both probed, and the block-scope case became `let g = { let y = 1; y }; y`.

##### SIX CLEAN PER-TASK REVIEWS, THEN FIVE FALSE CLAIMS THE WHOLE-BRANCH REVIEW FOUND IN FILES NO TASK TOUCHED

Every task review passed; three found nothing at any severity. The whole-branch review then returned **needs fixes**, and every Important finding was a claim this branch's changes had made false in a file the branch never edited — structurally invisible to a review scoped to a diff:

- `nav.rs`'s module doc still said the server maps a definition to a `SymbolKind` "at the one place that knows the document's language". After `outline_kind` there is no such place. **This was the surviving twin of a sentence a task-review fix round had already corrected in `redextape-lsp/src/lib.rs`** — the copy in the module the change was actually about outlived it.
- `tests/sourcemap_coverage.rs` still said "the method name has no span of its own in this AST". `Expr::Method` gained `name_span` in task 2, which corrected that exact sentence at the `desugar.rs` UFCS arm and nowhere else.
- `README.md` said `.rxt` navigation was "Still not built… needs `analysis` to keep resolved symbols", and counted the navigable forms as two.
- `plugin/redextape.lua` listed navigation for `.tm` and `.asm` only.
- `binder.rs`'s `resolve` doc claimed its cost is "bounded by nesting rather than by file length".

The review also found that **`textDocument/definition` and `textDocument/references` had no `.rxt` test at all** — two of the three surfaces this PR ships, exercised only at the `NameIndex` level and never through the server. Both now have one, against a shadowing fixture where a name-keyed resolver answers differently from a binding-keyed one in both directions.

##### THE COST CLAIM WAS WRONG IN THE SPEC FIRST, AND TWO CORRECTION ROUNDS EACH INTRODUCED A NEW FALSE CLAIM WHILE FIXING ONE

`resolve`'s cost is not bounded by nesting. `block` threads `cur = self.bind(cur, …)` across *consecutive* statements, so a flat run of N `let`s at one nesting depth still produces a chain N deep. The claim was written in the design spec first and copied faithfully into the code, which is the shape worth remembering: **a spec's prose gets reviewed before execution, and a defect in it becomes a defect in every place the implementation copies it.**

The correction rounds are the more useful finding. Round two fixed the bound and illustrated it with `let a0 = 0; let a1 = a0; … let a19999 = a0;`, asserting it walks the whole chain "well inside `MAX_TOKENS`". Measured: that program is **100,001 tokens against a limit of 100,000**, so `parse_inner` returns an empty `Block` and `nav_rxt` answers **zero occurrences** — an illustration demonstrating the exact opposite of the property its own paragraph existed to establish. (19,999 statements is 99,996 tokens and yields 39,997 occurrences.) The same round replaced a stale count in `nav.rs` with an enumeration of what separates two `.rxt` names — `.`, `,`, `(`, `|` or whitespace — which is false: `let a = 1;let b = a;b` separates two names with `;` alone, and `x+x` with `+`. The true reason needs no enumeration and covers all three forms at once: **two identifier tokens can never be adjacent, because a lexer that saw them adjacent would read them as one identifier.**

Round three fixed both, and its dispatch named only `binder.rs` for the mitigation clause — so the spec paragraph that clause came from kept the undifferentiated version, and a fourth sibling had to be closed by hand. The asymmetry now stated in both places: `TyEnv::lookup` pays the same reverse scan on every program that typechecks, but `lints.rs`'s walk runs only after typechecking added no error-severity diagnostic, so on a file that does not typecheck — or since B1 does not parse — the binder pays this cost and `lints.rs` never runs. Those are exactly the files navigation exists to serve.

**What ended the cycle was a review dispatched specifically to check whether a correction had introduced a new error**, rather than to re-check the feature. Two of the three rounds had, and neither was visible to anyone re-reading the sentence they had just written.

#### THREE OF #82'S FILED ENDS CLOSE, TWO OF THEM WERE ONE DEFECT — AND THE BRANCH'S REAL RESULT IS THAT CORRECTING A FALSE CLAIM REPEATEDLY PRODUCED ANOTHER ONE, THAT RUNNING THE SABOTAGE A CLAIM FORBIDS IS WHAT THE SURVIVING CLAIMS HAVE IN COMMON AND STILL DID NOT SAVE ONE WHOSE SABOTAGE RANGED NARROWER THAN ITS SENTENCE, AND THAT THIS ENTRY KEPT REPRODUCING THE PATTERN WHILE RECORDING IT — LATTERLY BY COUNTING A SERIES NOTHING CAN GATE (2026-09-08, branch `lsp-loose-ends`, `6e0ad6e..1cd4e05`, 25 commits, plus the entry commit and the rounds that corrected the entry itself)

Design: [`../specs/2026-09-08-lsp-loose-ends-design.md`](../specs/2026-09-08-lsp-loose-ends-design.md). Plan: [`2026-09-08-lsp-loose-ends.md`](2026-09-08-lsp-loose-ends.md).

**A cleanup slice, and the three ends it closes are small.** `ast::fn_run_at` replaces five hand-written scans for the maximal run of consecutive `Stmt::Fn` — four walk forward, one walks right-to-left and so asks at the run's last statement. `parse_inner`'s `bool` becomes `Completeness { Complete, Recovered, Refused }`, and a crate-private `parse_for_nav` answers `None` only for `Refused`, so `nav_rxt` returns `Option<NameIndex>` and a `.rxt` file over `MAX_TOKENS` inherits the `nav: None` path where handlers answer JSON `null` — *no outline for this document* rather than *this document has no symbols*. And `Role::Definition` gains `extent: Option<Span>`, which closes the last two filings at once because they were never two: the outline listing every `let` as a flat sibling, and `documentSymbol` folding a multi-line `fn` to its header, are both `document_symbol` starving for a span the index did not carry.

**#82's second filed end — folding `push_reference` into `push_resolved_reference` — is deliberately NOT done**, and the whole-branch review checked the reasoning rather than accepting it. The two `None`s are not the same value: `push_reference`'s is a placeholder `link` later fills, while the binder's is final, because `Binder::finish` never calls `link`. Folding would give one argument two meanings distinguished only by whether the caller later calls a different method. That is unlike `push_definition`'s new `extent`, whose `None` sites are enumerated at the field rather than assumed uniform: `.tm` records no state extent, `.asm` records no label extent, and a `.rxt` parameter has none of its own because its construct is the enclosing `fn`. **The first draft of this entry wrote "one fact at every site" here, reinstating the omission a review had already made this branch fix** — not the same wording, the same gap — which is why the paragraph now names all three.

##### CORRECTION ROUNDS, THE CLAIMS THEY INTRODUCED, AND WHY THIS SECTION CARRIES NO TOTAL

A correction round here means **a commit that fixed a false claim a review had found**. Below are those commits on `6e0ad6e..1cd4e05`, and what each introduced. **This section deliberately states no total, and the reason is a finding rather than a hedge.** Two earlier drafts each published one. The first was arithmetically wrong — its table could not produce the number its heading claimed. No error was ever found in the second's arithmetic; what was wrong was publishing a total at all, because the count is not a quantity the tree can settle:

- **The definition does not pin its own population.** `6fe9da3` fixed three plan commands that did not work, but an implementer found it, not a review. `4097345` is arguable in both directions — its message credits the implementer before the review, and while it mostly fixed a stale *instruction*, it also corrected an expectation that was false about the tree. Each falls out through a different half of "a commit that fixed a false claim a review had found", and nothing in the tree marks either exclusion.
- **The scoring is not uniform, and the total is what the non-uniformity buys.** `f4b0ae4` left a false paragraph standing that had been in the plan since `9c538e0`; `585c1f0` and `df815d8` likewise walked past copies that predated them. Score "left standing" as an introduction and the total rises; score it as an omission and it falls. Both readings are defensible and no gate holds either.

So the rows are the record. The number is not: **write the property when no gate can hold the count.** The count refused here is specifically *how many correction rounds there were and how many claims they introduced* — the counts elsewhere in this entry each resolve to a commit, a diffstat or a measurement, and are stated for that reason.

**This file predicted this, more than once, and an entry above already says so in as many words: "This file has now done this three times."** It names them — the encoding-site survey (filed at 6 sites, re-grepped to 13, a 14th found during execution, a 15th by a whole-branch review), the `unreachable!` list (5, 8, 9, 17), and the `brief` references (15, 45). Each was published and corrected; two of the three were corrected more than once.

**The first draft of this cross-reference then made the same error inside the sentence citing it**, twice: it read that entry's "second standing list" as naming the encoding survey when the same clause calls that one "the first", and it claimed a place in the series that a later entry had already taken. So this paragraph now names no ordinal at all. The series is the finding; a running count of it is one more quantity nothing gates.

| `f4b0ae4` + `024270a` | the outline pass's correctness argument, in spec, plan and code | **left the plan's very next paragraph standing** — the recursion-safety claim, false since `9c538e0`. An omission, not new prose; see the scoring note above |

| `9d90d3e` | the sweep's four false claims | **the `Completeness` enum doc now contradicted the variant doc it had just fixed** |
| `cd18fe9` | that contradiction | — |
| `60e67bc` | nine whole-branch findings | **"and at the right place", a check the test did not do; and a false rationale for `shape_with_spans`** |
| `ed09f10` | the paragraph `f4b0ae4` stopped short of | **a new sentence, false in both its clauses** |
| `e8292de` | the placement claim | **`nav.rs` strengthened a true vague sentence into a false checkable one; and the placement fix was still not universal** |
| `585c1f0` | two copies of claims a review had called false | — |
| `df815d8` | four more, every property sabotaged | — (its twin greps were scoped to `crates/`, leaving two plan copies that had stood since `9c538e0`) |
| `88d7019` | the sentence `ed09f10` introduced | — |
| `1cd4e05` | the last two plan copies, passed over by `df815d8`'s `crates/`-scoped greps and then by `88d7019`, which edited fifteen lines above one of them | — |

**Per claim — not per round — the ones that survived correlate with someone having run the sabotage that claim forbids. Correlate, not guarantee: the next paragraph is the counterexample.** The round-level version does not hold and is worth stating so nobody rebuilds it: several rounds that ran no sabotage at all introduced nothing, and every round that produced two claims had also run sabotages. `e8292de` is the sharp case *within* one round: it fixed three findings with a sabotage and one by reading the code, and the one read rather than run came back false — as did one of the three that were sabotaged, for the reason below.

**But sabotaging is not sufficient, and this branch has the counterexample.** `e8292de`'s *sabotage-tested* placement fix also came back false. Its sabotage used a tree with distinct names and confirmed misplacement is caught; the sentence it licensed claimed misplacement is caught **in general**, and two same-named parents produce an identical multiset when the compared tuple carries only a parent's name. The refinement, which is the transferable form:

> **A sabotage tests the property you aimed it at, not the property your sentence claims.** Before writing the sentence, ask whether the sabotage you ran actually ranges over everything the sentence quantifies.

**This entry then kept reproducing the pattern, and the last time was inside the paragraph above arguing against it.** Its first draft tabulated eight rounds, double-counted one, omitted another, asserted a clean controlled experiment that its own later section disproved, and restated the `extent` omission. The correction of that draft fixed all five and introduced more of its own — contradictory ordinals for one event, the missed plan copies attributed to a commit that was not responsible, an overstated "verbatim", and a pedantic claim that did not hold for `grammar-check`. How many is exactly the quantity this section says nothing gates, so it is not stated here either. Every draft was caught the same way — a review that re-ran every figure and checked every sentence against the tree — and that is why this section now carries no total at all, its own revision count included.

##### A SENTENCE CORRECTED IN ONE PLACE AND *MOVED* IN ANOTHER IS THE TWIN THAT SURVIVES

The design named **both** copies of one justification — *"the index stores name spans, and recording where each block ends is more than navigation needs"* — and said in as many words that it "was true of `.tm` and `.asm` and is not true of `.rxt`". One copy was corrected. The other was carried **verbatim into a brand-new file** by the task that created `outline.rs`, where the later claim sweep's grep hit it and read it as already-swept **because the whole file was new**. That sweep's own commit message then asserted no second copy survived.

**A grep hit in a file this branch created is not evidence the claim was reviewed. Code moved into a new file has not been read; it has been relocated.** Diff its doc comments against their origin, not against nothing.

The same mechanism ran twice more on scope rather than novelty: two sweeps bounded their greps to `crates/` and left twins standing in `docs/` — in this branch's *own plan*, which holds a full draft copy of the code being corrected. One of those survived a commit that edited the file fifteen lines above it while recording, in its own message, that it had swept that file for a different duplicate. **A copy sweep bounded by a directory finds nothing outside the directory.**

##### THE PLACEMENT CLAIM NOTHING COULD HAVE CAUGHT, BECAUSE NOBODY WROTE ITS SABOTAGE

The whole-file property test's doc claimed every definition reaches the tree *"exactly once, and at the right place"*. Its helper flattened the tree and **discarded the container**, so placement was never compared. Measured, in an isolated checkout: moving the push arm above the drain loop — a whole-tree misplacement that loses no node — reddened 6 of 10 outline tests and left **that one green**, with every node re-parented.

Two sabotages had been run against that test. Neither was ever aimed at "the right place", because nobody wrote one. **A doc line that names a property must be paired with the sabotage that property forbids** — and the property with no sabotage is the claim nothing catches.

The fix carried the parent into the compared tuple, and the *next* review found that a parent's **name** still could not tell two same-named parents apart. `fn f(p) { fn f(q) { let z = 1; z } f(0) } 0` under a wrong-parent sabotage produces an identical sorted multiset. It now carries `(name, selection_range)`, and the name-only form was re-run as a probe against the misplaced tree to show it passes — the counterexample is measured, not asserted.

##### A CORPUS THAT CANNOT EXERCISE THE PROPERTY ITS TEST NAMES, GUARDED BY A COUNT OF THE WRONG QUANTITY

The property test walks the tree's `.rxt` fixtures and guarded against a vacuous run with `assert!(files.len() >= 20)`. Measured: **22 files**, 10 of them contributing no outline-eligible definition at all, and two of the 22 are `.tm` source in a `.rxt` file on purpose. Of the other twenty-one, ten are depth-0 — they contribute no outline-eligible definition at all — and eleven are depth-1, so none of the twenty-one has a parent-child edge; the twenty-second, `run_nested_scopes.in/p.rxt` — a CLI end-to-end case for a program whose scopes actually nest, not a fixture written for this test — reaches depth 3 and gives the corpus its first real parent-child edges. One fixture is not the breadth this defect needs, so the corpus alone still cannot exercise it at scale, and a file count on its own cannot tell a corpus that built real trees from one that compared two empty lists twenty-two times.

**A count that proves the loop ran is not a count that proves the loop exercised anything.** The guard now counts nodes built — **20** measured (12 of them from the corpus's flat files, 8 from `run_nested_scopes.in/p.rxt`), with the floor raised from 10 to **15** so that losing the nesting fixture again, not just ordinary fixture churn, is what fails it — and a second floor requires the corpus's own max depth to clear 1, so a corpus that grew wide but stayed flat could not pass either. The generated nested source still supplies nesting at a scale the corpus, even with that one fixture, does not match. `nested_or_disjoint` turned the placement column's load-bearing premise into a check: **464** real pair comparisons, of which the corpus supplies **29** — 1 of them from `emit_overflow.in/p.rxt`'s two sibling `let`s, as before, and 28 from `run_nested_scopes.in/p.rxt`'s eight definitions.

**This closes the `WHAT STAYS OPEN` item this entry itself filed on exactly this point** — the corpus could not exercise nesting at all; now one fixture in it does, at depth 3, and the generated half is still what exercises the property at the breadth a single fixture cannot.
