#### ACCESSIBILITY ITEM 8 CLOSES — `[continue]` AND A FRONTIER `▶` ARE WITHDRAWN FOR THE WINDOW IN WHICH THEY PROVABLY CANNOT WORK — AND THE BRANCH'S SHARPEST FINDING IS A SABOTAGE THAT REDDENED NOTHING IN EITHER TIER, WHICH FALSIFIED THE DESIGN'S OWN JUSTIFICATION BEFORE ANY OF IT SHIPPED; THE CALL-SITE CENSUS THEN KILLED THE DESIGN'S PREFERRED SHAPE BY FINDING THE DEFECT'S OWN SHAPE ALREADY WAITING IN THE HARNESS THAT WOULD HAVE TESTED THE FIX, THE SENTENCE THE DESIGN QUOTED AS ITS AUTHORITY WAS THE ONE THIS BRANCH INVALIDATED IN A FILE NO TASK TOUCHED, EDITED ONLY TO FIX THAT COMMENT, THE RETRACTED JUSTIFICATION SURVIVED SUCCESSIVE SWEEPS BY CHANGING GRAMMATICAL FORM, AND MAKING A HEDGED NUMBER EXACT FALSIFIED THE CLAUSE BESIDE IT (2026-09-09, branch `extend-during-recompile`, `d5da8c8..ea04893`, 13 commits, plus the entry commit and the rounds that corrected the entry itself)

Design: [`../specs/2026-09-09-extend-during-recompile-design.md`](../specs/2026-09-09-extend-during-recompile-design.md). Plan: [`2026-09-09-extend-during-recompile.md`](2026-09-09-extend-during-recompile.md).

**ONE ITEM OFF THE DEFERRED-ACCESSIBILITY LIST, AND ONLY ONE.** `compile.ts`'s `schedule` claims a generation synchronously at dispatch and posts the run 300 ms later (`DEBOUNCE_MS = 300` at `compile.ts:11`; the supersede/post pair at `compile.ts:135-136`), while `session-worker.ts`'s `onExtend` returns in silence on `live?.gen !== req.gen` (`session-worker.ts:704`). For that whole window every `extend` addressed to the session is dropped on arrival — and `[continue]` and a frontier `▶` went on offering themselves, which is the *silence* item 8 filed rather than the inert click, which was always correct. Three small pieces close it. `SessionClient` gains `awaitingRun`, set in `supersede()` and cleared in the message listener **before** `onReply` runs, because `replies.ts` drives the repaint off that call and a repaint reading a still-set flag would paint the withdrawal one frame after the window it describes had closed. `SessionPool`'s constructor takes a required `onSupersede` — `main.ts:282` passes `() => draw()`, six test sites pass their own — so no `src/` site can claim a generation without the panes learning about it. And `canRecordFurther` takes the flag as a second parameter, which makes it the single gate that both `controlState`'s `continueLabel` and `transport.ts`'s frontier `▶` handler read. The step readout carries ` — recompiling` in place of the stop reason for the same window, and the `…` that means *this count is not final* drops with it, because the run being described will record nothing more whatever the new one goes on to do.

**ALL THREE `supersede()` CALL SITES ARE COVERED, AND A FIX KEYED TO THE DEBOUNCE ALONE WOULD HAVE MISSED TWO.** `compile.ts:135` is the ≥300 ms case item 8 names; `scratch.ts:859` (`#spawn`) and `scratch.ts:1001` (`recompile`) supersede and post in adjacent statements, so their window is one message hop rather than a debounce — the same defect, shorter. Putting the flag on `SessionClient` rather than on the debounce is what makes that automatic rather than remembered.

##### THE SABOTAGE THAT REDDENED NOTHING IS WHAT FALSIFIED THE DESIGN, BEFORE ANY OF IT SHIPPED

Every sabotage the plan names was run; three of them carry the branch's central argument, and **two of the three results are negatives that are findings rather than gaps** — one sabotage reddened nothing anywhere, and a second only reached its fourth assertion once that assertion stopped being unreachable behind an earlier hard failure.

- **`transport.ts` passes a literal `false` for `awaitingRun`: reddens nothing in *either* tier.** The node tier cannot see it because nothing there drives that handler — the only `.forward()` anywhere under `web/tests/node` is `History.forward()` in `history.test.ts`. The browser tier cannot see it either, and that is the sharper half: `forward.disabled` is rendered by `controlStrip` from `controlState`, which reads the flag through `sessions.ts`, a path wholly independent of this click handler's own gate. **This is what falsified design §4.1's justification for folding `awaitingRun` into `canRecordFurther` at all** — that the `▶` handler would otherwise keep posting a doomed extend under its own copy of the rule. It would not, and it cannot. The retraction landed in the design, in the plan and in the shipped doc comment before any of this merged.
- **`sessions.ts` passes a literal `false`: reddens all four in-window browser assertions, independently.** And it only *demonstrated* the fourth after those four became `expect.soft`. Before that the first failure aborted the test, so `forwardButton()?.disabled` — the assertion the browser file exists to reach, since no node test can observe a rendered `disabled` — had never been shown capable of failing at all.
- **`main.ts` passes `() => {}` instead of `() => draw()` to `new SessionPool`: reddens every in-window assertion.** The flag is correct and nothing repaints. This is the only check that the repaint wiring is load-bearing rather than incidental, and it is what makes design §3 a decision rather than a coincidence.

##### THE CALL-SITE CENSUS KILLED THE DESIGN'S PREFERRED SHAPE BEFORE A LINE OF CODE WAS WRITTEN

Design §3 first prescribed threading `onSupersede` through `SessionClient` **and** `SessionPool.bind`. The census that shape asked for is what rejected it, and not on the count. At the merge base, `git grep -c 'new SessionClient(' d5da8c8 -- web | awk -F: '{s+=$NF} END {print s}'` gives 20 (1 in `src`, 19 in tests) and `git grep -c 'pool\.bind(' d5da8c8 -- web | awk -F: '{s+=$NF} END {print s}'` gives 25 (2 in `src`, 23 in tests) — 45 sites. **The decisive one is not among them.** `web/tests/node/scratch.test.ts:113-114` replaces the method with a **two-parameter interceptor** (`const bind = pool.bind.bind(pool)`, then `pool.bind = (id, onReply) => …`). A required third argument on `bind` would have had to be hand-added there, and omitting it drops the callback in silence — **the defect being fixed, reinstalled inside the harness that tests the fix.** The constructor takes it instead: 7 `new SessionPool(` sites, `bind`'s two parameters untouched.

##### ONE OF THE TWO CONSUMERS CANNOT REACH THE HALF OF THE GATE IT WAS GIVEN, AND THE GATE IS KEPT ANYWAY

`canRecordFurther`'s second caller is the frontier `▶` handler at `transport.ts:127`. **While `awaitingRun` holds, that caller cannot reach the gate's `awaitingRun` half.** `controlStrip` renders `forward.disabled = !c.canForward` (`pane-chrome.ts:696`); a disabled `<button>` receives no click from a user gesture; and while the flag holds, `canForward` reduces to `head < length - 1`, which is exactly the case where `leg.hist.forward()` succeeds and short-circuits before the gate is consulted. The repaint that sets the flag is synchronous, so no click lands between the transition and the paint. `play()` (`transport.ts:87-94`) is the only other `hist.forward()` caller and stops at the frontier without posting anything.

**The gate is kept, and the reason is one gate rather than two.** What makes the second copy unreachable is a rendering decision in `pane-chrome.ts` — a module `controls.ts` does not own and does not get to depend on. A narrower rule in `controls.ts` would be a second opinion about the same question, held correct only by a distant file's current choice. **No test was written for it**: nothing can exercise an unreachable branch, so this is prose rather than coverage, and it is stated as a property of today's rendering rather than as a ranking of the two callers. The reachability question was asked only because the sabotage aimed at that gate reddened nothing, and answering it took reading the code rather than running anything.

##### THE FOCUS HALF IS A MEASURED NEGATIVE, WHICH IS WHY NO FOCUS CODE SHIPS

Item 8 invokes item 1 (*"a control that hides itself on click strands the keyboard"*), so the branch had to answer whether withdrawing `[continue]` strands focus. `web/tests/browser/extend-focus-probe.test.ts` answers it in three parts and all three are load-bearing:

- **The mechanism is real.** Focusing `[continue]` and setting `hidden`, and focusing the frontier `▶` and setting `disabled`, each leave `document.activeElement` on `<body>`. Item 1's recorded hazard holds in this browser, against these controls.
- **No user gesture reaches it.** Typing into the source editor keeps focus on `view.contentDOM`; selecting a different encoding keeps it on `#encoding`. Each sub-case first asserts the readout contains ` — recompiling`, so it is evidence about the hazard rather than about a window that never opened.
- **One programmatic route does reach it**, named so the finding is falsifiable rather than an absence of evidence: a document dispatch made while focus sits on `[continue]` strands focus on `<body>`. No user gesture performs one.

**The trigger enumeration covers all three `supersede()` call sites**, and the third needs no focus answer for a structural reason rather than an empirical one: `#spawn` registers the session with `available: false` (`scratch.ts:822`, `#reg.add` at `:827`) before superseding at `:859`, so `controlState` takes its `!v.available` early return (`controls.ts:90-99`) — neither `[continue]` nor a frontier `▶` renders for that session, and there is no control to withdraw. **So no focus code ships, and that is a measurement rather than an omission.** Item 1's two standing instances — `tm-pane.ts`'s reattach and `[continue]`'s own click path — are reachable independently of this change and stay filed.

##### FIVE WAYS A FALSE CLAIM SURVIVED A CORRECTION, AND A REVIEW FOUND EVERY ONE

Not one of these was found by re-reading.

- **A false claim in a file the branch never edited, invalidated by the branch's own change — and it was the design's cited authority.** `compile.ts:120-122` **at `d5da8c8`** said *"nothing here changes a binding now, so there is nothing for this path to repaint"*. `schedule` now repaints on every dispatch, through `supersede()` → `onSupersede` → `draw()`. Design §3 **quotes that very comment** as its evidence for "nothing repaints at dispatch today". The sentence the branch relied on is the sentence the branch invalidated, and no diff-scoped review could have seen it, because the file was not in the diff until the whole-branch review put it there.
- **The retracted justification survived successive sweeps by changing grammatical form.** After §4.1's doomed-extend claim was retracted, a sweep grepped its wording and found nothing. It survived three times more anyway: first as a **test obligation** in the design's own §6.3 list (*"Assert a frontier `▶` click during the window posts no `extend`"*, 95 lines below the paragraph that had just been rewritten to say the path is unreachable and nothing can exercise it), then as a **coverage attribution** in the plan's Task 2 sabotage table, which read *"this is Task 3's browser assertion, and that it does not fire here is the finding that says so"* — while Task 3's own row, written after that sabotage had actually been run, records it reddening nothing in the browser tier either — and a third time as a **standing instruction**, in the plan's own Task 5 (`2026-09-09-extend-during-recompile.md:891-892`), telling whoever wrote this entry to report the node-tier silence as the reason Task 3's browser assertion exists rather than as the negative that falsified the design — corrected in this commit. That the third copy sat inside the instructions for writing the entry that names the first two is the point worth recording. A sweep that greps a claim's wording finds none of the three forms.
- **Making a number more precise falsified its neighbour.** `session-client.ts:263` read *"`bind` keeps the two parameters its ~20 test call sites pass, one of which replaces the method with a two-parameter interceptor of its own."* Replacing the hedge with the exact **23** made the membership clause beside it false: that interceptor is spelled `pool.bind.bind(pool)` and `pool.bind =`, matches neither of the greps the 23 came from, and so contributes zero to it — `grep -c 'pool\.bind(' tests/node/scratch.test.ts` is **0**. The vague figure had absorbed the error and the precise one exposed it, so precision moved the falsehood rather than removing it. The line now reads *"…its 23 test call sites pass, plus one more site that replaces the method…"* — the interceptor as a separate conjunct rather than as a member.
- **A correction round installed a false argument about another item on this list, and the round after it deleted the argument rather than replacing it.** The reading was checked against item 1's own words at roadmap:1367-1374 and did not survive them. It is deliberately not restated here: what is worth keeping is that a correction round invented it, not the thing invented.
- **A test made *more faithful* to the gesture it models found a real cross-test coupling the inert version hid.** The encoding sub-case had dispatched a bare `change` event without ever reassigning `picker.value` — modelling the event rather than the gesture. Selecting the other option first (there are exactly two, `unary` and `binary`) made it a real gesture, and it then leaked into the test that runs after it, because `compile.ts`'s `schedule` reads `picker.value` **lazily inside its debounce timer** rather than at dispatch. Fixed by restoring the picker's value inside the sub-case. The faithful-looking-but-inert version could not have found it.

##### WHAT STAYS OPEN

- **Thirteen accessibility items remain: 1–7, 9, 10, and 13–16.** Sixteen were filed; 11 and 12 were fixed in the branch that filed them; item 8 closes here. **This is one item, not the pass** — the trigger for the pass is unchanged and remains *"when the web UI is close to actually being done"*, a condition on the UI rather than on a slice. (The 2026-08-18 decision entry above still reads *"so fourteen remain"*. That is a dated observation, true when written and superseded by this closure; it is left standing, as this file's frozen-entry convention requires.)
- **Nothing here is announced.** The step readout is a plain `<span class="step">` (`pane-chrome.ts:686`) with no live region, so ` — recompiling` appearing and vanishing reaches a screen reader through nothing at all; `grep -rn 'aria-live' src/ index.html` still finds nothing anywhere in this app. Item 6 already holds that question for `#link-status`, so this is a second surface with the same gap rather than a new question.
- **`awaitingRun` is a superset of the worker's drop condition, not an equality.** The worker sets `live.gen` when it *starts* a run and its first reply follows, so between those two moments `onExtend` would accept an extend this flag still answers `true` for. That gap is a message queued behind a run already in flight on a single-threaded worker, so being conservative there costs nothing — but the two predicates are not the same one, and anything that makes the worker concurrent makes the difference matter.
- **`controlStrip`'s doc and its code do not say the same thing.** `pane-chrome.ts:670` states *"THE CONTINUE BUTTON IS ADDED AND REMOVED, NEVER DISABLED"*, while `update` sets `extend.hidden` (`:700`/`:702`). `hidden` does remove the button from the tab order and the accessibility tree, so **nothing in this branch depends on closing the gap** — the withdrawal is real either way. But the doc claims an idiom the code does not use, and the pass should decide which of the two moves.
- **`canRecordFurther`'s doc comment and the plan's copy of it are held byte-identical by nothing.** `controls.ts:61-87` and `2026-09-09-extend-during-recompile.md:430-456` are 1,930 bytes each and currently `diff`-clean, so a plan re-execution reproduces the shipped comment exactly. No hook enforces that. The pre-commit hook named *"shared doc regions match their source"* (`scripts/check-shared-docs.sh`) scans only `.md` files carrying explicit `<!-- BEGIN shared: name -->` markers sourced from `grammars/shared/*.md` — three sources, four consumer READMEs, all Neovim grammar install prose — and the plan carries no such marker. Same shape as the four-files-explain-`MAX_TOKENS` item the previous branch filed.
- **Seven sites still say `main.ts` owns a pane handler that lives in `transport.ts`.** Pre-existing drift from PR #37 (plan 5d-ii-a), which moved `play` and `events` out of `main.ts` verbatim into the new `transport.ts`; each verified still reading that way at `ea04893`: `web/tests/browser/app.test.ts:630`, `:666` and `:894` (all naming *"`main.ts`'s `forward`"*), plus `web/src/sessions.ts:67` and `:583` and `web/tests/browser/running-focus.test.ts:246` (three naming *"`main.ts`'s `play`"*), plus `web/tests/browser/app.test.ts:920` (naming *"`main.ts`'s `back`"* — the same file as the three `forward` sites above, and `back`'s sibling in the same `events` object). The two sites this branch made self-contradictory — `controls.ts:123` and `controls.test.ts:155` — were fixed here; these seven were filed rather than swept, because the branch has no other reason to touch them.
- **In `web/tests/browser/extend-during-recompile.test.ts`, the tail that `expect.soft` lets the run reach passes vacuously inside an already-red run.** Because the four in-window assertions are soft, execution continues past them to the closing pair of hard `expect`s — and if the withdrawal never happened, the readout still contains `history is full`, so the trailing `until` returns immediately and that pair reads un-withdrawn state as success. Vitest still fails the run at teardown, so this misleads a reader of the tail alone and never the verdict — a diagnostic wrinkle, not a false test.
- **The browser tier duplicates its shell and helpers across files, and this branch added to it.** Measured at `ea04893` across the 49 files in `web/tests/browser`: **29** declare a `const SHELL`, **28** of them byte-identical 11-line blocks (the one exception, `scratch-fork.test.ts`, differs only by indentation), and `async function until` exists in **six distinct bodies across 22 files**. At `d5da8c8` it was 27 and 20 over 47 files — this branch's two new files copied both helpers, following the existing convention rather than fixing it. **A tree-wide extraction is filed as a follow-up and deliberately not done here**; the `until` drift is the evidence that it is warranted, because six implementations of one idea is not a convention with a reason.
- **This entry's own insertion moves every line below item 8 in this file**, so the `roadmap:NNNN` citations in the specs and plans that cite the accessibility list drift again — the class 5d-ii-c's closing entry already filed and measured under *CITATION ROT, AND WHAT IT COST*, where a sixteen-line insertion into this same list moved twenty distinct line references across eight documents in a single edit — and the whole-branch review that re-derived all twenty found fifteen of them already wrong for other reasons before that shift. Nothing gates it. That section's own conclusion is the durable form and is why this bullet cites it by name: the citations that never go stale are the ones naming a symbol instead of a line.

#### THE BROWSER TIER'S `SHELL` AND `until` COLLAPSE TO ONE MODULE EACH, AND THE DUPLICATION WAS HIDING A DEFECT NEITHER COPY COULD REVEAL ALONE — `vite.config.ts` SETS NEITHER `testTimeout` NOR `hookTimeout`, BROWSER MODE TRIPLES BOTH NODE DEFAULTS TO 15,000 AND 30,000, AND TWELVE FILE-LEVEL CEILINGS PLUS ELEVEN CALL-SITE CEILINGS COULD NEVER FIRE; THE CALL-SITE COUNT ITSELF TOOK THREE SCANNERS, BECAUSE THE SECOND ONE'S OWN SELF-TEST PROVED THREE SHAPES OF CALL WHILE WHAT IT MISSED WAS A SHAPE OF COMMENT, AND THE SITE IT MISSED WAS THE ONLY ONE WHOSE NUMBER HAD A REASON (2026-09-09, branch `browser-harness-dedup`, `7258986..f554d9b`, 25 commits — the implementation range, fixed and re-countable, including seven review-fix commits of which three touch code — plus this entry and whatever corrections follow it, a number this heading does not commit to)

Design: [`../specs/2026-09-09-browser-harness-dedup-design.md`](../specs/2026-09-09-browser-harness-dedup-design.md). Plan: [`2026-09-09-browser-harness-dedup.md`](2026-09-09-browser-harness-dedup.md).

**#84's own filing named the duplication and nothing else.** 29 of the browser tier's **49** test files declared a local `SHELL` and 23 declared a local `until` in seven distinct bodies; both now live once, in `web/tests/browser/harness.ts` (71 lines), and every one of the 29 importers was verified importing it (`grep -l "from './harness'" tests/browser/*.test.ts` → **29**; zero files still declare either locally). The denominator is 49, not the 46 that `pnpm run test:browser` runs: `pane-floor.test.ts` is one of the 29 importers and is also one of `vite.config.ts`'s three `PROBE_FILES`, excluded from the browser project unless `REDEXTAPE_PROBE` is set — so one of the 29 files sharing this module never runs under the count this entry's own verification section reports. `SHELL` is an inert template string and `until` closes over nothing, so importing both into 29 files shares no page — the directory's standing "one page per file" idiom is about the *mount*, not about a fixture that touches no DOM. **Deleting the copies removed more than the two new gate files added**: `git diff --stat 7258986..f554d9b -- web/` is **32 files changed, 644 insertions(+), 605 deletions(-)** — net positive by 39 lines in the `web/` tree despite the duplication removed being substantially larger than the fixtures added, because the gate's own growth across the review rounds has taken the tier's total slightly positive.

**But the filing understated its own scope, and what it missed is the branch's real result.** `web/vite.config.ts` sets neither `testTimeout` nor `hookTimeout` — confirmed by reading the installed package rather than the docs: `node_modules/vitest/dist/chunks/coverage.DM_a_rWm.js:538` resolves `testTimeout` to `15e3` when `browser.enabled` and `5e3` otherwise; `:539` resolves `hookTimeout` to `3e4` and `1e4` the same way. **Browser mode triples both of the node project's defaults**, and nothing in the repository was reading either. Eleven of the 23 file-level `until` declarations shipped a default of `60_000` with no override anywhere in the file — `buffer-restore`, `buffer-cool-warm`, `scratch-app`, `scratch-edit`, `scratch-buffers`, `tm-blank-buffer-cap`, `scratch-rebind-editor`, `scratch-cap`, `tm-buffer-restore`, `tm-scratch-fork`, `tm-blank-buffer` — every one above both 15,000 and 30,000, so none could ever fire ahead of Vitest's own kill. A twelfth, `buffers-quota-empty`, declared `30_000`; that *ties* the hook bound rather than exceeding it, and is dead for a different reason — its one call site sits inside an `it`, bound at 15,000, not inside a hook. **An earlier draft of this paragraph counted a thirteenth file, `scratch-fork`, alongside the eleven, and said "every one above both bounds" of it too — wrong, on the exact shape the plan's own Task 6 instructions warned about for `buffers-quota-empty` and this paragraph avoided there.** `scratch-fork`'s file-level default is also `60_000`, but its one `beforeAll` carries an explicit `}, 60_000)` override, so at the two call sites inside that hook the declaration *ties* the bound rather than exceeding it — the design states this correctly at §2, as one of three ties (with `link-truncated` and `running-focus`). Its other ten call sites, in plain `it`s with no override anywhere reachable from them, are dead the ordinary way, at 15,000. The design's twelve is {the eleven above} + `buffers-quota-empty`; `scratch-fork` is not a member of it, and belongs with the ties instead. On top of the declarations, 18 further timeouts were passed at individual call sites across 7 files (re-derived by running the shipped scanner against a `git archive` of `7258986`, reproducing the plan's own figure exactly): **11 at `60_000`** (`active-pane` ×2, `buffers-quota` ×2, `pane-kind-switch` ×2, `pane-picker` ×5) — dead at either bound, since 60,000 exceeds both — plus 4 at `10_000` and 3 at `30_000` that were not uniformly dead. A test whose wait never returned printed `Test timed out in 15000ms.` (or `Hook timed out in 30000ms.`) with no name for what never arrived, because the `until` call that would have named it had already lost the race to a ceiling nobody had checked against the runner it ran under.

##### TWO WRONG INSTRUMENTS, AND THE SECOND SAT INSIDE THE PARAGRAPH ANNOUNCING THE FIRST WAS FIXED

The first probe of that default ran `pnpm exec vitest run --project node`, read `Test timed out in 5000ms.`, and that 5,000 was carried into an argument about the *browser* tier — the right kind of experiment, pointed at the wrong project. It was caught by the one comment in the tier that already had the mechanism right: `buffer-cool-warm.test.ts` passed an explicit `10_000` at one call site and explained it was "BOUNDED BELOW VITEST'S OWN 15s `testTimeout`" — a file whose own file-level `until` default was `60_000`, four times the bound its own comment named correctly. The correction that followed measured `testTimeout` on both projects and declared the instrument error over — and never measured `hookTimeout` at all, the same class of miss, one paragraph below the sentence closing the first one. All four numbers (`node` test/hook, `browser` test/hook) are now read from the installed package rather than argued from one probe, for exactly that reason.

##### THE CALL-SITE COUNT TOOK THREE SCANNERS, AND THE MISS WAS A SHAPE OF COMMENT, NOT A SHAPE OF CALL

1. **The first anchored on the end of the argument list** (`,\s*[\d_]+\s*$`) — every multi-line call in this tier ends `60_000,` then a newline and `)` — and reported "these two call sites and no others": **2 of 18**.
2. **The second did a balanced-paren split that tracked string literals**, self-tested against three known call shapes before its count was trusted, and found **17 of 18**. What it missed is `buffers-quota.test.ts`'s first-compile wait, whose argument list carries a comment reading *"A wider budget than this file's own default…"* — the apostrophe in *file's* opened a string the scanner had no way to close, which ate the separator ahead of the number. **The self-test bounded the instrument's error only over the shapes it contained.** It proved three shapes of *call*; the miss was a shape of *comment*.
3. **The third strips comments and string literals before splitting anything**, and finds **18**. This is what shipped: `web/tests/node/browser-timeout-invariants.test.ts`'s `stripped()` + `argsOf()`, re-run here against the same `7258986` archive and reproducing 18 sites across the same 7 files independently of the plan's own count.

**The site the second scanner missed was the only one whose value had a reason, and losing it cost the reason too.** `buffers-quota.test.ts`'s `30_000` was a deliberate wider budget — the one `beforeAll` in the tier paying for `main()`'s own wasm `init()` with no sibling test in the file having amortised it first. Because the count feeding Task 2's migration table was 17 at the time, that site had no comment-handling step, and the migration deleted the reasoning along with the number; `c71162f` restored it as a standalone comment above the `await until(...)` call (verified still present: `web/tests/browser/buffers-quota.test.ts:50-53`, reading "THE LONGEST SINGLE WAIT IN THE BROWSER TIER, AND IT DELIBERATELY HAS NO OVERRIDE"). **The ceiling-lowering measurements never covered that site until the end, either**: every bracket in the design's own table (`4_000`, `2_000`, `1_000` over subsets of the 23 file-level declarations) lowered *declaration* defaults while this call site kept its own explicit value throughout, so none of those rows says anything about it. Only once no override remained anywhere — the shared default lowered to `2_000` with every call-site number gone — was the whole tier measured green including this wait: `pnpm run test:browser` reported 273/273 at that setting, which is the measurement that justifies shipping `10_000` (five times the slowest observed wait) as the one number the tier now carries.

##### THE GATE WAS GREEN AND BLIND, AND A REVIEWER PROVED IT BY CONSTRUCTION

The gate's first numeric-literal detector was `/^[\d_]+$/` — decimal digits and underscores only. `0xea60` and `6e4` both equal `60_000` and both passed it clean, and so did a named constant (`until(p, 'x', SLOW_TIMEOUT)`) for an unrelated reason. `a3d58b0` replaced the regex with a function that strips underscores and asks whether `Number(...)` parses, which is verified still shipping: `web/tests/node/browser-timeout-invariants.test.ts`'s `isNumericLiteral` (lines 90-93) and its dedicated test `'the scanner finds a numeric timeout in every shape a call site can take'` (lines 124-138) exercises hex, scientific-notation, and decimal-point forms alongside the three original call shapes — all six re-run clean at `HEAD`. **A named constant remains uncatchable**, and that is written down as the gate's boundary rather than left implicit: `'the scanner correctly ignores a named constant'` (lines 175-181) asserts `SLOW_TIMEOUT` passes through untouched, because seeing through a symbolic reference to the number it holds needs type or dataflow analysis the gate does not have.

##### CORRECTING CLAIMS KEPT PRODUCING NEW ONES

`harness.ts`'s module doc, in its first shipped form, narrowed the directory's "every sibling states this" idiom claim to a count — "25 of the 29" (`181bc19`) — which fixed the over-quantification but replaced it with a figure nothing re-checks: it goes stale the moment a browser test file is added or a comment reworded, exactly the failure class it was written to correct. `ac43abb` replaced the count with the load-bearing *property* instead — Vitest gives each test file its own page — which is what the argument actually needs and cannot drift. The current text (`web/tests/browser/harness.ts:6-14`) states no count at all. **A distinct, correctly-scoped version of the same claim survives in the design** (`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-09-browser-harness-dedup-design.md:207`): "3 of 29 files state it", anchored to a literal `grep -rniE` pattern over the idiom's own wording rather than the broader "gets its own page" reasoning — re-run here, `grep -rniE "standing idiom|duplicating the shell|rather than importing|nothing to import" tests/browser/*.test.ts` returns exactly **2 hits across 2 files** (`tm-blank-buffer.test.ts`, `tm-buffer-restore.test.ts`), not the four hits across three files the design measured at `7258986`. 4-across-3 is the base-tree census; this branch's own Task 4 rewrote `tm-scratch-fork.test.ts`'s prose and its comment no longer contains any of the four phrases, so it dropped out. The design's "3 of 29" describes the pre-change tree, and this is the post-change count — the branch's own edits moved the figure, which is not the same thing as the figure holding. **A reviewer separately confirmed `scripts/check-doc-figures.sh` covers only the root `README.md` and the four grammar READMEs** — every row in its table is scoped to `.` (repo root) or one `grammars/tree-sitter-redextape*` directory; nothing under `web/` or `docs/superpowers/` has a row — so neither the "25 of the 29" figure nor its replacement was ever going to be caught by the pre-commit gate this repo already has for exactly this failure class. The identifiable correction commits on this branch are `bcd6269` (17 → 18 call sites, and the comment-handling gap that caused it), `c71162f` (restoring the deleted wasm-init reasoning), `181bc19` + `ac43abb` (the idiom claim, corrected twice), `9925a26` (a stale "4/4" against a 5-`it` test file, and two missing `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` casts), and `a3d58b0` (the decimal-only gate). **This entry does not restate the plan's own claim of "two review rounds, 11 errors, 7 then 4" as a figure**: nothing in the tree marks a round boundary or an error tally for pre-commit draft review, so that count is not one this entry can verify — the five commits above are what is checkable, and they are named instead.

#### THE SEVEN FILED SITES WERE TWENTY-SIX, AND THE TIER THAT NEVER SPLIT A GOD-MODULE NEVER DRIFTED AT ALL — `crates/` CARRIED 150 SYMBOL CITATIONS AND NOT ONE NAMED THE WRONG FILE, WHILE `web/` CARRIED 339 AND 26 DID; THE GATE WRITTEN TO STOP A RECURRENCE FIRST REPORTED 467 VIOLATIONS OVER 492 SITES AND WAS WRONG ABOUT 441 OF THEM, BECAUSE `grep -q` KILLS ITS OWN PIPELINE UNDER `pipefail` AND SO FAILED HARDEST EXACTLY WHERE THE TREE WAS CLEANEST; THE PERFORMANCE FIGURE IN ITS HOOK WAS WRITTEN BEFORE ANYTHING WAS TIMED AND WAS WRONG BY 2x IN THE FLATTERING DIRECTION, AND THE PROFILE THEN NAMED A COST THE SENTENCE HAD NOT GUESSED AT (2026-09-10, branch `attribution-drift-sweep`, `96bf3ad..68ba8d2`, 4 commits, plus this entry and whatever corrections follow it)

PR #84 filed it as *"Seven sites still say `main.ts` owns a pane handler that lives in `transport.ts`"* — pre-existing drift from PR #37 (plan 5d-ii-a), which moved `play` and `events` out of `main.ts` verbatim into the new `transport.ts`. The filing was accurate about every site it named and wrong about the size of the class by a factor of nearly four.

##### THE CLASS IS `check-citations.sh`'s SUCCESSOR, NOT ITS NEIGHBOUR

That gate exists because `file:line` citations rot, and the convention it enforces is **cite the symbol**. This is that convention's own rot, and it is worse in one specific way: **the symbol survives the move and the filename does not.** After an extraction the citation is still greppable, still spelled correctly, and still resolves to real code — so it reads correct to anyone who does not go and look, and no review of the extraction diff can see it, because the citing files are not in that diff. A line citation at least breaks visibly when you follow it.

##### THE SPLIT BETWEEN THE TIERS IS THE FINDING, AND IT IS ABOUT HISTORY RATHER THAN LANGUAGES

Measured by the gate at the branch point: **492** attribution sites — **339** under `web/`, **150** under `crates/`, **3** under `grammars/` — and **31** flagged. **All 26 of the real ones are under `web/`.** `crates/` produced two flags and neither is drift: both deliberately name something no file holds in code (a `MAX_SHARED_LOGICAL_NODES` guard that was measured, falsified and reverted; a `PATH_ENTRY_BYTES` wire term that would exist only if a `serde(skip)`ped field were restored), and both now carry the escape-hatch marker.

Rust's modules were split along boundaries that existed before the code did. `main.ts` was a god-module that PR #37 and its successors carved into `transport.ts`, `link-wiring.ts`, `compile.ts`, `panes.ts` and `buffer-list.ts`, and every citation written before the carve kept pointing at the file the symbol left. **The drift is not a property of TypeScript; it is a property of extraction**, which is why the gate covers both tiers rather than the one that was dirty. It is armed for the next carve, wherever it happens.

The 26 resolve to five destinations, and the shape of the list is the argument: `play`/`forward`/`back`/`detach` → `transport.ts` (8), `lambdaLinkState`/`linkable`/`detachedPanes` → `link-wiring.ts` (6), `onNewTm` → `buffer-list.ts` (2), `DEBOUNCE_MS` → `compile.ts`, `LegState`/`resetLegs` → `sessions.ts`, `redex_span` → `protocol.ts`, `extend` → `pane-chrome.ts`, `setEditor` → `replies.ts`, and two naming a `write_term` that **does not exist anywhere in the workspace** — the recursive printer in `lambda/syntax.rs` is `write`, and two files had been citing a plausible name for it.

##### THE GATE WAS WRONG IN THE LOUD DIRECTION, AND THAT IS THE FAILURE MODE THIS PROJECT HAS NOT RECORDED BEFORE

Its first run over the unfixed tree reported **467 violations across 492 sites** — a 95% violation rate on a tree with 26. The cause is three characters in the gate's own `set` line. `symbol_in_code` was `strip_code … | grep -qwF`; `grep -q` exits at the FIRST match, `awk` upstream dies of SIGPIPE, and `set -o pipefail` reports the pipeline as failed. **So every site whose symbol WAS present failed in exactly the way a site whose symbol was absent fails, and the gate was at its reddest precisely where the tree was cleanest.**

The roadmap has several entries about a check being green and blind. This is the inverse and it is not automatically safer: a 95% violation rate is loud, but the obvious reading of it is *"the tree is a disaster"*, and the fix that reading suggests is to start rewriting 467 comments. What said otherwise was a single spot-check — `SessionRegistry` is plainly defined in `sessions.ts` — against a claim the instrument made about it. **A rate that high is evidence about the instrument, not the tree**, and the cheapest way to tell them apart is to verify one claim by hand rather than to read the summary.

##### THREE BLIND SPOTS, EACH OF WHICH SHIPPED GREEN IN A DRAFT

Recorded in the gate's own header, because a reader of the gate is who needs them:

1. **A presence test that does not strip comments passes on any file that merely MENTIONS the symbol.** The first scanner asked whether `forward` appears in `main.ts` and got yes — from a comment in `main.ts` about the handler that had moved out of it. It reported the seven filed sites clean. A file that talks about a symbol does not own it.
2. **A Rust `'` is a lifetime far more often than a char literal.** Blanking from `'` to the next `'` deletes the code between two annotations: the draft reported `impl Drop for Core` missing from `core.rs`. That direction produces FALSE POSITIVES, so it inflated the Rust count rather than hiding it — the tier's clean result survived the bug, and 3 of its 5 flags did not.
3. **A symbol written `` `play()` `` escapes a pattern that stops at word characters.** This is how the seventh of PR #84's seven filed sites escaped the first scan written to find all seven.

##### A PERFORMANCE FIGURE WRITTEN BEFORE ANYTHING WAS TIMED, AND A PROFILE THAT NAMED A DIFFERENT COST

The pre-commit stanza for the new hook first read *"self-test plus scan is 3.6-3.9 s"*. Nothing had been measured; the number was a guess, and it was wrong by 2x in the flattering direction — the real figure was **7.5 s**, against 574-594 ms for the slowest hook already there.

The profile then contradicted the sentence's own explanation. That comment blamed comment-stripping (*"because it strips comments from every cited file"*), and stripping every `.ts` file under `web/src` costs **182 ms**. The seven seconds were **486 forks, one per SITE**: a command substitution inside the symbol test and another at the resolver call, each copying a whole file's text through a pipe. Both now return through globals and a bash word test, and the scan is **2.57-2.61 s**. **The explanation was written down with the same confidence as the number and was wrong about a different thing** — which is why the header now carries the profile rather than the reasoning that preceded it.

##### THE FIGURE GATE CAUGHT THIS BRANCH'S OWN COMMIT, AND WHAT IT CAUGHT WAS ALREADY STALE

`scripts/check-doc-figures.sh` refused the commit that added the tenth pre-commit hook: `README.md` claimed nine, twice. Fixing that exposed a second claim the gate does not hold — *"roughly **150x** the ~1.5 s the **three** unscoped pre-commit hooks cost together"* — which was **already wrong before this branch**, because there were four unscoped hooks, not three. Re-measured in one minute rather than scaled: 1,127 + 494 + 253 + 181 + 2,603 ms for the five. **A ratio goes stale when EITHER of its two figures moves, which is twice the exposure of the figures it compares** — and this one had no row in the gate, so only a human reading the paragraph for another reason would ever meet it.

##### THE PRE-MERGE CHECK FOUND THE GATE HAD STOPPED TESTING ITSELF, IN THE FILE WHOSE SUBJECT IS EXACTLY THAT

Three findings, none of which any green check reported:

- **The self-test no longer covered the parse the scan runs.** Removing the per-site forks inlined the parse into the scan loop and left `parse_attribution` reachable only from `--self-test` — two implementations of one idea, with the tested one no longer the one that executes. Nothing was red: the scan was correct and the self-test passed. **What makes this the sharpest finding on the branch is where it sits** — a gate whose entire subject is a claim that stops matching what it describes had acquired exactly that defect, and its own CI comment promised the opposite in as many words (*"All five run through the same `strip_code` and `symbol_in_code` the scan uses, so the self-test cannot drift into agreeing with a broken scan"* — true of those two functions, and silently false of the parse). `parse_attribution` now sets globals: one implementation, no fork, and sabotaging it reddens **3 of 5** checks where before it reddened **0**.
- **Two of the 26 rewrites moved a false claim rather than removing it, and both passed the gate.** `app.test.ts` cited *"`types.ts`'s `redex_span` doc"*; `types.ts` re-exports `LambdaState` from a **gitignored generated** binding, so the symbol is genuinely not in its code and the gate flagged it — correctly by its own rule, and misleadingly, because the citation was pointing at a barrel rather than at a moved symbol. It was "fixed" to `protocol.ts`, which discusses `redex_span` in a byte-budget argument. The doc it actually wanted — the pre-step-redex-versus-contractum semantics the citing comment is about — is on the Rust field in `viewmodel.rs`. **The gate cannot tell "names a file that owns this symbol" from "names a file that mentions this symbol in code"**, and that gap is precisely where a correction round can land another falsehood while turning the check green. The second was `scratch.ts`'s *"`replies.ts`'s `setEditor`"*: `replies.ts` CALLS it, `LambdaPane` declares it, and the possessive claimed ownership the file does not have. Rewritten to *"nothing in `replies.ts` ever calls `setEditor`"*, which asserts what the sentence needs and creates no attribution site at all.
- **The new hook's comparison timings were quoted rather than measured.** The stanza read *"against 574-594 ms for `check-text-bytes` … on the same machine"* — two figures lifted from the hook comments above it, not run. Re-measured in one minute, `check-text-bytes` is **1,070 ms**, nearly 2x the quoted figure. This is the same paragraph that had already been wrong once by guessing its own runtime, so the correction round reproduced the class it was correcting, one clause over.

##### LEFT FOR THE READER

- **A bare `` `:N` `` line citation is invisible to `check-citations.sh`**, whose pattern requires a filename before the colon. Four exist: three in `web/src/session-client.ts` (`` `:15` ``, `` `:16` ``, `` `:18` ``) and one in `crates/redextape-core/examples/owner_probe.rs` (`` `:125` ``). They are the same rot that gate exists for, arriving one character short of its pattern, and they rot faster than the form it catches because they name no file to anchor against. Filed rather than fixed: widening that pattern is that gate's decision, not this one's.
- **The quoted-doc shape is fixed by hand and gated by nothing.** Two sites attributed a verbatim quotation to the wrong file — both quoting `link-wiring.ts` while naming `main.ts`. They are sharper than the 26, because the quotation is *correct*: someone read the real doc, copied it accurately, and got the filename wrong, so the accuracy of the quote is what hides the misattribution. Not gated because two sites is not a corpus and matching prose quotes needs fuzziness whose false-positive rate would be unmeasured.
- **The gate cannot see through a re-export.** A citation naming a barrel file rather than the defining one reads clean, because the symbol genuinely appears in the barrel's code.
- **A named constant defeats it the same way it defeats `browser-timeout-invariants.test.ts`'s scanner** — the boundary that file already states for its own class.

##### WHAT STAYS OPEN

- The four bare `` `:N` `` citations above, and the quoted-doc shape.
- **The five escape-hatch markers are the measured false-positive rate of the strict rule: 5 in 491, ~1%.** Three cite something deliberately absent from all code; two cite the `compiled` reply tag, which lives in `protocol.ts` as a quoted string that `strip_code` blanks ON PURPOSE. That last pair will recur — every citation of a discriminated-union tag needs a marker — and the alternative is reading string literals as code, which is exactly blind spot 1.
- Thirteen accessibility items remain: 1-7, 9, 10, and 13-16, unchanged by this branch.

#### EVERY NUMBER THE DESIGN COMMITTED TO WAS FALSIFIED BY BUILDING IT — 7.75 ESTIMATED STATES PER ORIGINAL STATE AGAINST 21.199662 MEASURED, THEN 19.201354 AFTER ONE OPTIMISATION, AND THE EXTRAPOLATION FROM THERE TO THE WORST SHIPPED DEMO WAS WRONG A SECOND TIME BECAUSE THAT MACHINE IS A DIFFERENT SHAPE RATHER THAN A BIGGER ONE (36.858736, 1,811,054 STATES AGAINST A 1,000,000 CAP, SO THE LARGEST SHIPPED MACHINES CANNOT BE REDUCED AT ALL) — AND THE REQUIREMENT THAT NUMBER MISSES WAS ITSELF THE WRONG REQUIREMENT; ALL SIX IMPORTANT FINDINGS OF THE CLOSING REVIEW WERE ABOUT WORDS WHILE THE ONE FINDING THAT CHANGES WHAT THE CODE RETURNS WAS FILED AS A MINOR, AND THE WAVE THAT CLOSED NINETEEN FINDINGS THEN WROTE TWO NEW FALSE CLAIMS ACROSS FOUR SITES AND FALSIFIED THREE STANDING SENTENCES OF ITS OWN (2026-09-10, branch `single-tape-reduction`, `9d598a0..15af549`, 33 commits, plus this entry and whatever corrections follow it)

Design: [`../specs/2026-09-10-single-tape-reduction-design.md`](../specs/2026-09-10-single-tape-reduction-design.md). Plan: [`2026-09-10-single-tape-reduction.md`](2026-09-10-single-tape-reduction.md).

**This is the "Single-tape TM" item above, and stage 1 of "Machine-model reductions — a PIPELINE".** It delivers `single_tape.rs`'s `to_single_tape` (`Machine(k-tape) -> Machine(1-tape)`), `interleave` and `deinterleave` (the tape layout and its inverse), and a fourth oracle leg asserting `reference == λ == multitape-TM == singletape-TM` by TAPE IDENTITY rather than by decoded value — `single_tape_oracle.rs`'s `the_single_tape_leg_agrees_on_small_programs` compares head *and* contents on all five tapes, so there is no second decode path to drift. **The architectural claim the roadmap states for this whole track held exactly**: `git diff --name-only 9d598a0..15af549 | grep -v '\.md$'` lists three files — `crates/redextape-core/src/tm.rs` (one `pub mod` line), the new `crates/redextape-core/src/tm/single_tape.rs`, and the new `crates/redextape-core/tests/single_tape_oracle.rs`. Nothing in Core, asm or `encoding` is touched, and the whole branch is `5 files changed, 2530 insertions(+)` with **zero deletions**.

**The roadmap's own sketch of the mechanism does not fit this tree, and the spec corrects it on measured grounds rather than as a preference.** The sketch asks for "a product alphabet" and to "keep the alphabet a tuple, not a blown-up power set". `machine.rs`'s `Symbol` is `char` — there is no tuple to keep, a product symbol has to *be* a `char` — and `build.rs`'s `TAPES` is 5 for every machine this project lowers, so under the checked-in Γ = `{#, 1, @, _}` a product alphabet is 4⁵·2⁵ = **32,768** symbols against the BMP private-use area's **6,400** code points (100,000 under `binary`). The state cost is the harder half: the textbook sweep *collects* the k marked symbols into the control state, which is 146 × 4⁵ = **149,504** states for the smallest real machine there is, against `build.rs`'s `MAX_MACHINE_STATES` of 1,000,000, before any phase multiplier. The shipped mechanism verifies one candidate rule at a time instead of collecting anything, so the |Γ|ᵏ factor never appears; and the marker symbol carries the tape index (`head_here(i)` is `'A' + i`, `head_away(i)` is `'a' + i`) so no walk ever has to count its offset within a block to learn which tape it is on.

##### THE DESIGN'S OWN COST MODEL WAS FALSIFIED BY BUILDING IT, AND THE SECOND ESTIMATE FAILED IN A DIFFERENT WAY FROM THE FIRST

The design projected `rules/state × (1 + concrete-reads/rule + acting-tapes/rule) + 1` and got **7.75** states per original state for `sum(5)`, 8.12 for `count_down(4)`, 7.26 for `[1, 2, 3]` — while already warning, in its own capitals, that the formula "COUNTS THE CHECK AND APPLY STATES AND NOT THE SCAN, REWIND, FAIL AND SEEK STATES AROUND THEM". It was right about the direction and wrong about the size. The built construction emits, per rule, three states of scan/rewind/fail scaffolding, one `chk` per concrete read, and four or five per acting tape. Measured on that same `sum(5)`: **21.199662**, 2.7x the estimate, over a ceiling of 20.352091.

An earlier draft of that same section had said 287,000 total states; it counted three fixed phases and never counted the apply passes at all. **So the section was wrong twice before anything was built, and the version that survived to be falsified was already the corrected one.**

**Then the extrapolation from `sum(5)` to the machine that sets the ceiling was wrong on top of that, and wrong about a different thing.** `sum(5)` is first-order recursion. The machine that actually sets the 49,135-state floor — the `map`/`ap2` demo, byte-identical to `guard_counterexamples.rs`'s `WORST_SHIPPED_DEMO` — reaches the backends through `defunc`, and it is a different SHAPE. Both terms the cost is built from move against it at once: **1.7143** acting tapes per rule against 0.8698 / 0.8964 / 0.9285 on the first-order fixtures, and **53.2086%** of acting-tape passes with no write against 89.4161% / 87.3646% / 91.4441%. Its wildcard-read share — the property the whole construction rests on — is **65.9997%** against 81.1934%-82.0065%. Measured: **39.505220** before the no-write split and **36.858736** after, or 1,811,054 states against a 1,000,000 cap. **The largest machines this demo suite ships cannot be reduced.**

**The one optimisation this branch made is worth exactly one state per no-write acting-tape pass, and that is checkable rather than argued.** `emit_one_tape_pass`'s no-write arm stops on the marker (`Move::S`) instead of stepping onto a content cell to write nothing and stepping back off it. Building the same seven machines in a worktree at `cb1c105` (the commit before the split) and at `15af549`, the single-tape state counts differ by 245 / 242 / 432 / 1,194 / 2,362 / 2,943 / 130,035 — and those seven numbers are, to the unit, each machine's own count of acting-tape passes whose `write` is `None`. On the worst demo that is 130,035 states, **6.70%**, against a gap of 1.81x: real, and nowhere near enough.

**What the split did change is which first-order programs are reducible at all.** Three of the six first-order machines measured here were over the ceiling before it and are under it after: `sum(5)` 21.199662 → 19.201354, the `while`-loop demo 22.542435 → **20.339483**, and `count_down(4)` 22.304029 → 20.147985. The `while`-loop demo now sits **0.062%** under the ceiling, the tightest margin on record, and it became a reducible program at all only because of a change that saves one state per no-write pass.

##### THE REQUIREMENT WAS WRONG, NOT JUST THE NUMBER

The ceiling the branch spent two tasks measuring against is `MAX_MACHINE_STATES / 49,135` = **20.352091**, and the question it asks is *can the largest shipped demo be BUILT as a single-tape machine*. **Nothing needs it to be.** The reduction is quadratic in tape length: the slow-tier table below measures `sum(5)` — a 1,182-state machine, forty times smaller than the worst demo — at **303,610,850** single-tape steps against 50,542 multi-tape ones. The single-tape image of a 49,135-state machine is unrunnable in STEPS by a margin far wider than the 1.81x it misses in states. It was never going to execute, only exist.

So the figure stays in the spec as the boundary it is — the point past which a program can no longer be reduced — rather than as a gate the construction failed, and the requirement that earns its place is the one the artifacts actually exercise: the oracle leg's corpus and the slow-tier cost table, every member of which fits. **Both times a number on this branch came out wrong, the measurement itself was correct; what was wrong was the sentence saying what it was for.**

##### A COST TABLE THAT WOULD HAVE MEASURED A CONSTANT I CHOSE

Task 6 shipped its first blowup figures at `PAD = 64`, a value its brief supplied as "generous rather than computed". Every simulated single-tape step sweeps the WHOLE block skeleton — both sentinels, every marker, every content cell, padding included — so absolute step counts scale with TOTAL blocks, and at that pad **82.1%-88.9% of the blocks were padding**. Re-measured here, at three pads, on the three programs that table used:

| program | multi | `PAD = 1` | `PAD = 2` | `PAD = 64` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `1 + 2` | 152 | 88,339 (581.2x, 18 blocks) | 99,559 (655.0x, 20) | 795,199 (**5,231.6x**, 144) |
| `3 - 5` | 253 | 238,856 (944.1x, 30) | 257,216 (1,016.7x, 32) | 1,395,536 (**5,516.0x**, 156) |
| `[1, 2]` | 422 | 365,990 (867.3x, 28) | 397,970 (943.1x, 30) | 2,380,730 (**5,641.5x**, 154) |

The shipped `PAD` is **2**, and it is not the minimum: `PAD = 0` overflows this corpus and `PAD = 1` clears it, so 2 is the measured minimum plus one block of margin. **A blowup ratio quoted without the pad it was measured at is not a property of the reduction**, and `single_tape_oracle.rs`'s `PAD` now carries that sentence directly above the constant.

The fix is not "choose a smaller constant", because a smaller constant is still a constant. `the_single_tape_cost_table` divides the padding back out, and the resulting column is this branch's actual answer to the roadmap's "polynomial slowdown is normally a hand-wave; here step counts are exact integers":

| program | multi-tape steps | single-tape steps | raw ratio | blocks | steps per multi-tape step per block |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `1 + 2 * 3` | 1,020 | 1,606,768 | 1,575.3x | 50 | **31.505** |
| `let x = 40; x + 2` | 2,870 | 22,505,781 | 7,841.7x | 265 | **29.591** |
| `fn sum(n) … sum(5)` | 50,542 | 303,610,850 | 6,007.1x | 192 | **31.287** |

The raw ratios span **4.98x**; the last column spans **6.5%**. That near-constant is the reduction's cost. The raw ratio would have been a hand-wave with better typography.

##### THE SABOTAGE DID NOT REDDEN THE GATE, AND THE ORACLE LEG STRUCTURALLY CANNOT

The construction fits only because `emit_candidate` emits no `chk` state for a wildcard read position, and on the three `SOURCES` machines 81.19%-82.01% of read positions are wildcards. Task 7's sabotage deleted that skip — emitting a `chk` for every position instead of only `Some(_)` ones — and **reported that the gate stayed green as its finding, rather than reporting a success.** Reproduced here in a worktree at `15af549` with the same sabotage applied: `cargo nextest run -p redextape-core single_tape --no-fail-fast` runs 24 tests and reddens exactly **one**.

- `the_construction_stays_inside_the_state_budget`, the gate written for this exact property, moves its three toy fixtures from 3.00 / 3.67 / 7.50 to **4.00 / 4.67 / 8.00** and **PASSES**. A 2-3 state hand-written fixture has neither the rules-per-state nor the reads-per-rule of a lowered machine; the gate was scored against inputs too small to fail.
- `the_single_tape_leg_agrees_on_small_programs` — the strongest correctness check the slice exists to build — **PASSES**, and that is structural rather than a gap to close. A bloated construction is still a correct one. **No oracle leg can ever redden for a pure cost regression**, which is why the spec's original sabotage instruction ("confirm the leg reddens") could not have been carried out by anyone.
- `real_lowered_machines_cost_far_more_than_the_toy_fixtures` **FAILS**, at `1 + 2 * 3` measuring **26.4895** against the 20.3521 ceiling.

Task 7b added the assertion that reddens. **The reason it gave for gating only `sum(5)` was that no sabotage measurement showed the other two rows were sensitive enough.** The closing review took the measurement. `1 + 2 * 3` goes 17.510490 → **26.489510** and `cons(1, cons(2, nil))` 17.089041 → **25.767123**; both cross, as `sum(5)` does at 19.201354 → 28.756345. All three `SOURCES` rows now carry the assertion. A reason given for not measuring something, standing in for the measurement, and false.

**Task 6's review sabotaged `Names::entry_name` and the fourth oracle leg kept passing while three unit tests inside `single_tape.rs` went red** — the strongest check in the slice was weaker than three tests beside it, on the dimension that file's own doc warns about.

##### TWO DEAD PARAMETERS, DOCUMENTED AS LOAD-BEARING, THROUGH THIRTEEN COMMITS

The spec's Surface section named `to_single_tape(&Machine, blocks: usize)`. The plan's first commit (`bcfed89`) reconciled that into a pad pair — `to_single_tape(&Machine, left_pad: usize, right_pad: usize)` — and wrote all seven of its call sites with it. The transition table is independent of block count; padding belongs to `interleave`, which is what actually builds the skeleton. So the parameters did nothing, and the whole of their use in the body, at `git show 028b7a8:crates/redextape-core/src/tm/single_tape.rs` line 143, was:

```rust
let _ = (left_pad, right_pad); // consumed by `interleave`, not by the transition table
```

The function's doc said "`left_pad`/`right_pad` fix how far any head may travel outside the initial contents". **The comment on the dead line was accurate and the doc above it was not**, and the doc is what a caller reads. They landed in code at `521e43b` (Task 2) and were removed at `80f008f`; `git rev-list --count 521e43b..80f008f` is **14**, so thirteen commits and every per-task review carried them, including a review that ran its own k=2 / k=3 / k=5 differentials against a multi-tape simulator. **Seeing it needs a differential nobody runs unless they already suspect it** — `to_single_tape(&m, 0, 0)` against `to_single_tape(&m, 1000, 7)`, which return byte-identical tables — and no correctness differential can reach it, because a parameter that does nothing breaks nothing.

##### A PARAGRAPH REFUTED BY THE NUMBER BELOW IT

The closing review's fix wave was 19 findings across 11 commits (`git rev-list --count 028b7a8..40b83e2`). One further round was dispatched briefed on a single question — *did this correction introduce a new error?* — and it found **eight defects**.

The sharpest is `40b83e2`, the wave's last commit, whose entire job was to record measured unreachable-state figures. It wrote, in one paragraph:

> When `rule` is an all-wildcard catch-all **(every lowered state's last rule, per this function's own doc)** … unreachable states are **1.25%-2.65%** of every real first-order lowered image measured … exactly one `fail` plus one `stuck` per state whose last rule is an all-wildcard catch-all

**The second half refutes the parenthetical.** If every lowered state's last rule were an all-wildcard catch-all, `1 + 2 * 3`'s 141 rule-carrying states would mint 141 `fail` plus 141 `stuck` unreachable states — 282 of 2,504, or 11.3%. The measured figure is **54**: exactly 27 `fail` and 27 `stuck`, with nothing else unreachable, because **27 of those 141 states**, 19.1%, actually have that shape. The other 114 `stuck` states are reachable from `start`. The same universality claim had been written twice more at `9358c83`, as the justification for a new fixture and for the test that uses it.

The wave's other new defects: a causal clause at `7b418dc` explaining a READ statistic (the worst demo's 66.0% wildcard reads) by a WRITE-and-MOVE statistic (its 1.71 acting tapes per rule) — both figures real, the relation between them invented; a `[`interleave`]` rustdoc intra-doc link written into a *Markdown* spec by `80f008f`, which is the commit whose own message says it fixed a doc citation naming the wrong file; and two 121- and 143-column lines introduced by `fefe749`'s margin table, in a file whose `max_width` is 120 and which `cargo fmt` reports clean because it does not reflow comments. **Three more sentences were not written by the wave but were made false by it**: the spec still said "`to_single_tape` takes a **block count**" after `80f008f` removed its padding arguments, the spec still described an oracle corpus `6086b9c` had replaced, and the plan still showed all eight three-argument call sites.

**Eight of eight defects in that round trace to the eleven commits immediately before it, and nothing green ever noticed** — `cargo fmt`, `cargo clippy -D warnings`, `check-citations.sh` and `check-attributions.sh` were clean at every commit in the wave and are clean now. A correction is an edit like any other, and the tree has no gate that reads what an edit says.

##### THE ONE FINDING THAT CHANGES WHAT THE CODE RETURNS WAS FILED AS A MINOR

The closing review's verdict was *"Not ready to merge — but nothing in the code is wrong."* Per the branch's progress ledger — the closing review's own report was never written to disk — it wrote its own absolute-position multi-tape simulator and compared head and contents on all five tapes across eight programs, ran the wildcard sabotage on ten machines plus five further construction sabotages, and BFS'd the state graph. The construction survived all of it. **All six Important findings were claim or coverage defects** — a sabotage instruction that cannot be carried out, an unchecked reason for gating one row of three, the dead parameters, a margin figure naming the wrong program as tightest, an oracle corpus whose members were not `FIRST_ORDER_DEMOS` entries so the four-way chain held for one program of three, and "the demo suite" describing three hand-copied programs of 46.

The one finding that changes what `to_single_tape` returns for any input was filed as **M-4, a Minor**: the tape count was never checked. `head_here(i)` is `'A' + i` and `head_away(i)` is `'a' + i`, so past 26 tapes the markers walk out of their two letter ranges. At 27 tapes the failure is loud — `head_here(26)` is `'['`, which `machine.rs`'s `validate` reserves — but a machine declaring 31 tapes whose rules touch only tape 30 emits `head_here(30)` = code point 95 = `'_'` = `BLANK`, and `validate()` returns **clean**: a head marker indistinguishable from a blank cell, in a machine that would report an ordinary accept over a tape that no longer deinterleaves.

**The boundary now sits at 26 and it is not off by one.** `MAX_ENCODABLE_TAPES` is 26 and `to_single_tape` refuses on `m.tapes > MAX_ENCODABLE_TAPES` BEFORE any marker is minted, so 26 tapes means indices 0..=25: `head_here` spans 65-90 and `head_away` spans 97-122, with `BLANK` at 95 and the sentinels at 60 and 62 all outside both ranges. Two tests hold both directions — `a_machine_with_too_many_tapes_is_refused_not_silently_corrupted` and `a_machine_at_the_encodable_tape_limit_is_not_refused_on_tape_count_alone`, the second building a machine at exactly 26 — so the check cannot quietly become off-by-one in the conservative direction either.

**The inversion is a finding about the review, not about the code.** Every Important was about words; the only finding that reaches runtime was a Minor. It is a defensible Minor — `build.rs`'s `TAPES` is 5, and nothing this compiler emits comes within twenty tapes of the limit — but the gap existed because `to_single_tape` is `pub` and stated a precondition it did not enforce, and it was found by constructing an input the compiler cannot produce. **A severity scale that ranks by what the shipped pipeline can hit will always rank a `pub` function's unenforced precondition last**, and that is exactly the finding no test in the tree was going to surface.

##### LEFT FOR THE READER

- **`normalize` discards the head position on an all-blank tape, and every tape-identity assertion in the oracle leg is built on it.** With no non-`BLANK` cell to anchor against, `normalize(&[BLANK; 5], 0) == normalize(&[BLANK; 5], 4)` — so on any tape that ends all-blank, which the normal-tier corpus does for most of its five, the comparison is satisfied by ANY head on either side. `normalize_discards_the_head_on_an_all_blank_tape` pins it as an instrument weakness. Nothing in `to_single_tape` or `interleave` loses head information; only the comparison does.
- **`assert_single_tape_agrees_capped`'s `got_steps > want_steps` can never fire.** Every single-tape/multi-tape ratio measured on this branch at the shipped `PAD = 2` falls between **655.0x** and **7,841.7x**. It is a sentence with an `assert!` in front of it.
- **`interleave`'s dangerous direction is guarded by a `debug_assert!`**, which a release build compiles out. `k > inits.len()` is safe — the extra tapes read as permanently empty — while `k < inits.len()` silently drops `inits[k..]` from the output while still counting them in the skeleton's width.
- **`to_single_tape`'s alphabet refusal is structurally incapable of being the whole precondition.** `Machine::alphabet` collects symbols from rules' `read`/`write` only; initial tape contents are a separate argument to `interleave` and are not part of `m` at all. A machine whose only rule is an unconditional wildcard has an empty alphabet and sails through no matter what its caller's tapes hold. The doc says so and names `layout_collision(m, inits)` as the caller's obligation — and `single_tape_oracle.rs` is the only place in the workspace that wires both together and discharges it.
- **`entry_name`'s "ONE FUNCTION BECAUSE TWO SPELLINGS IS A BUG THAT TESTS GREEN" overstates what the code enforces.** The same two strings are independently re-derived in `emit_state`'s accept branch, in its empty-rules branch, and by `emit_candidate`'s own `scan` name whenever `c == 0`. All three are correct today because each knows its own state's accept-ness locally. Latent, not live.
- **Every `fail`, and for the last candidate every `stuck`, is minted unconditionally**, including for all-wildcard candidates that nothing can ever mismatch into.
- **One 135-column doc line survives in a file whose `max_width` is 120, and `cargo fmt --all --check` exits 0 on it.** `rustfmt.toml` sets no `wrap_comments`, so rustfmt reflows no doc comment at all; `awk '{ if (length($0) > 120) print NR }' crates/redextape-core/src/tm/single_tape.rs` returns exactly one line, 1113, introduced at `22be61a`. This is the second shape of fmt blindness this one file has produced — the first was a 128-column `proptest` line that rustfmt left alone because it **cannot parse** `ident in expr`, now wrapped by hand with a comment saying why. Two different mechanisms, the same green check.

What would close it is collapsing the per-acting-tape passes into one sweep, which needs a **third marker per tape** so a head already moved in this sweep is not moved again. That is a redesign of the apply phase, nothing this slice delivers requires it, and it is filed rather than done. **ANNOTATED 2026-09-15 (`reduction-state-guard`):** still true, but `to_single_tape` now refuses the demo with `too-many-states` instead of building its 1,811,054 states.

The figures are recorded in the spec and in `real_lowered_machines_cost_far_more_than_the_toy_fixtures`'s doc so the tradeoff is visible rather than silent.

Pruning takes `sum(5)` from 19.201354 to 18.886633 and the worst demo from 36.858736 to 36.687819 — real, and nowhere near enough alone to close either gap.

- **Nothing gates the doc figures in `single_tape.rs` against drift.** `check-doc-figures.sh` has rows for the root `README.md` and the four grammar READMEs only; every ratio, margin and percentage this branch wrote into a Rust doc comment is outside its table — the same exposure the previous entry recorded for `web/`.
